Delighted to see the successful launch of Invest Europe’s Independent Sponsor Roundtable last week, a great initiative supporting a fast-growing and increasingly important segment of the private equity ecosystem.

Bringing together independent sponsors and their investors, the Roundtable will ensure the community is better represented, while creating a platform to share insights, address regulatory challenges, and contribute to tailored professional standards. It will also play a key role in showcasing activity and strengthening understanding of this evolving model.

Through the Roundtable, Headway Capital Partners looks forward to supporting the continued development of this growing community under the leadership of Christiaan de Lint and James Almond, CFA.

If you are active in this space and an Invest Europe member, we would encourage you to get involved!

To learn more, please contact Deborah Botwood Smith, Business Development Director, at deborah.botwoodsmith@investeurope.eu.

#PrivateEquity #IndependentSponsor

His research explores the intersections of gender, religion, caste, and colonial politics. Sandeep’s current work focuses on researching the history of epidemic disease, religious healing, and political authority, particularly how Kanphata Yogis, local kings, and the colonial state engaged with the healing cult of Pateshwari Devi to claim spiritual and political power. Most companies don’t have a technology problem… they have a redundancy problem. Over the past decade working across large enterprises (including IBM), I have seen the same pattern repeat: ➡️ Multiple on-prem applications doing the same job ➡️ Rising maintenance costs with limited ROI ➡️ Fragmented data across systems ➡️ Slow delivery despite heavy IT investments And yet, the go-to solution is still: “Let’s move everything to the cloud.” 👉 The real question should be: “What should we NOT move at all?” 💡 Modernization isn’t migration. It’s elimination + simplification. Here’s what actually drives impact: ✅ Rationalize first Cut redundant and low-value applications (often reduces portfolio by 30%+) ✅ Consolidate platforms Standardize core systems like CRM and ERP to reduce complexity ✅ Adopt cloud with intent Leverage Amazon Web Services / Microsoft Azure strategically—not just lift & shift ✅ Build API-led architecture Use integration layers (e.g., MuleSoft) to avoid point-to-point chaos ✅ Drive data & governance Create a single source of truth with strong controls 🎯 The outcome? Lower operational cost 💰 Faster time-to-market 🚀 Better decision-making 📊 Scalable, future-ready systems ☁️ 🔥 The biggest mistake I see? Companies modernize everything… except their mindset. 💬 How is your organization tackling redundant legacy systems? Her goal is to contribute to the advancement of a socially just, inclusive, tolerant and sustainable Viet Nam.

Awarded the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master scholarship thanks to her academic excellence and dedication to international development, she is passionate about collaborating with people from all walks of life to turn ambitious goals into tangible realities, making a meaningful impact on everyday lives.

Outside of work, she enjoys walking in nature and watching movies, finding inspiration and relaxation in both activities.

Loan lives by the motto “Hate cannot drive out hate, only love can do that.” - Martin Luther King Jr

post_text: Carrying out appropriate research to identify wealth, or possible wealth, and where this practice intersects with privacy law has been much in the news in the charity sector over the last year or so. The latest "news" piece was the Daily Mail's outrage that universities had, as they put it, been "snooping" on former students. The BBC's News programme, reviewing the next day's headlines, suggested that the real surprise was not that universities were doing this, but that they were paying anyone to do so, given that "all the information was available on Google anyway." This is a post about one particular source of that public domain data - data obtained from Companies House. As you read it, please assume that any charity using that data has been entirely transparent about the fact that it does use it. An example is here at Manchester University's alumni privacy notice. Here's the conundrum. In its conference paper for the charity sector in February 2017 (which itself says is not to be regarded as definitive) the ICO said "The fact that personal information is publicly available doesn’t make it ‘fair game’. And it doesn’t make further use of that personal information for any purpose fair." And the paper specifically mentions Companies House as a source of public domain data. What I want to suggest is that while ICO's comment quoted above is entirely capable of being true in some contexts, it is not universally true. Indeed, ICO does not claim it to be universally true, but many have interpreted this as such. So, because Companies House data is widely used since it's useful, I want to have a look at the use of that data. UK Company Officers have no choice about their data being made public. The law says it must be public, and this aids the good governance of our corporate life. Few would argue against officers of businesses being publicly accountable for the way in which they run those businesses, and that access to information on those officers is a critical part of ensuring that accountability. The same argument might be made about shareholders since they elect the officers. But is it "fair game" to use that data, including data on the profitability of a company and its ownership structure, to assess the value of someone's holding in that company, or if they are a director of some larger companies, their remuneration. It is a DP principle that data obtained for one purpose should not, in general, be used for another, especially if the person concerned is unaware of the extra uses, or had no choice about its publication. So it could be argued that the purpose of putting all the company information referred to above into the public domain is good corporate governance, and not so a charity can work out how much to include in a proposal to one of the company officers. And, remember that a company officer has little choice about the publication of the information. So, does this put a lid on the use of Companies' House data for fundraising research, at least without the direct consent of the data subject, something which will usually be very odd to obtain at the point in the relationship between charity and potential donor where it is useful. (And bear in mind that ICO advises that if consent is hard to get then it might not be right ground for processing.) So can we use Companies House data for prospect research? Can we have a lawful ground for processing, and not be unlawfully re-purposing the data? ICO says that if someone expects their data to be used in a particular way then it is far more likely that the "purpose" principle will be satisfied. "In deciding whether the two [purposes] are compatible, you should consider things such as: the individuals’ reasonable expectations, the potential effect on them of the processing and what they’ve been told." ICO Conference Paper. There is heaps of evidence in the fundraising world that wealthy potential donors expect fundraisers to come to them properly prepared. As one said to me "without this, you are saying that the demand side can't talk to the supply side." A dig around some Freedom of Information requests shows that Companies House did a privacy impact assessment before the broad release of data into the public domain on their beta web site, as rightly they should have. Amongst other conclusions, they found that beta users were "overwhelmingly positive with any negatives being a request for more functionality." Mitigating factors for people who were concerned about their data being in the public domain were "We will review the instructions given to new company officers to ensure that they are clear that part of the consequence of limited liability is that certain information about them and their company will be made available to the public." This is an interesting insight into the trade-off between having the protection of the limited company status afforded by national legislation and the window into a company officer's world which is required to benefit from this status. The Government's Information Fair Trader Scheme produced a report in July 2016 on Companies House's accreditation to its scheme. This scheme ensures that "re-users of public sector information can be confident they will be treated reasonably and fairly by public sector information providers." Part two of this report refers to the "Maximisation Principle." The report authors said that they "find Companies House to be working at a best practice level against the Maximisation principle. Staff across the organisation are keenly aware of the Companies House public task of making information from the Company Register freely and easily available for any re-use with as few restrictions as possible. " Meanwhile, recommendation 7 of this report says: "Companies House should promote innovative uses of Register data through holding ‘hack days’ and should consider other methods to promote the innovative use of its data." So here we have our own government supporting the innovative use of public domain data and in a context where there are "as few restrictions as possible" on the use of that data. An August 2017 note from a member of staff at Companies House on their developer forum, said "We do not expect GDPR to have any impact on the re-use of information on the public register, or on the basis on which this information is published." Now, before anyone runs away thinking this merits a free-for-all on the use of Companies House data, please stop. If you were to use this data for prospect research you would still need a lawful ground for processing and to be entirely open about your use of this data. But, it seems to me that, if there is a business need within a charity to use such data to help find and verify potential donors, the Companies House PIA and the Fair Trader report add significant extra pieces of evidence to the Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) that would be necessary to use that ground for lawful processing. These two documents add substantial weight to the argument that the processing should not be unexpected and that use of the data is not unreasonable. There is a caveat, but this is followed by a "good practice" note. The caveat is that Companies House data is not any old public domain data. It's there as the result of legislation about the good governance of companies and so arguments about the use of its public domain data will not necessarily be applicable to other public domain data. The good practice note is to suggest that any use of public domain data should be subject to the same sort of inspection as this article has covered. You should look at the conditions under which the data was put in the public domain, and treat it accordingly. If you can identify what the person was likely to expect when the data was made public, or what the publisher says about the data, then you are far more likely to be able to satisfy a legitimate interest condition than if you can not answer those questions. For Social Media you should look at the terms and conditions under which people provide their data to those platforms, and the context. Personally, I think you are much more likely to be able to pass an LIA in respect of using LinkedIn or Twitter information than Instagram or Facebook. Why? Because the main intention of biographical information on the first is all about making one's persona known, and the second is so very obviously public. (And its T&C say in its second paragraph, in big letters "What you share on Twitter may be viewed all around the world instantly. You are what you Tweet!" ) Facebook, on the other hand, is much more personal and far less based on a professional, public persona. (Some would argue it's based on a desired or manipulated persona, but that's a different article.) Some may disagree with my conclusions and argue that the re-purposing of data put in the public domain is inherently unfair. In answer to that I would ask whether we can lawfully use any data about anyone else in that case, since a piece of general public information rarely comes tagged with a note to say why it got there and what the person was expecting when it leaked from their own persona. And I'd still want to question how one government agency seems to think it's actually its duty to encourage "new and innovative uses of the data" while another implies you can't do it except in very restricted circumstances.

Monday marked the conclusion of the 2025 Spring Training season at the Peoria Sports Complex, and I am incredibly grateful for the opportunity to have served as a Ticket Sales Associate this season. This role allowed me to gain invaluable experience in the ticketing industry, providing insight into the behind-the-scenes operations of professional baseball.

Under the leadership of my manager, Nash Thompson, and in collaboration with my sales partner, Ty Petersen, Ty and I successfully generated over half a million ($549,411.50) in ticket revenue, selling a total of 19,152 physical tickets. Our sales efforts spanned beyond single-game tickets to include season ticket memberships, fundraising, and, my personal favorite, group sales.

Additionally, I had the privilege of working closely with the marketing and operations departments, where I expanded my knowledge of promotions, sponsorships, and facility operations. Collaborating with marketing and operations coordinators Kyle Bloms, M.S., and Katherine Reis, as well as my fellow associates Aysa Crocker and Chloe Kaminski, was an incredibly rewarding experience.

Thank you to everyone who has made this season unforgettable. I am so grateful for the learning opportunities and career development I have gained, and I am excited to carry these experiences forward in my career!

post_text: Day 10 of the 30 day “Win Ugly Challenge!” Standardization = Speed + Quality Some leaders think standardization slows things down. The truth? It does the opposite, it gives you time back. People often say “hiring is how you buy back your time.” That’s true. But implementing processes and creating efficiencies is another way to do it, often at a lower total cost and with a greater long-term impact. When processes are consistent: --Training is faster → new hires get productive in weeks, not months. --Mistakes reduce → less rework, less scrap, fewer delays. (And let’s be honest, a lot of rework never gets fully captured on a line item or tied back to a sales order.) --Quality improves → customers see your product as the reliable standard. Standardization isn’t red tape. It’s the foundation of speed, quality, and scalability. 💬 What’s one process in your business that would unlock speed if everyone followed it the same way? #IWillTakeThatChallenge #WinUglyChallenge #Manufacturing #ServantLeadership #ScalingWithoutChaos #30daywinuglychallenge Donnie Boivin | Success Champion Networking (SCN) | Badass Business Summit

Day 10 of the 30 day “Win Ugly Challenge!”
Standardization = Speed + Quality

Some leaders think standardization slows things down.
The truth? It does the opposite, it gives you time back.

People often say “hiring is how you buy back your time.”
That’s true. But implementing processes and creating efficiencies is another way to do it, often at a lower total cost and with a greater long-term impact.

When processes are consistent:

--Training is faster → new hires get productive in weeks, not months.

--Mistakes reduce → less rework, less scrap, fewer delays. (And let’s be honest, a lot of rework never gets fully captured on a line item or tied back to a sales order.)

--Quality improves → customers see your product as the reliable standard.

Standardization isn’t red tape. It’s the foundation of speed, quality, and scalability.

💬 What’s one process in your business that would unlock speed if everyone followed it the same way?

post_text: Introduction Infrastructure as Code (IaC) has become an integral part of modern software development, allowing teams to define and manage their infrastructure in a code-like manner. Terraform is one of the leading IaC tools, widely adopted for its simplicity and versatility. TFlint, an open-source linting tool for Terraform, has been gaining popularity for its ability to catch errors and improve the quality of Terraform code. The version v0.47.0 of TFlint introduces an innovative feature: auto-correction. In this article, we'll delve into the significance of this new feature and how it enhances the Terraform development experience. What is TFlint? TFlint is a framework for Terraform that helps developers catch potential errors and improve the overall quality of their Terraform code before deployment. It analyzes the code for issues such as syntax errors, resource duplication, and best practices violations. By providing instant feedback during the development process, TFlint enables developers to write cleaner and more efficient Terraform code. Auto-Correction Feature from v0.47.0 The auto-correction feature in TFlint takes the tool's capabilities to the next level. Instead of merely identifying issues, TFlint can now automatically correct certain types of errors in the Terraform code. This feature aims to streamline the development workflow by reducing the manual effort required to fix common mistakes. Key Benefits: Increased Developer Productivity: Auto-correction minimizes the need for developers to manually address common errors identified by TFlint. Developers can focus more on designing and refining their infrastructure code, rather than spending time on routine corrections. Reduced Human Error: Manual corrections often introduce the possibility of human error. With auto-correction, the chances of introducing new mistakes during the resolution process are significantly reduced. Consistency in Codebase: Auto-correction ensures a consistent coding style and adherence to best practices across the entire codebase, as corrections are applied uniformly. Faster Iterations: By automating the correction of certain errors, developers can iterate more quickly, accelerating the development lifecycle. How to Use Auto-Correction Enabling auto-correction in TFlint is a straightforward process. Developers can use the --fix flag when running TFlint to instruct the tool to automatically correct issues identified during analysis. For example: tflint --fix It's important to note that while auto-correction is a powerful feature, developers should still review the changes made by TFlint to ensure they align with the intended behavior of the infrastructure code. If you would like to use it in pre-commit, you can update your pre-commit file this way: # Please see docs for installation: https://pre-commit.com/#installation repos: - repo: https://github.com/antonbabenko/pre-commit-terraform rev: v1.83.3 hooks: - id: terraform_tflint args: - --args=--fix - --args=--recursive Conclusion: TFlint's auto-correction feature marks a significant advancement in the realm of Terraform development. By automating the resolution of common errors, this feature not only enhances developer productivity but also contributes to the overall reliability and consistency of Terraform codebases. As the adoption of Infrastructure as Code continues to grow, tools like TFlint play a crucial role in ensuring the resilience and efficiency of cloud infrastructure deployments.

review how we approach LLN and digital literacy across different learner cohorts — particularly in the context of the RTO Standards 2025. Our discussion focused on the reality that LLN and digital capability are not static requirements. They need to be: scaled differently for skill sets vs full qualifications reconsidered for returning learners and thoughtfully applied for students with higher-level qualifications (such as teaching degrees), where the risk is often over-supporting rather than under-supporting. We also talked through how this thinking must be clearly reflected in the Training and Assessment Strategy (TAS) — not as generic statements, but as: documented decision-making clear rationale for support pathways and evidence that strategies are appropriate, proportionate, and defensible. is a growing disconnect between education and reality, and most people can feel it even if they cannot yet name it. Learners spend years consuming content. Videos, textbooks, slides, lectures, assessments. By the end of it, they are certified, qualified, and often completely unprepared for the real world. Education has become very good at transferring information and very poor at developing capability. We have confused exposure with competence. Knowing the language of a subject is treated as the same thing as being able to do the work. It is not. You can explain how a solar dehydrator works and still be unable to build one. You can recite principles and still freeze when reality introduces friction, constraints, and uncertainty. The real world does not reward recall. It rewards application, judgment, adaptability, and execution. Reality gives feedback. Things break. Assumptions fail. Context matters. Most education systems are designed to avoid this messiness rather than engage with it, because it is harder to standardise and harder to control. The solution is not more content. It is a different sequence. Practice must lead and theory must support. Learners should be doing real work early, making mistakes, receiving feedback, and refining their thinking through experience. Assessment must shift from exams to evidence. Portfolios of work. Projects that solve real problems. Artefacts that demonstrate competence over time. Educators become guides and mentors, not content dispensers. Their role is to design learning environments that mirror reality closely enough to matter. When education realigns with reality, competence stops being assumed and starts being demonstrated. previous posts, I argued that attendance functions as an ROI signal rather than a motivation issue. This post looks at why that signal is so consistently ignored. Universities say they want quality assurance, continuous improvement, and evidence of effective teaching. But look at what their feedback instruments actually ask. Most questions fall into three categories. 1. Affect management - Was the teacher nice? - Was the atmosphere pleasant? - Did you feel supported? This measures emotional comfort, not learning. It tells the institution whether friction stayed low, not whether understanding increased. 2. Method visibility - Were different methods used? - Were lessons varied? - Were tools or media employed? This measures performative pedagogy. Teaching that looks active scores well; cognitive change is not measured. 3. Curricular compliance - Was the course covered? - Were objectives addressed? - Was the syllabus followed? This measures contract fulfilment, not instructional effect. It answers “Was the service delivered?”, not “Did learning happen?” What is almost never asked are questions that measure learning: - What can you do now that you couldn’t do before? - What concept became clearer? - Where did your thinking change? - Which sessions had the highest learning payoff? Those would be ROI questions. And that omission is not accidental. Learning-value feedback is avoided because it would: - expose variance (some sessions would show low return), - threaten standardisation (comparability would collapse), - shift accountability (from personality and compliance to design and effectiveness), - create pressure to redesign (which “nice” feedback never does). So institutions ask questions they can afford to hear answers to. The uncomfortable implication Universities do not ask: “Did this session justify your time?” Because that would make attendance a measurable ROI signal. Instead, they ask: “Did you enjoy the experience?” Bottom line Universities collect feedback they can safely process, not feedback that would force change. They don’t want to know whether learning was worth the cost. They want to know whether the experience was pleasant, the process was followed, and no one caused trouble. Because standardisation depends on avoiding variance, questions that would expose uneven learning value are excluded. That’s why attendance signals are ignored. And why asking the wrong questions keeps producing the same answers. #HigherEducation #StudentEngagement #LearningDesign #GenZ #EducationInnovation Acquisition at Schools and Colleges Do we truly acquire knowledge at school, or do we merely junk our minds with the prescribed thinking of others? This question has followed me through much of my life. Looking back at my own learning and teaching journey, I often feel that instead of nurturing my natural and inborn abilities, the system gradually weakened them. What was meant to enlighten sometimes ended up overshadowing what was already within me. Most school and college systems are built on transmission, not discovery. Knowledge is treated as something external—created by experts, packaged into subjects, and delivered to students. The learner’s role becomes passive: absorb, memorize, reproduce, and move on. In this process, curiosity is slowly replaced by compliance, and originality by conformity. What is rarely acknowledged is that every human being is born with a unique configuration of talents, instincts, and ways of understanding the world. True education should help individuals uncover these inner capacities—what they are naturally inclined toward, what energizes them, what problems they are wired to solve. Instead, we often force everyone through the same narrow pathways, regardless of whether those paths align with who they are. As a result, many students graduate knowing a lot about things yet knowing very little about themselves. They can pass exams but struggle to find meaning. They can repeat theories, but hesitate to question assumptions. In some cases, the imposed knowledge even conflicts with their natural ways of thinking, creating confusion, self-doubt, and a sense of inadequacy. This is not an argument against knowledge, teachers, or institutions. Knowledge matters. Structure matters. Guidance matters. The real issue is balance. Education should not be an act of replacement—swapping a learner’s innate intelligence for borrowed frameworks—but an act of integration, where external knowledge refines, expands, and gives language to what already exists within. Imagine an education system that starts with exploration rather than prescription. One that helps students identify their strengths early, encourages diverse forms of intelligence, and treats questioning as a skill—not a disruption. A system where curricula are flexible, not rigid; adaptive, not uniform; human-centered, not exam-centered. True knowledge acquisition is not about stuffing minds; it is about awakening them. It is not about shaping everyone into the same model, but about helping each individual become more fully themselves. This week in my #NeededNow in L&T series with Jason M. Lodge
Curtin University Mollie Dollinger
👇 We credential them, but we've never met them. What online education must confront

👏 Quality fully online degrees critical for #Equity+ #UniversitiesAccord ambitions for an expanded, more inclusive #HigherEducation sector
BUT...
🤔Assuring learning for fully online degrees is extra difficult
SO...
👍New: Assurance of Learning in Fully Online Credentialled Programs
->Best assessment minds in the business considered:
1️⃣What are the dimensions of the assurance of learning?
2️⃣What models of assurance of learning for online credentialled programs? 
3️⃣Systemic challenges the sector must address
PROPOSE:
3 comprehensive verification models:
1️⃣Supervised assessments at approved locations,
2️⃣Accredited workplace supervision and assessment
3️⃣Longitudinal synchronous learning partnerships

💯 Big, impressive piece of thoughtful work with robust analysis of pros + cons

The year over year Spring peaks have fallen 15% for 2022 and 11% for 2023. This year's summer/early fall has seen a deceleration in sales compared to last year. This makes sense with rates being between 0.5% and 1% higher and money existing homeowners reluctant to give up their low mortgage rates.

New Home sales had a pretty poor Spring season as well but have been showing resilience in recent months. Perhaps this is due to the lack of resales coming on the market and/or builders offering rate buy downs to assist buyers.

#realesate #iowa #realtors #newbuild #housing

post_text: Redefining Credentials in a Disrupted World For decades, India’s colonial-era education system has filtered talent through a rigid classroom-to-job model. This model, designed for a bygone era, now stands as a barrier in a tech-led, AI-disrupted economy. While millions of graduates hold traditional degrees, many are unprepared for a market that increasingly values real-world ingenuity over rote learning. Entrepreneurs, especially those operating profitable businesses in India’s hinterlands, are often left on the fringes. By introducing vocation-based, reflective degrees, as Dr. Ankit Shah radically suggests, we can transform credentials from obstacles into enablers—validating practical skills and innovative thinking. Insights from Harvard Business Review and Forbes highlight that alternative, non-traditional learning models better capture the entrepreneurial spirit, similar to the narratives of Silicon Valley icons like Steve Jobs and Bill Gates . These reflective degrees would recognize real-world success and encourage an ecosystem where entrepreneurial drive is the true measure of potential. The Challenge: Outdated Systems in a Digital Age Mismatch of Skills: The existing curriculum is heavily skewed towards academic theory, leaving graduates ill-equipped for the demands of an AI-driven economy . Traditional degrees often fail to capture the creativity and adaptability needed in today’s fast-paced business environment. Unrealized Potential: Millions of young Indians, especially in rural and semi-urban regions, are sidelined by a system that prioritizes formal education over practical expertise. This underemployment and unemployment among degree holders reflect a significant misalignment between educational outcomes and market needs. Innovation Stifled: The current education framework tends to favor standardized testing and conventional pathways, which can stifle the innovative mindset required to tap into emerging opportunities. Recognizing vocation-based skills through reflective degrees would incentivize creative problem-solving and real-world impact. Bridging the Gap: Strengthening Government Initiatives India’s vision for a “ Viksit Bharat by 2047 ” is already being advanced through flagship programs designed to nurture entrepreneurship ( see my earlier blog about this ): Startup India: Promotes innovation and startup culture by providing funding, mentorship, and regulatory support. This initiative is a critical platform for nurturing entrepreneurial talent, especially when combined with a reformed credentialing system. Learn more about Startup India Mudra Yojna: Facilitates access to credit for micro, small, and medium enterprises, empowering entrepreneurs from all regions—including the hinterlands—to launch and scale their businesses. Visit Mudra Yojna PMEGP and PM Svanidhi Yojana : These schemes provide essential support for self-employment and sustainable livelihoods, ensuring that funding, mentorship, and incubation reach even the most underserved communities. Details on PMEGP Integrating these initiatives with a system that awards reflective, vocation-based degrees would ensure that every young Indian—regardless of geography or formal education background—has the opportunity to unleash their full potential. Three Strategic Steps for Transformation 1) Establish an Independent Accreditation Board for Entrepreneurial Degrees Action: Form a board comprising academic experts, industry leaders, and successful entrepreneurs. Objective: Develop comprehensive evaluation metrics that validate entrepreneurial success through innovation, business growth, and social impact. Outcome: Recognize and formalize non-traditional learning paths, creating a seamless link between education and the dynamic job market. 2) Forge Public-Private Partnerships to Modernize Curricula Action: Collaborate with industry leaders and educational institutions to embed practical, real-world skills into the academic framework. Objective: Transition from rote-based learning to experiential education that aligns with the demands of an AI-driven economy. Outcome: Equip youth with the necessary tools to thrive and innovate, regardless of traditional academic limitations. 3) Implement a Multi-Metric Evaluation Framework Action: Design assessment tools that encompass both quantitative measures (such as business performance and revenue growth) and qualitative factors (like innovation and community impact). Objective: Ensure that reflective degrees hold equal credibility to conventional academic credentials. Outcome: Create a robust system that not only validates entrepreneurial achievements but also attracts funding, partnerships, and opportunities for startup ecosystems nationwide. A Future-Ready India: Empowering Every Young Dream The shift towards vocation-based, reflective degrees can serve as a powerful enabler—turning traditional filters into catalysts for innovation. By recognizing the entrepreneurial spirit inherent in every young Indian, and by seamlessly integrating with government initiatives like Startup India, Mudra Yojna, PMEGP, and PM Svanidhi Yojana, we could pave the way for an inclusive, dynamic future. This approach can not only address current skill gaps and underemployment but could also turbocharge India's startup ecosystem and unlock its demographic dividend, ensuring that every aspiring entrepreneur, regardless of their background, has the opportunity to spread their wings and achieve impactful success. (This article is inspired by a pathbreaking response given by Dr. Ankit Shah during the Q/A on his latest podcast )

There is something powerful happening at Franklin School, and it is becoming more than a moment, it is becoming a tradition.

This week, we welcomed P. Alex Shaurette from NYSAIS - New York State Association of Independent Schools to campus to learn more about the innovative and collaborative work taking place within our professional learning model.

What makes this visit particularly meaningful is that it reflects a growing pattern at Franklin. Increasingly, thought leaders, school teams, education experts, and passionate educators are visiting our campus each week to share ideas, learn together, and experience firsthand the work happening across our school community.

At the center of this particular work is Amanda Katagiri. The embedded weekly professional learning program Amanda has designed and led is not only exceptional in its structure and impact, it is genuinely valued and loved by the faculty who experience it every week. It has created a culture where professional growth is not an event or a workshop; it is woven directly into the rhythm of school life.

Very proud of Amanda and very proud of Franklin for continuing to build a culture where educators learn as deeply and intentionally as our students do.

From reading fluency to outdoor learning, controlled school leaders are driving sustained improvement for pupils in #ControlledSchools through CSSC's #BuildingCapacity programme. Informed by high performing education systems across the world, the programme challenges leaders to identify a clear improvement priority, gather evidence, test approaches in practice, and evaluate real impact in their own schools. It is disciplined, collaborative, and ongoing. The event ‘Sharing Impact in School Improvement’ marked the sharing of that work and launch of the publication Building Capacity: Leading Improvement which brings together 23 case studies from participating schools, organised around five themes: Under Great Teaching First, leaders including David Corbett of Gilnahirk Primary strengthened reading fluency and writing across their schools. Every Learner Included, Nuala McGranaghan of Cedar Lodge School developed communication and sensory support for pupils with complex needs. Melissa McCombe of Kilrea Primary led work under Ethos as a Priority. Ross Coulter of Ballycarrickmaddy Primary developed collaborative professional practice under Growing People. And in Spaces That Shape Learning, leaders transformed outdoor environments to enhance engagement and wellbeing. There is something powerful happening at Franklin School, and it is becoming more than a moment, it is becoming a tradition.

This week, we welcomed P. Alex Shaurette from NYSAIS - New York State Association of Independent Schools to campus to learn more about the innovative and collaborative work taking place within our professional learning model.

What makes this visit particularly meaningful is that it reflects a growing pattern at Franklin. Increasingly, thought leaders, school teams, education experts, and passionate educators are visiting our campus each week to share ideas, learn together, and experience firsthand the work happening across our school community.

At the center of this particular work is Amanda Katagiri. The embedded weekly professional learning program Amanda has designed and led is not only exceptional in its structure and impact, it is genuinely valued and loved by the faculty who experience it every week. It has created a culture where professional growth is not an event or a workshop; it is woven directly into the rhythm of school life.

Very proud of Amanda and very proud of Franklin for continuing to build a culture where educators learn as deeply and intentionally as our students do.

post_text:
As the conversation around AI continues to mature, it's becoming increasingly clear that frontier AI models represent both opportunity and risk.
 
This thought provoking article explores how advanced AI capabilities could become a force multiplier for adversaries, enabling cyber threats to operate at greater scale, speed and sophistication than ever before. It serves as a timely reminder that organisations must consider not only how to leverage AI, but also how to secure against its misuse.
 
Thank you Aditya K Sood, Ph.D, for highlighting this important perspective. The discussion reinforces the need for robust AI governance, cyber resilience and security strategies that can keep pace with rapidly evolving technologies.

AI introduces new pathways for risk. Sensitive data exposure. Excessive access. Unintended information disclosure. Weak governance and oversight. These are not AI challenges alone. They are security, risk, and governance challenges. What organisations should focus on ✅ Applying existing security controls to AI platforms and agents ✅ Protecting sensitive information used by and exposed to AI systems ✅ Monitoring AI activity and outputs for unexpected behaviour ✅ Establishing clear ownership and accountability for AI risks ✅ Continuously assessing how AI changes the organisation’s attack surface The question is no longer whether organisations will adopt AI. But here's what I've learned from working with businesses of different sizes: The biggest cybersecurity challenge isn't detecting threats. It's responding to them fast enough. Most organizations don't fail because they lack tools. They fail because alerts are missed, systems aren't monitored properly, or security is treated as a one-time project instead of a continuous process. That's where advanced AI models could make the biggest impact. Not by replacing security professionals, but by helping them focus on what matters most while the AI handles the noise. The future of cybersecurity won't be human vs AI. It will be organizations using AI effectively vs those that don't. And just like cloud adoption a decade ago, the companies that start learning and adapting today will have a significant advantage tomorrow. From where I stand, AI isn't becoming another cybersecurity tool. It will be built on AI assurance. A recent announcement caught my attention. The goal is to identify dangerous behaviors, vulnerabilities, and misuse risks before these models reach more users. Think about that for a moment. Some of the world's most advanced AI systems are now being stress-tested before deployment, much like critical infrastructure. That reflects a major shift. For years, organizations asked: \"How can AI improve our business?\" Now the question is: \"How do we prove our AI is safe to deploy?\" Every enterprise adopting AI should start thinking the same way. Before an AI model reaches production, ask: ✅ Has it been red teamed? ✅ Can it resist prompt injection and misuse? ✅ Are high-risk capabilities restricted? ✅ Are outputs monitored after deployment? ✅ Can every AI decision be audited? The future belongs to organizations that don't just build intelligent AI. They build trustworthy AI. Because in cybersecurity, confidence without validation is simply another vulnerability. We are delighted to be featured in the latest regional publication by Waterford Press Ltd! The article highlights our Employer of the Year nomination at the Wellington Gold Awards and perfectly captures our core people strategy: 'Brilliant people; connected, enabled, and unleashed'. 

The timing of this feature could not be better, as tonight our team is attending the Auckland Business Chamber 2degrees Business Awards as a finalist for Employer of the Year (Central region)! We are incredibly proud to be recognised across multiple regions for our people first culture, and we have our fingers crossed for a win this evening.

In the article, our General Manager of People, Katie Ham, shares some fantastic insights into how we actively support our team in a demanding industry. It is this proactive care that allows our consultants to confidently derisk major digital transformations for organisations like Inland Revenue NZ Revenue and the Ministry of Social Development (MSD). 

A special shout out to our long time hardware and infrastructure partner, iTops, for their ongoing support and for sharing this piece. 

Check out the article to read more about our recent growth and what makes Assurity such a rewarding place to work!

the course of this year there’s been a lot of commentary about the employment market being “soft”. At the executive level across transport, rail and logistics in Australia and New Zealand, I think the picture is more nuanced. The market is certainly more cautious and more selective. Organisations are taking longer to approve senior appointments, scrutinising remuneration and expecting more from every leadership hire. But the demand for genuinely strong executives hasn’t disappeared. If anything, I’m seeing a flight to quality. Businesses are looking for leaders who can do more than simply run their function. They want executives who can lead transformation while maintaining operational performance, improve asset reliability and productivity, navigate complex safety and regulatory environments, lead large dispersed workforces and bring strong commercial judgement to operational businesses. And while there may be more people open to conversations, the pool of executives with the right combination of sector knowledge, leadership capability, commercial judgement and a demonstrated record of transformation remains relatively tight. For organisations recruiting at this level, that creates an interesting dynamic: You can afford to be selective — but you can't afford to be slow. The strongest executives are rarely sitting in the active candidate market waiting for an advertisement. They need to be identified, approached and given a compelling reason to consider moving. It’s also an interesting time for me personally. Having recently relocated to Melbourne, I’m looking forward to building on the relationships I already have across Victoria while continuing to work with clients and executives throughout Australia and New Zealand. I’m particularly keen to connect with more CEOs, C-Suite executives, GMs and senior leaders across rail, transport, logistics and infrastructure here in Melbourne. So, if we’ve been connected on LinkedIn for years but have never actually met — or if you're in the sector and our paths haven't crossed yet — I'd be very happy to grab a coffee and change that. From the conversations I’m having across the market, I’d describe conditions right now as: Cautious. Selective. Competitive. But still very active for the right leadership talent. We are delighted to be featured in the latest regional publication by Waterford Press Ltd! The article highlights our Employer of the Year nomination at the Wellington Gold Awards and perfectly captures our core people strategy: 'Brilliant people; connected, enabled, and unleashed'.

The timing of this feature could not be better, as tonight our team is attending the Auckland Business Chamber 2degrees Business Awards as a finalist for Employer of the Year (Central region)! We are incredibly proud to be recognised across multiple regions for our people first culture, and we have our fingers crossed for a win this evening.

In the article, our General Manager of People, Katie Ham, shares some fantastic insights into how we actively support our team in a demanding industry. It is this proactive care that allows our consultants to confidently derisk major digital transformations for organisations like Inland Revenue NZ Revenue and the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).

A special shout out to our long time hardware and infrastructure partner, iTops, for their ongoing support and for sharing this piece.

Check out the article to read more about our recent growth and what makes Assurity such a rewarding place to work!

The document introduces the “Triad of Bird Immunity”, showing how the bird, the environment, and pathogens interact across all stages of production — from breeders and hatchery to grow-out and production. post_text: The "Safety-Assured High-Speed Aerial Robot," aka SUPER, Boasts Hummingbird-Like Agility The most impressive new drone technology doesn’t come from DJI (or FAA-approved "research drones") but rather from the University of Hong Kong. And it’s called the "Safety-Assured High-Speed Aerial Robot," also known as SUPER. But is it really that super? The autonomous SUPER micro aerial vehicle (MAV) has a diameter of about 28 cm and features the speed and agility of a hummingbird reaching over 72 km/h. What sets SUPER apart from other racing drones, which can exceed 160 km/h and make sharp turns on the spot, is that SUPER is AI-powered and equipped with an onboard 3D LiDAR. In other words, it uses pulse lasers for light detection and ranging (LiDAR), giving SUPER eagle-like vision, capable of seeing with precision down to less than 1 cm at a distance of 70 meters. Imagine being able to clearly see a thumbtack on the sidewalk from the top of an 18-story building. Yes, that’s what SUPER’s 3D LiDAR is capable of. What also makes this thing pretty insane is its level of obstacle avoidance while moving at maximum speed. Again, it’s not on par with an extreme racing drone in a drag race, but its ability to autonomously choose a clear path through tons of thin branches at 72 km/h while chasing a human almost like it has a bounty on them—is next-level. (If AI ever flips the switch, it’s pretty much "game over, humanity.") SUPER’s 3D LiDAR system can detect wires as thin as 2.5 mm in high definition. That’s about the size of a low E guitar string or a small twig on a tree. In the research paper published by the University of Hong Kong—along with data and video footage—there’s a whole lot of math on parameterization, trajectory optimization, formulas, and “kinodynamic constraints” that go way over my head, but they work. Even in complete darkness, the drone can navigate obstacle courses at incredible speeds while avoiding collisions. In fact, its onboard AI simultaneously calculates two trajectories: one optimized for maximum speed and the other as a "safety net" in case it needs to make an emergency maneuver. Thanks to this "pull-the-pin" approach, SUPER has reduced failure rates (i.e., the classic crash and burn) by a factor of 35.9 while reaching speeds over 45 mph. That makes it nearly 40 times safer—even at high speeds. Watching SUPER map its surroundings in detail with 3D LiDAR in real time feels like playing Command & Conquer or StarCraft as you explore the map. The SUPER MAV boasts a thrust-to-weight ratio greater than 5.0, making it incredibly agile and capable of rapid direction changes. For comparison, the cutting-edge Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II, a 5th-generation multirole stealth fighter, has a meager thrust-to-weight ratio of around 0.87. This is undeniably cool technology (or terrifying for those wary of AI’s growing capabilities) with a wide range of practical applications—disaster response, search and rescue, infrastructure inspection… or, in a dystopian nightmare scenario, AI-powered drone fleets patrolling the skies like hawks, straight out of Skynet Hunter Killers . Hopefully, we’re looking at the first scenario—where drones like SUPER can quickly assess hard-to-reach situations and relay crucial information to rescuers to help save lives. SUPER is far from being commercially available. However, search-and-rescue drones already exist on the market, such as the DJI Matrice 30T. It’s highly valued by police and emergency response teams for its ruggedness, ease of use, weather resistance, and a full suite of potentially life-saving features like thermal imaging, optical zoom, and laser ranging. Perhaps combining the technology from both could lead to the ultimate search-and-rescue drone. 🎉 Zehn Jahre Verbund: Aldra & Ewitherm feiern Jubiläum

Die Ewitherm Holzbau aus Thedinghausen feierte am 2. Oktober 2025 ihr zehnjähriges Bestehen – und zugleich blickt Aldra Fenster und Türen GmbH auf zehn Jahre Vollsortiment im Fenster- und Türbereich zurück.
Durch die Integration des Holzsortiments bietet das norddeutsche Familienunternehmen seit einem Jahrzehnt Elemente aus Kunststoff, Aluminium sowie Holz und Holz/Aluminium – und deckt damit nahezu jede Anforderung vom Einfamilienhaus bis zum Objektbau ab.

💬 „Um Fachpartnern die Möglichkeit zu geben, alle Produkte im Fenster- und Türbereich aus jedem Werkstoff über einen Hersteller beziehen zu können, haben wir das Holzsortiment bei Aldra aufgenommen“, sagt Jan-Peter Albers, geschäftsführender Gesellschafter von Aldra.

👉 Mit über 7.000 produzierten Holzelementen im Jahr 2024, einem stetig wachsenden Premiumsegment und kontinuierlichen Investitionen in moderne Fertigungstechnik zeigt sich: Der Verbund aus Aldra und Ewitherm ist eine Erfolgsgeschichte aus Handwerkskunst, Innovation und Teamgeist.

Hier geht's zum Beitrag: https://lnkd.in/ewVBhZuE

post_text: Ipsos announces the acquisition of Seventh Decimal, a research technology company specialising in Out-Of-Home (OOH) audience measurement. Established in 2019 and headquartered in the UAE, Seventh Decimal is still in the initial phase of its development and will benefit from Ipsos to scale. Leveraging proprietary, state-of-the-art mobility intelligence, the company delivers advanced OOH media exposure measurement for brands, media agencies, and media owners. Its platform provides predictive planning and post-campaign analytics, reporting on OOH exposure, frequency of exposure and granular results for both static and digital OOH. By integrating Seventh Decimal’s technology, Ipsos will further establish itself as a market-leader for OOH. Read more: https://ow.ly/XSVs30sSZXx

Ipsos announces the acquisition of Seventh Decimal, a research technology company specialising in Out-Of-Home (OOH) audience measurement. Established in 2019 and headquartered in the UAE, Seventh Decimal is still in the initial phase of its development and will benefit from Ipsos to scale.

Leveraging proprietary, state-of-the-art mobility intelligence, the company delivers advanced OOH media exposure measurement for brands, media agencies, and media owners. Its platform provides predictive planning and post-campaign analytics, reporting on OOH exposure, frequency of exposure and granular results for both static and digital OOH.

By integrating Seventh Decimal’s technology, Ipsos will further establish itself as a market-leader for OOH.

Read more: https://ow.ly/XSVs30sSZXx

in Industry 4.0: It’s Not the Tech, It’s the Fit That Matters (13 Underrated Drivers of Real ROI from Transform Partner) 1. Use Case Fit - Alignment with a real operational pain point. - Clear KPIs defined from the start (e.g., downtime reduction, defect rate, energy savings). 2. Process Integration Complexity - Ease or difficulty in integrating with legacy systems (ERP, MES, SCADA). - Disruption to existing workflows during deployment. 3. Data Readiness - Availability of clean, structured, contextualized data. - Latency and accessibility of real-time data streams. 4. Change Management and Workforce Buy-In - Training, adoption speed, and frontline engagement. - Resistance from operators or middle management can delay ROI. 5. Scale of Deployment - ROI on a pilot line vs. enterprise-wide rollout differs drastically. - Proof-of-value efforts deliver faster ROI than end-to-end transformations. 6. Organizational Agility - Speed of decision-making, budget reallocation, and vendor coordination. - Bureaucratic friction adds months to ROI timelines. 7. Regulatory and Industry Constraints - In industries like aerospace, pharma, or energy, ROI is slowed by compliance, certification cycles, and safety validation. 8. Vendor Capability and Accountability - Partner’s ability to deliver measurable outcomes (e.g., SLA-driven delivery). - Strong vendor-client collaboration accelerates time-to-value. 9. Infrastructure Maturity - Whether the digital backbone (cloud, edge, connectivity) is already in place. - Tech upgrades may be needed before value realization starts. 10. Business Ownership - Strong executive sponsorship and cross-functional alignment. - ROI stalls when the initiative sits in a tech silo without business accountability. 11. Cybersecurity & Operational Technology (OT) Security Posture - Resilience against cyber threats to the new connected infrastructure. - Skills and processes for ongoing security maintenance, not just initial deployment. A security breach can instantly wipe out any accumulated ROI. 12. Long-term Evolution & Interoperability - Avoiding new \"vendor lock-in\" and ensuring new systems can integrate with future technologies. - Scalability and adaptability of the solution to accommodate new business models (e.g., Product-as-a-Service). This ensures the ROI continues to grow rather than plateau. 13. Sustainability Impact - Measuring contribution to ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) goals. For many modern companies, ROI is not purely financial. Use cases that reduce energy consumption or material waste are increasingly prioritized and can have a significant \"soft\" ROI in terms of brand value and compliance This checklist can serve as a diagnostic lens before any investment — to pressure-test expected ROI timelines and set realistic expectations at the leadership table. Process Integration Complexity - Ease or difficulty in integrating with legacy systems (ERP, MES, SCADA). - Disruption to existing workflows during deployment. 3. Data Readiness - Availability of clean, structured, contextualized data. - Latency and accessibility of real-time data streams. 4. Change Management and Workforce Buy-In - Training, adoption speed, and frontline engagement. - Resistance from operators or middle management can delay ROI. 5. Scale of Deployment - ROI on a pilot line vs. enterprise-wide rollout differs drastically. - Proof-of-value efforts deliver faster ROI than end-to-end transformations. 6. Organizational Agility - Speed of decision-making, budget reallocation, and vendor coordination. - Bureaucratic friction adds months to ROI timelines. 7. Regulatory and Industry Constraints - In industries like aerospace, pharma, or energy, ROI is slowed by compliance, certification cycles, and safety validation. 8. Vendor Capability and Accountability - Partner’s ability to deliver measurable outcomes (e.g., SLA-driven delivery). - Strong vendor-client collaboration accelerates time-to-value. 9. Infrastructure Maturity - Whether the digital backbone (cloud, edge, connectivity) is already in place. - Tech upgrades may be needed before value realization starts. 10. Business Ownership - Strong executive sponsorship and cross-functional alignment. - ROI stalls when the initiative sits in a tech silo without business accountability. 11. Cybersecurity & Operational Technology (OT) Security Posture - Resilience against cyber threats to the new connected infrastructure. - Skills and processes for ongoing security maintenance, not just initial deployment. A security breach can instantly wipe out any accumulated ROI. 12. Long-term Evolution & Interoperability - Avoiding new \"vendor lock-in\" and ensuring new systems can integrate with future technologies. - Scalability and adaptability of the solution to accommodate new business models (e.g., Product-as-a-Service). This ensures the ROI continues to grow rather than plateau. 13. Sustainability Impact - Measuring contribution to ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) goals. For many modern companies, ROI is not purely financial. Let’s stop treating TCO as a procurement checkbox as projects starts with $amount and ends with multiples of this $ amount. Even better? This approach doesn't just help identify risk—it helps prevent it. The goal isn’t to slow things down or overwhelm teams with alerts. The goal is to build controls into the flow of business—quietly, intelligently, and sustainably. It’s a shift from reacting to issues... to anticipating and eliminating them early. For those working in internal audit, risk, compliance, or operations: How are you thinking about embedding risk detection into everyday operations? It’s the ability for a process to run end-to-end — from initiation to completion — without manual intervention. No emails back and forth, no spreadsheets bridging systems, no human “glue” holding things together. When STP works, it delivers: ✅ Accuracy — no data loss or duplication. ✅ Efficiency — faster turnaround and reduced costs. ✅ Scalability — processes that can grow without adding people. And that’s where DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act) comes in. DORA isn’t just about compliance — it’s a mindset. It’s a reminder that digital speed means nothing without digital resilience. post_text: Do you need a dental insurance plan? Oral hygiene is a major component of your overall health and wellness. However, Statistics Canada reported that more than 2 in every 10 Canadians skipped dental visits due to cost constraints. This is a concerning statistic as a lack of oral care can cause serious problems down the road that can become unavoidable and highly expensive. Dental insurance plan coverage categories While dental insurance plans can vary from provider to provider, there are three general categories that you will likely find included in your plan. The first is basic care which includes preventative services including X-rays, dental cleaning, fluoride applications, fillings, and other minor or routine dental work. Major restorative services is another category. This category includes major dental work such as crowns, dentures, bridgework, inlays and onlays. The last category is orthodontic services which include coverage for specific procedures and appliances including braces and other aids that help to straighten your teeth, fix your bite alignment, etc. How dental insurance works By buying a dental insurance policy , you enter into a contract with your insurance provider. Similar to any other insurance policy that you buy, you have to pay monthly premiums to the insurance company in exchange for the benefits that they pay out. There are also several other components to your insurance plan. 1- Deductible Most dental insurance policies will not cover the entirety of your dental expenses. A deductible is the amount that you are responsible for paying before your insurance coverage kicks in. For example, imagine you have a deductible of $250 on your policy and your treatment cost $700. In that case, you would be responsible for paying $250 out of pocket and your insurance provider will cover the remaining $450. 2- Co-payment Your insurance policy may also carry a co-payment feature wherein you are accountable for paying a specific percentage of the total cost over and above your deductible. Usually, this percentage is around the 10% mark, but can be higher depending on the policy you purchase. It should also be noted that your insurance provider will not reimburse you for the co-payment you make. 3- Maximum limit The insurance policy will also likely stipulate a limit on the benefits you are eligible to receive under the coverage option you choose. For example, the policy may only allow 2 annual dental check-ups in a year. 4- Waiting period Some insurance providers may have a waiting period before your benefits kick in while others do not. When selecting a policy, it is particularly important to check coverage for major services as some policies only allow holders to become eligible after several years of coverage. What to look for in a dental insurance plan Purchasing a dental insurance plan does not have a one-size-fits all solution. Different plans may be useful for different people. Some of the main things you should assess are: 1- Premiums One of the most important considerations is the monthly premium you have to pay. Make sure that this premium is affordable to you and in line with your income. 2- Offered coverage All things equal, greater coverage options translate to higher premiums. Depending on your oral history, needs and preferences, you may want to choose a plan that offers coverage of more than just basic dental services. You may also choose greater coverage options as the parent of children who may need braces as opposed to an adult individual with strong oral health. 3- Deductibles and co-payments Some plans have higher deductibles and lower co-payments while the vice versa applies for others. For plans with a large deductible, you have to pay a higher fee upfront. However, if you have significant dental care costs, this may still be worth it since most plans with higher deductibles come with lower co-payments. 4- Group vs. individual insurance plan If you have access to a group plan from your employer, it is worth at least reviewing it. Group coverage generally offers more cost-effective premiums than individual plans and can often offer more attractive benefits as well. 5- Limits and waiting periods Based on your and/or your family’s dental needs, you may need plans with higher limits or shorter waiting periods to start availing of your benefits. text":"It’s I’ve chosen LinkedIn as my primary platform. I’ve dabbled with video before and copped criticism - usually behind my back, not to my face. That’s fine. It comes with putting yourself out there. What I find interesting is that the loudest critics are often producing the least. Plenty of opinions. Very little output. Meanwhile, the people actually doing the work - starting podcasts, creating content, organising guests, investing time with no immediate return - are the ones moving the industry forward. They’re the ones trying to raise the floor. And that’s how I see competition. Not as something or someone to tear down. As something that should lift the standard for everyone. We’ve got competitors who throw mud at us. Some replicate our marketing. Others undercut fees to win work. We don’t chase them down. We assess. We refine. We improve. Then we go again. That’s the game. To stay ahead you have to keep pushing to another level. Same with fees. We constantly come up against competitors charging half of what we charge. We don’t match them. We sharpen our message. We articulate value better. We focus on outcomes - not price. Because discounting your worth isn’t strategy. It’s surrender and lack of belief. At the end of the day, looking sideways is dangerous. Look too long at what others are doing and you lose sight of where you’re going. Focus on your lane. Keep testing. Keep refining. I just had to find smarter ways to bring in leads.

Through trial, error, and a lot of learning, I discovered how to leverage Facebook ads, automate systems, and use communication to my advantage. These strategies helped me build a business that wasn’t just about quick wins but about long-term success.

It stands as a powerful reminder of the country’s remarkable journey transforming deserts into hubs of innovation and leadership. Beyond the skyscrapers and technological marvels, the UAE’s dedication to sustainability is its true legacy.

In the words of His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum: 

“We will continue pursuing ambitious investments with an emphasis on projects that have a positive impact on people’s lives. Clean and renewable energy is key to sustainable development and the UAE has set an example for its rapid adoption,”

This vision is now a reality with the UAE leading the way in renewable energy projects like the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park and Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant.

From world-leading solar parks to the Net Zero 2050 goal, the UAE is proving that true progress is built on a foundation of sustainability. As we move forward, let’s remember that our actions today shape the world of tomorrow.

Navigating the job market can be a daunting challenge, but with the right strategies, success is within reach.
Your mindset totally shapes how you tackle the job hunt! 
Stay Tough: Job hunting is tough, but keeping a positive mindset helps you bounce back from setbacks and keeps you going. 

Believe in Yourself: Confidence is key! If you believe in yourself, you're more likely to nail those interviews and land the perfect role. 

Take Charge: Don't wait around for opportunities to come to you. Go out there, network, and hustle for what you want. 

Roll with the Punches: Stay flexible and open-minded. Sometimes, you might need to switch gears or try something new.

Set Goals: Break down your job search into bite-sized goals. It keeps you focused and motivated. 

Chill Out: Job hunting can stress you out, but finding ways to relax and stay balanced is key. 

Build Connections: Your network is gold! Keep those relationships strong—it could lead to your next job opportunity. 

Learn from Feedback: Don't take criticism to heart. Use it as fuel to improve and grow. 

Keep pushing forward, stay positive, and remember that the right opportunity is out there waiting for you.

post_text: The Mechanical Licensing Collective and Pandora filed competing summary judgment motions in their ongoing dispute over mechanical royalties owed to songwriters and publishers. The MLC argues that features on Pandora's ad-supported free tier, including on-demand listening sessions, unlimited skips and replays, and personalized programming, qualify the service as "interactive" under Section 115 of the Copyright Act. This classification would require Pandora to pay mechanical royalties for the reproduction and distribution of musical works. The MLC claims Pandora has been underpaying mechanical royalties and points to language on Pandora's website that describes features allowing users to "search and play what you want" on Pandora Free. The collective says Pandora "has not correctly reported royalty payment and accounting information as required." Pandora disputes this classification, arguing its free tier operates as noninteractive internet radio, which would exempt it from mechanical licensing requirements under Section 115. The company claims the MLC is engaged in "gross overreach" and attempting to impose "a novel and incorrect interpretation of the Copyright Act." Why this matters: This case could set precedent for how streaming services are classified under mechanical licensing law, directly affecting royalty flows to your songwriter and publishing clients. The interactive vs. noninteractive distinction determines whether platforms owe mechanical royalties under Section 115, making this outcome critical for understanding rights administration obligations and ensuring proper compensation. The Mechanical Licensing Collective and Pandora filed competing summary judgment motions in their ongoing dispute over mechanical royalties owed to songwriters and publishers.

The MLC argues that features on Pandora's ad-supported free tier, including on-demand listening sessions, unlimited skips and replays, and personalized programming, qualify the service as "interactive" under Section 115 of the Copyright Act. This classification would require Pandora to pay mechanical royalties for the reproduction and distribution of musical works.

The MLC claims Pandora has been underpaying mechanical royalties and points to language on Pandora's website that describes features allowing users to "search and play what you want" on Pandora Free. The collective says Pandora "has not correctly reported royalty payment and accounting information as required."

Pandora disputes this classification, arguing its free tier operates as noninteractive internet radio, which would exempt it from mechanical licensing requirements under Section 115. The company claims the MLC is engaged in "gross overreach" and attempting to impose "a novel and incorrect interpretation of the Copyright Act."

Why this matters:

This case could set precedent for how streaming services are classified under mechanical licensing law, directly affecting royalty flows to your songwriter and publishing clients. The interactive vs. noninteractive distinction determines whether platforms owe mechanical royalties under Section 115, making this outcome critical for understanding rights administration obligations and ensuring proper compensation. Nova is aangesloten bij Jeugdstroom, een samenwerkingsverband van organisaties die zich gezamenlijk inzetten voor kinderen, jongeren en gezinnen in de regio.

Binnen Jeugdstroom bundelen Chinski Groep, Jij, Ik en Wij, Praktijk Carpe Diem, Dokter Bosman, FIVE2CONNECT en Nova hun kennis en expertise. Iedere organisatie brengt daarbij haar eigen specialisme mee. Hierdoor kunnen organisaties elkaar aanvullen wanneer een hulpvraag specialistische expertise vraagt die niet binnen één organisatie aanwezig is.

De samenwerking biedt daarnaast mogelijkheden om gezamenlijk aanbod en collectieve interventies te ontwikkelen. Groepsgerichte ondersteuning kan voor veel jeugdigen een waardevolle aanvulling zijn op individuele hulp. Door kinderen en jongeren met vergelijkbare hulpvragen samen te brengen, ontstaat ruimte voor herkenning, sociale verbinding en het oefenen van vaardigheden in een veilige omgeving.

Wat ons verbindt is een gezamenlijke visie op samenwerking, preventie en passende ondersteuning. Daarbij staat steeds de vraag centraal welke ondersteuning nodig is voor het kind, de jongere en het gezin.

🐕🐶🤖🐺🐩 Quand nos étudiants ne sont pas là, nos robots dansent. 😉

Notre chenil robotique était de sortie aujourd'hui pour la visite d'étudiants en L3 de la Faculté des Sciences et Technologie de Nancy actuellement en stage au Loria. 💻🔬

Ils ont été accueillis par Amaury Saint-Jore, doctorant en robotique au Loria, ainsi que par les stagiaires du Techlab Mines Nancy, qui viennent de CESI Nancy et EpiTech Nancy. Au programme, Intelligence Artificielle, Robotique, Cybersecurité et Réseaux 5G. 📚🏫

L'occasion pour nos robots de se promener pendant les vacances scolaires, quand nos étudiants ne sont pas là... 😸

Ecole Nationale Supérieure des Mines de Nancy Université de Lorraine CESI EPITECH - European Institute of Technology Mines Nancy Alumni Boston Dynamics Unitree Robotics Petoi

post_text: 🌟 Anyone Can Be Called “Boss.” Few Earn the Title “Leader.” 🌟 Being a boss is about authority — a position granted by title. Being a leader is about influence — a position earned through trust, vision, and action. A boss commands. A leader inspires. A boss demands results. A leader develops people. A boss manages tasks. A leader shapes purpose. In every organization, the true measure of leadership isn’t how many people report to you — it’s how many people believe in you, grow because of you, and follow you even when they don’t have to. 👉 Lead with empathy. 👉 Empower instead of control. 👉 Build others, and you’ll build something that lasts. #Leadership #Inspiration #GrowthMindset #TeamCulture #LeadByExample

🌟 Anyone Can Be Called “Boss.” Few Earn the Title “Leader.” 🌟

Being a boss is about authority — a position granted by title.
Being a leader is about influence — a position earned through trust, vision, and action.

A boss commands.
A leader inspires.

A boss demands results.
A leader develops people.

A boss manages tasks.
A leader shapes purpose.

In every organization, the true measure of leadership isn’t how many people report to you — it’s how many people believe in you, grow because of you, and follow you even when they don’t have to.

👉 Lead with empathy.
👉 Empower instead of control.
👉 Build others, and you’ll build something that lasts.

#Leadership #Inspiration #GrowthMindset #TeamCulture #LeadByExample

post_text: Back in 2011, BlueStone set out to do what many thought was impossible: convince Indians to buy gold and diamonds online. At its core was a bold belief that India’s jewelry market, dominated for generations by family jewelers, was ready to be reshaped by design, technology, and above all, trust. What began as a 33-slide idea deck is today a billion-dollar public company, proving that conviction paired with clarity can rewrite an entire category. On PitchCraft Season 2, Founder Gaurav Singh Kushwaha and early investor Prashanth Prakash , revisit that very first deck, surfacing lessons every founder can carry forward: 𝟭. 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝗮 𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗼𝗮𝘁 From his Amazon years, Gaurav saw that horizontal players could swallow many verticals. Jewelry was different: it demanded specialist supply chains, design expertise, and a trust equation outsiders couldn’t easily replicate. Lesson: When giants loom, pick a space where differentiation is baked into the category itself. 𝟮. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 Buying jewelry online in 2011 seemed absurd. BlueStone answered with 3D renders more lifelike than photographs, alloy replicas for home try-ons, and a 30-day money-back promise. These weren’t features; they were trust signals. Lesson: In high-friction markets, innovation lies in reducing anxiety, not just in refining the product. 𝟯. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗱, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁 The first roadmap imagined solitaires, watches, and even men’s accessories. Reality forced discipline. Solitaires were too spec-driven, margins too thin. What clicked was everyday, design-led jewelry. Lesson: Ambition sets direction, but survival depends on pruning fast and doubling down on where you’re truly distinct. 𝟰. 𝗦𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗲𝗱 Jewelry isn’t built in a funding cycle. Even Tanishq struggled for its first decade. Credibility compounds over years, not months. Lesson: In brand-heavy categories, patience and persistence are as important as capital. 𝟱. 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿’𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 As Prashanth recalls, 'It was the person behind the deck first.' What stood out wasn’t just jewelry, but Gaurav’s conviction that India wouldn’t follow the US diamond-centric path, and gold and design would define this market. Lesson: First-principles insight often outweighs the TAM slide. 𝟲. 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲, 𝘀𝗼 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 BlueStone’s early bet that internet-savvy men would buy gifts didn’t hold. The real customers? Married women, 25-45, building new lives away from their family jeweler. Lesson: Hypotheses will fail. Winners are those who grow with their customers. 19‑year‑old from a tiny chawl in Mumbai built what billion‑dollar companies still can’t. He slept on a folded mattress that smelled of jasmine incense and street‑food oil. Every morning the rooster from the neighbor’s rooftop sang at 5 am, and he was already at the tiny tea stall, buying a cup of chai for 5 rupees, notebook in hand. The idea was simple: a platform that let local artisans showcase handcrafted jewelry without a middleman. But the first prototype was a crumpled sketch on a torn newspaper, and the first pitch was met with laughter in a glass‑walled conference room of a venture firm. He walked out, heart pounding like the monsoon drums, and sat on the steps of the railway station. The rain began, soaking his shoes, but the sound of droplets on metal gave him a rhythm. He realized he was trying to sell a polished product before he’d built the trust. That night, under a flickering bulb, he called his grandmother. She reminded him of the old loom in the courtyard, how each thread was woven with patience. He turned that patience into a promise: 'Every artisan will keep 90 % of the sale.' He built a tiny website on a borrowed laptop, using free tools, and posted the first 12 artisans he knew from his street. Within weeks, a fashion blogger from Delhi discovered the site, posted a photo, and the orders started flowing like the Ganges after the monsoon. The first shipment of brass bangles arrived at a boutique in London, wrapped in a handwritten note that read, 'Made in Mumbai, loved worldwide.' Today his company ships to over 30 countries, employs a team of 45, and still runs its weekly 'Chai & Chat' calls where every employee shares a story of a customer’s smile. The secret isn’t the technology; it’s the humility of remembering where you started and the courage to keep walking when the world says 'no'. Takeaway: Real impact grows when you turn your own struggle into someone else’s advantage. Success isn’t a straight line; it’s a series of rain‑soaked steps that lead to sunrise.
