This Tuesday I had the chance to present our research on reliability analysis of composite poles manufactured by Resilient Structures during Resilient Structures Symposium in Houston, Texas. Our results show that composite poles have superior performance against wind and wildfire hazards with minimal maintenance. I also had the chance to visit Resilient Structures’ new factory and get to know how composite poles are manufactured. These composite poles have superior performance against UV, salt, and moisture and are a fantastic choice for hardening the power grid.

Many thanks to Resilient Structures for organizing the symposium. Also, special thanks to John Higgins, Scott Holmes, Shawn van Hoek-Patterson, P.Eng and Ian McKerlich  for their collaboration on the research project.

Finally,  I am so grateful for my students Saeed Sohrabi, PhD, Amir Tajik, and Amirmohammad Rabbani for their dedication and hard work on this project.

This Tuesday I had the chance to present our research on reliability analysis of composite poles manufactured by Resilient Structures during Resilient Structures Symposium in Houston, Texas. Our results show that composite poles have superior performance against wind and wildfire hazards with minimal maintenance. I also had the chance to visit Resilient Structures’ new factory and get to know how composite poles are manufactured. These composite poles have superior performance against UV, salt, and moisture and are a fantastic choice for hardening the power grid.

Many thanks to Resilient Structures for organizing the symposium. Also, special thanks to John Higgins, Scott Holmes, Shawn van Hoek-Patterson, P.Eng and Ian McKerlich for their collaboration on the research project.

Finally, I am so grateful for my students Saeed Sohrabi, PhD, Amir Tajik, and Amirmohammad Rabbani for their dedication and hard work on this project.

Spot it. Shape it. Sell it.

If I could boil down 25 years of account management into three simple sentences, this would be it. You can apply these to any level, any title, any part of the job.

Need to hire? First you've got to spot exceptional talent. Once in the door, you have to nurture and shape them to be better versions of themselves. Then you may eventually have to sell their capabilities to others for a promotion.

Creative review? First you've got to spot the nuggets of brilliance that best align to the brief. Then you've got to help shape the work in a way that uplevels it - adding value, not noise. Finally, you help clients see how this idea will transform their business. Bonus points if they feel they arrived at this decision without your aid.

Reviewing scope? First you spot whether the staffing is accurate and you've got the right teams in place. Then you shape the timeline and budget to make success possible. Finally, you sell the client on why this approach will get them where they need to go.

Every good account person is part talent scout, part coach, part closer. I can't promise you job security - nobody can anymore. But spotting opportunities, shaping outcomes, and selling vision?  These skills travel with you.

The next bottleneck nobody's talking about? PCB drill bits.
As someone who's been in the PCB design and fabrication space for over 20 years, I've watched supply chain crunches come and go, copper foil, laminates, substrate lead times. But what's happening right now with high-end drill bits is different.
AI infrastructure is driving demand for high-layer-count boards through the roof and drill bits, once treated as a commodity consumable, are now one of the sharpest pinch points in PCB manufacturing. We're looking at a projected supply-demand gap of 2.2 billion units in 2026, getting worse through 2027.
At Palpilot, we're getting ahead of this for our customers managing material allocation, prioritizing build schedules, and making sure critical programs don't get caught off guard when capacity tightens.
If you're building AI servers, networking gear, or any high-layer-count hardware and haven't had this conversation with your PCB partner yet let's talk. 🤙

Post 5｜As Features Shrink, Manufacturing Tolerance Becomes the Real Challenge When discussing AI servers, CoWoS, and advanced packaging, most conversations focus on performance, bandwidth, and I/O density. From a PCB manufacturing perspective, another challenge is growing just as quickly: The available tolerance budget is shrinking. As line widths, spacing, and via structures become smaller, variations that were once acceptable can become yield-limiting factors. For example: ✓ Material dimensional changes ✓ Layer-to-layer registration errors ✓ Drill-to-pad offset ✓ Lamination shrinkage variation ✓ Etching tolerance ⸻ What makes this challenging is that these variations rarely occur independently. A few microns from material movement, combined with a few microns from drilling and imaging, can quickly consume the entire process window. This is why registration control is often not about a single process. It is about managing the cumulative variation across the manufacturing flow. ⸻ From my experience, improving registration performance is not simply about tighter machine accuracy. It often involves: • Selecting materials with better dimensional stability • Optimizing lamination profiles • Understanding X-Y movement behavior • Applying scaling compensation based on process data The goal is not perfection. The goal is ensuring every process step moves in a predictable direction. ⸻ Key Takeaway As PCB features shrink, process capability becomes just as important as design capability. The next bottleneck nobody's talking about? PCB drill bits.
As someone who's been in the PCB design and fabrication space for over 20 years, I've watched supply chain crunches come and go, copper foil, laminates, substrate lead times. But what's happening right now with high-end drill bits is different.
AI infrastructure is driving demand for high-layer-count boards through the roof and drill bits, once treated as a commodity consumable, are now one of the sharpest pinch points in PCB manufacturing. We're looking at a projected supply-demand gap of 2.2 billion units in 2026, getting worse through 2027.
At Palpilot, we're getting ahead of this for our customers managing material allocation, prioritizing build schedules, and making sure critical programs don't get caught off guard when capacity tightens.
If you're building AI servers, networking gear, or any high-layer-count hardware and haven't had this conversation with your PCB partner yet let's talk. 🤙

AI infrastructure is driving demand for high-layer-count boards through the roof and drill bits, once treated as a commodity consumable, are now one of the sharpest pinch points in PCB manufacturing. We're looking at a projected supply-demand gap of 2.2 billion units in 2026, getting worse through 2027.
At Palpilot, we're getting ahead of this for our customers managing material allocation, prioritizing build schedules, and making sure critical programs don't get caught off guard when capacity tightens.
If you're building AI servers, networking gear, or any high-layer-count hardware and haven't had this conversation with your PCB partner yet let's talk. 🤙

🎤 ONE Tech Talk – Austausch, Impulse und neue Erfahrungen 📽️✨
 
Ein Livestream, rund 20 zugeschaltete Standorte und für mich? Eine völlig neue und ganz besondere Erfahrung. ✨
 
Die ONE Tech Talks bringen Führungskräfte zusammen, um standortübergreifend Erfahrungen zu teilen, sich über die Geschäfte hinweg zu vernetzen und voneinander zu lernen – mit dem gemeinsamen Ziel, die Zukunft von #Siemens in Richtung ONE Tech Company zu gestalten.
 
Wir starteten mit einer Reise in einem Impulsvortrag zu unseren DI Werken über disruptiven Veränderungen, neue Technologien bis hin zu AI und der Frage, wie wir als Werke im Netzwerk Tempo aufnehmen – ohne die Menschen zu verlieren.
Die Botschaft hierbei ist klar:
One Tech Company ist kein Projekt. Es ist ein Mindset.
 
💡 Was ich für mich mitgenommen habe:
 
👉 Transformation lebt von offenem Dialog und Vernetzung
👉 Perspektiven teilen schafft Klarheit und Verständnis
👉 Lernen und Verlernen sind zwei Seiten derselben Transformation
👉 Mut, Neues auszuprobieren, lohnt sich
 
Danke für den inspirierenden und offenen Austausch – vor Ort als auch virtuell! 🙌
Danke an unseren Impulsgeber, das Transformationsteam sowie allen die bei der Organisation unterstützt haben. 
 
Ein besonderes Danke an Alexandra Kleinlein für die harmonische und zugleich spaßige Co-Moderation! 🤝😊

#ONETech #ONESiemens #Transformation #Siemens

post_text: Conference Direct provides comprehensive meeting and event solutions designed to simplify the complexities of meeting planning, from initial site selection to final billing. Their approach leverages industry relationships and collective buying power to secure favorable terms and save valuable time. Core Services include: - **Site Selection & Contract Negotiation**: Utilizing a global network to identify the right venue and negotiate contracts that minimize risks, such as attrition and cancellation fees, while maximizing concessions. - **Conference Management**: Offering end-to-end logistics, including project management, floor plan design, and on-site execution. - **Housing & Registration**: Streamlining the attendee experience with integrated software solutions for room block management and seamless event registration. - **Virtual & Hybrid Events**: Providing technical expertise to create digital experiences that replicate the engagement of in-person meetings. - **Strategic Meetings Management (SMM)**: Assisting organizations in standardizing their meeting processes for better visibility into spending and ensuring corporate compliance. Strategic benefits include: - **Cost Savings**: With experience managing thousands of events annually, Conference Direct has the leverage to negotiate rates and terms that individual planners may not access. - **Risk Mitigation**: Experts focus on the details of hospitality contracts, ensuring protection against unforeseen market shifts or event disruptions. - **Resource Efficiency**: Acting as an extension of your team, they manage time-consuming administrative tasks, allowing you to concentrate on the content and strategy of your event. The company is recognized for its professional network, with associates involved in major industry milestones and a strong presence in key hubs like the Washington DC-Baltimore area.

Proper budgeting covers venue rental, catering, technology, and marketing to ensure profitability or cost recovery. Here is a breakdown of what typically comes in conference costing: 1. Essential Fixed Costs (The Foundation) These expenses remain relatively stable regardless of how many people attend. Venue Hire: The primary rental fee for the main plenary room and breakout rooms. Audio-Visual (AV) & Technology: Costs for microphones, projectors, lighting, sound systems, and IT support. Marketing & Promotion: Website creation, social media ads, graphic design, and promotional materials. Conference Software/Apps: Platforms for registration, mobile apps for attendees, or virtual conferencing tools. Speaker Fees & Expenses: Honorariums for speakers, plus their travel and accommodation. 2. Variable Costs (Per-Delegate Costs) These costs increase as more attendees sign up. Catering: The largest variable cost, including breakfast, lunch, coffee breaks, and gala dinners. Attendee Kits/Swag: Conference bags, branded merchandise, name badges, and printed programs. Delegate Materials: Lanyards, handbooks, and notebooks. Wi-Fi Fees: High-speed, high-density Wi-Fi for all attendees is often a separate, scalable expense. 3. Staffing and Human Resources Expenses associated with running the event on-site. Registration Desk Staff: Personnel to manage check-ins. Security Personnel: Protective services. Greeters & Event Staff: Seasonal causal staff for kitchen and service, stewards, and assistants. 4. Hidden and Miscellaneous Costs Easy-to-overlook expenses that can drain a budget. Contingency Fund: An essential 10%–20% buffer for unexpected costs or last-minute changes. Insurance: Coverage for event cancellation or liability. Taxes and Fees: Service charges and VAT/taxes on venue and catering. - **Virtual & Hybrid Events**: Providing technical expertise to create digital experiences that replicate the engagement of in-person meetings.

- **Resource Efficiency**: Acting as an extension of your team, they manage time-consuming administrative tasks, allowing you to concentrate on the content and strategy of your event.

It also helps you avoid common pitfalls like unclear roles, outdated wills or missed tax-saving opportunities. “Isn’t philanthropy just for billionaires?” Not at all. This is how influence moved through an educational organization.

While the 6 C-suite leaders 🟣 are tightly connected to themselves, real change depends on a small group of people operating in the shadow of the org chart. That's why they made the right decision to identify the 3% outside leadership ⚫ who influenced 87% of the whole organization.

These leaders knew that change doesn't fail because they lack commitment! It fails because influence isn't where we think it is. It's the #ThreePercentRule.

Now that their 3% were identified, this is what they did:
1. Got c-suite leaders out of their echo chambers by creating direct dialogue between them and the 3% to hear what's really happening on the ground.
2. Kept the 3% in the loop by giving them access to the "why" behind changes so they can authentically spread the word.

----

post_text: Satisficing: “Satisficing implies that a consumer, when confronted with a plethora of choices for a specific need, will select a product or service that is “good enough”, rather than expending effort and resources on finding the best possible or optimal choice.” I believe we see this everyday, in fact, do this everyday. Choosing a lesser, easier, and safer path instead of riskier, harder, and uncertain path. It’s fear of failure. Logically, choosing satisficing makes sense, because what if a negative result of a risky decision causes someone to lose his or her job? Every men and women want to take care of their family, pay their bills, and go on vacation, which is the reason for satisficing. Now, it is easy to justify, but what if everyone was willing to settle? It is easy to see in product recalls, failed accounting practices and scandals, unsafe work environments, faulty electrical, and the list goings on. Catastrophic events often occur because it was “good enough.” The question remains, will you take a risk and take the path of the most resistance, overcome fear to become something great? History is full of great heroes who weren’t going to settle for good enough, Martin Luther King Jr., Abraham Lincoln, Benjamin Franklin, Margaret Thatcher, Jackie Robinson, Lou Gehrig, Howard Hughes, and the list goes on. So… Will you satisfice?

It's was disappointing for me and HR both because she was good candidate.

post_text: It Begins "Tim, we want to double your salary and also give you this sign-on bonus in the same amount. You will get an equity stake in the new venture. We are supplying $10 million up front and there is more behind that. All you need to do is build a company that will decrease the incidence of chronic disease. Not slow the growth. Decrease it. In other words, make it so people are healthier so fewer and fewer will need medical diagnostics and treatments. Free up our hospitals and clinics and medical staff to treat diseases where medical intervention is the only way. When can you start?" That was my dream last night... well it was a dream until I woke up and had time to think about it. Yesterday I read a very sad article by Mandi Bishop , Quantifying the Patient Experience in Healthcare: One LEAN Expert Calculates Her "Care"'s Value . Mandi highlighted the frustrating and agonizing last two years of Jess Jacobs' life. Jess died at age 29 from rare diseases that required medical attention from institutions that are inundated and inefficient. I took a quick look at some of the links Mandi included where Jess documented her observations of waste. Lean Six Sigma expert, Mark Graban, showcased Jess' work in an article RIP Jess Jacobs (#UnicornJess): The Healthcare System Wasted Her Time, But She Inspires Many to Fix the System that had, for me, one particularly gut-wrenching line in a fabric of tragedy: "She calculated the value-added percentage for outpatient visits to be 16.6% and 1.7% for inpatient care." This was the inverse of how Jess should have experienced healthcare and starting a venture to fix it would be no picnic. The Nightmare Jess already lived the nightmare. Other patients experience it now. Clinicians experience it daily... until some finally retire, leave medicine, or worse. So maybe my dream offer is really just part of this nightmare. Like Jess, I have a green belt in Six Sigma... Design for Six Sigma actually. Basically, Design for Six Sigma is for something brand new or when something is so broken the process must be invented anew. This sounds about right. Let's start with a definition. Six Sigma is about reducing defects. Borrowing from isixsigma.com : A defect is defined as any part of a product or service that: -does not meet customer specifications or requirements, or -causes customer dissatisfaction, or -does not fulfill the functional or physical requirements. Jess was obviously dissatisfied and the process was nowhere near meeting her (or any reasonable person's) expectations or requirements. There were undoubtedly defects in the service for her healthcare. So let's back up and look at health . The World Health Organization (WHO) has a pretty simple definition of health : Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. What if a "defect" in the US healthcare system was not just the wasted months of Jess' short life, waiting in lines and waiting for clinical attention. What if the defect in the US healthcare system was not just the bureaucracy that pummels and burns out clinicians? What if a defect in the US healthcare system was every human being who shows up for medical care when more attention to other factors that determine health would have kept them healthy? The Dream The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (RWJF) has partnered with the University of Wisconsin's Population Health Institute to develop a weighted impact of various "health factors" based on reviews of health data for every US county. They found that "clinical care" accounts for 20% of a person's health! Yet, the US healthcare system spends over $3 trillion annually focused on clinical care and is inefficient / ineffective for today's growing epidemic of chronic diseases which represent 86% of the $3 trillion. Source: http://www.rwjf.org/content/dam/farm/reports/reports/2015/rwjf418649 What if the waste that Jess found in the healthcare system during her final two years could be dramatically reduced and the human suffering associated with so many chronic diseases could be avoided while saving billions of dollars? That is a dream! OK, dream benefactor. I accept the offer. post_text_html:
It Begins


"Tim, we want to double your salary and also give you this sign-on bonus in the same amount.  You will get an equity stake in the new venture.  We are supplying $10 million up front and there is more behind that.  All you need to do is build a company that will decrease the incidence of chronic disease.  Not slow the growth.  Decrease it. In other words, make it so people are healthier so fewer and fewer will need medical diagnostics and treatments.  Free up our hospitals and clinics and medical staff to treat diseases where medical intervention is the only way. When can you start?"


That was my dream last night... well it was a dream until I woke up and had time to think about it. Yesterday I read a very sad article by Mandi Bishop, Quantifying the Patient Experience in Healthcare: One LEAN Expert Calculates Her "Care"'s Value. Mandi highlighted the frustrating and agonizing last two years of Jess Jacobs' life.  Jess died at age 29 from rare diseases that required medical attention from institutions that are inundated and inefficient.


I took a quick look at some of the links Mandi included where Jess documented her observations of waste.  Lean Six Sigma expert, Mark Graban, showcased Jess' work in an article RIP Jess Jacobs (#UnicornJess): The Healthcare System Wasted Her Time, But She Inspires Many to Fix the System that had, for me, one particularly gut-wrenching line in a fabric of tragedy: "She calculated the value-added percentage for outpatient visits to be 16.6% and 1.7% for inpatient care."  This was the inverse of how Jess should have experienced healthcare and starting a venture to fix it would be no picnic.


The Nightmare


Jess already lived the nightmare. Other patients experience it now. Clinicians experience it daily... until some finally retire, leave medicine, or worse.  So maybe my dream offer is really just part of this nightmare. 


Like Jess, I have a green belt in Six Sigma... Design for Six Sigma actually. Basically, Design for Six Sigma is for something brand new or when something is so broken the process must be invented anew.  This sounds about right.


Let's start with a definition.  Six Sigma is about reducing defects.  Borrowing from isixsigma.com:


A defect is defined as any part of a product or service that:
-does not meet customer specifications or requirements, or
-causes customer dissatisfaction, or
-does not fulfill the functional or physical requirements.


Jess was obviously dissatisfied and the process was nowhere near meeting her (or any reasonable person's) expectations or requirements.  There were undoubtedly defects in the service for her healthcare.  So let's back up and look at health.


The World Health Organization (WHO) has a pretty simple definition of health: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.


What if a "defect" in the US healthcare system was not just the wasted months of Jess' short life, waiting in lines and waiting for clinical attention. What if the defect in the US healthcare system was not just the bureaucracy that pummels and burns out clinicians? What if a defect in the US healthcare system was every human being who shows up for medical care when more attention to other factors that determine health would have kept them healthy?


The Dream


The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (RWJF) has partnered with the University of Wisconsin's Population Health Institute to develop a weighted impact of various "health factors" based on reviews of health data for every US county.  They found that "clinical care" accounts for 20% of a person's health! Yet, the US healthcare system spends over $3 trillion annually focused on clinical care and is inefficient / ineffective for today's growing epidemic of chronic diseases which represent 86% of the $3 trillion.





Source: http://www.rwjf.org/content/dam/farm/reports/reports/2015/rwjf418649 


What if the waste that Jess found in the healthcare system during her final two years could be dramatically reduced and the human suffering associated with so many chronic diseases could be avoided while saving billions of dollars? That is a dream!


OK, dream benefactor. I accept the offer. Let's build something to keep people healthy and reduce chronic disease, let clinicians practice medicine, and let patients like Jess no longer cry out:



There’s no reason that I spent two solid months (1540 hours, 64.2 days) of this year waiting instead of healing.

So, please, stop wasting my time. Stop wasting my life.

Tim Perry, MPA, MS, CPHIMS, PCMH CCE, CISSP is a visionary Chief Information Officer who has a deep passion for transforming and improving healthcare. Tim is blessed with a wonderful wife and two inspiring children. Tim has practiced Taiji Chuan for over 15 years and enjoys cooking wholesome (and easy) meals.

A strong focus on Health and Safety has always been a top priority of the Nordex Group, and this week marks 6 months since we launched the #SafetyTogether campaign. As we further improve our safety culture, it is important for all of us to remain mindful of best practices and behaviors when it comes to keeping ourselves and others safe in the workplace.

For that reason, our #TeamNordex HSE specialists identified and analyzed the main risks and previous incidents across all our activities and used this to develop 10 Life Saving Rules. These 10 Life Saving Rules underline our commitment to safety and, more importantly, act as a safeguard for our employees and subcontractors moving forward.

Each rule addresses a specific topic as part of a defined minimum acceptable HSE standard which must not be broken. This is the key message that the 10 Life Saving Rules aim to firmly reinforce within our Nordex Group safety culture and all our mindsets. 

These rules are fundamental to the safety of everyone working as part of and alongside our company, and it is our duty to uphold them in everything we do here at the Nordex Group.

A strong focus on Health and Safety has always been a top priority of the Nordex Group, and this week marks 6 months since we launched the #SafetyTogether campaign. As we further improve our safety culture, it is important for all of us to remain mindful of best practices and behaviors when it comes to keeping ourselves and others safe in the workplace.

For that reason, our #TeamNordex HSE specialists identified and analyzed the main risks and previous incidents across all our activities and used this to develop 10 Life Saving Rules. These 10 Life Saving Rules underline our commitment to safety and, more importantly, act as a safeguard for our employees and subcontractors moving forward.

Each rule addresses a specific topic as part of a defined minimum acceptable HSE standard which must not be broken. This is the key message that the 10 Life Saving Rules aim to firmly reinforce within our Nordex Group safety culture and all our mindsets.

These rules are fundamental to the safety of everyone working as part of and alongside our company, and it is our duty to uphold them in everything we do here at the Nordex Group.

#SafetyTogether #SafetyFirst #LSR #TeamNordex

🤝 Visite du Directeur général de l’RS La Réunion au sein de la Fondation Père Favron

La semaine dernière, la Fondation Père Favron a eu l’honneur d’accueillir, Jean-Jacques Coiplet, Directeur général de l’ARS La Réunion, pour une visite de terrain au cœur de nos établissements.

➡️ Cette rencontre a débuté par un déjeuner au restaurant d’application L’Atelier à Saint-Pierre, privatisé pour l’occasion, illustrant notre engagement en faveur de l’insertion, de la formation et du savoir-faire de nos équipes et des travailleurs handicapés.
L’après‑midi s’est poursuivie sur le site de Bois d’Olives avec :
➡️ un temps d’échanges avec les administrateurs de la Fondation autour des actualités, des enjeux et des perspectives de la Fondation,
➡️ et la visite de l’EHPAD de Bois d’Olives et la présentation de nos dispositifs d’accueil de jour et d'accueil de nuit ainsi que le service d'accueil mobile (SAM), notre camping‑car, véritable outil "d’aller‑vers" au service des personnes âgées isolées dans les Hauts du secteur Sud.

Tout au long de ces visites, le Directeur général a pu échanger avec les bénéficiaires et les professionnels, au plus près des réalités du terrain, des pratiques et des besoins.

👉 Ces temps de rencontre sont essentiels pour renforcer le dialogue, partager une vision commune et continuer à construire ensemble des réponses adaptées, humaines et innovantes.

🙏 Merci à l’ARS La Réunion pour son écoute, son intérêt et son engagement aux côtés de la Fondation Père Favron.

Agence Régionale de Santé La Réunion - ARS La Réunion

post_text: The "IIoT", a common buzzphrase as of late within the industrial world, tends to create more confusion than answers. What does IIoT actually mean? The concept of IoT, or Internet of Things, is simple at it's core: allow machines to communicate with one another on a variety of parameters and process information. In practice, we often find this concept to be easier said than done. IIoT is the industrial version of this, focusing on integrating equipment and machinery to better operate facilities, improve production and optimize processes. Many manufacturing plants have initiatives to move further into IIoT by implementing high tech devices and machines for condition monitoring, conducting expensive integrations and program roll outs, or by retrofitting existing infrastructure with WiFi enabled devices through an elaborate wiring schematic. Integrating new, high tech equipment into existing infrastructure has created a mountain of tasks for many plants; determining best applications, running conduit or getting special permission from IT to access the networks, securing and managing third party WiFi or cellular plans, sourcing and purchasing software to analyze the data pulled from machines, and training someone in-house to make sense of that data. All of this leads to increased wait time and cost for the plant, while machines continue operations as usual. There are other options out there, just do a quick search of "Remote Condition Monitoring" and you will get page after page of expensive, comlicated equipment meant to monitor and diagnose machine health and early fault modes. In my opinion there is no end all be all system, even with the most expensive and complicated system for 24/7 condition monitoring, there will always be a human element to diagnosing machine troubles. Look at it this way; when your car's check engine light comes on, you don't go out and buy a new transmission without having a qualified mechanic inspect your vehicle. You may be mechanically inclined yourself, or have an OBDII scanner, to check codes or troubleshoot by yourself, similar to RCA in any maintenance plan. These are additional tools to supplement, not replace, the human element of diagnosis and troubleshooting. I believe the concept of PdM and IIoT should be leveraged to help point your team in the right direction, not be the absolute voice of reason when it comes to diagnosing faults or failures in your plant. This is the true essence of PdM and condition monitoring; looking for trends in machine health or data points that stick out from the norm that indicate decreased efficiency and life of the machine. This data is then analyzed and used in diagnosing the issue, taking corrective action if needed. In the example above, data was leveraged to identify and correct a misalignment on a motor driven pump. A quick fix when the data is available and easy to digest (in this case vibration monitoring), but without the insight into machine health, this issue could have escalated into machine failure or degradation of life. This is just one example of a real world scenario where vibration monitoring helped a plant maximize their uptime and prevent unexpected machine failure. If your plant is on the road to zero downtime, focusing on PdM, IIoT initiatives, or if you're just curious about remote vibration sensors and condition monitoring, I'd love to connect and share our experiences here at ProAxion and answer any questions I can.

post_text: 6.Planning 6.1 Actions to address risks and opportunities This clause replaced “preventive action” in the 2015 revision of the 14001 standard. The standard states that the organization should establish, implement, and maintain the processes required to address the requirements of the whole of the planning section itself. When planning the EMS, considerations need to be made on the context of the organization (section 4.1) and the needs and expectations of interested parties (section 4.2), as well as the scope of the EMS. Risk and opportunity must be considered in respect of these elements, as well as legal and regulatory issues, and the organization’s environmental aspects themselves. This outcome needs to ensure that the EMS can meet its intended outcomes and objectives, that any external factors that may affect performance are avoided, and that continual improvement can be achieved. In terms of emergency situations, the organization is required to determine any situations that may occur and have a resulting environmental impact. Again, it is vital that documented information is retained concerning the risks and opportunities considered and addressed in the planning phase in order to satisfy the terms of the clause. 6.1.2 Environmental aspects ISO 14001:2015 asks organizations to consider, from a life cycle perspective – which includes carriage, disposal, and recycling as well as production – all environmental aspects of its products, services, and activities that are deemed to be within the organization’s control. Changes or planned future changes to services also have to be taken into account, as do any abnormal situations that may arise that are reasonable for the organization to predict – for example, if you are about to launch a new product that needs radically new packaging materials. Again, the organization needs to maintain documented information on this clause and its elements, and communication to the appropriate levels with effective frequency needs to be planned and undertaken. In terms of documented information, if you ensure that all actual and associated impacts, the criteria you use to define them, and your significant environmental impacts are documented, then you will satisfy the terms of this clause. 6.1.3 Compliance obligations This is a relatively straightforward, but obviously vital part of the ISO 14001:2015 standard. The organization must decide what obligations are related to its environmental aspects and how to best access them, decide how they apply to the organization, and take them into consideration when establishing, operating, and delivering continual improvement through the EMS. Documented evidence needs to be recorded for these obligations, also. 6.1.4 Planning actions In this clause, the standard states that the organization shall plan to take actions to address its environmental aspects, risks and opportunities, and compliance obligations, all of which we have discussed above. These also need to be implemented into the organization’s EMS and associated business processes. The task of evaluating the effectiveness of these actions also must be considered, with technological, financial, and operational considerations all taken into account. 6.2 Environmental objectives and planning to achieve them 6.2.1 Environmental objectives The standard advises that environmental objectives should be established at appropriate levels and intervals, having considered the identified environmental aspects, risk and opportunities, and compliance obligations. The characteristics of the set objectives are important, too; they need to be consistent with the organization’s environmental policy, measurable where possible, able to be monitored, communicated effectively, and be such that they can be updated when circumstances require. Once more, it is mandatory that documented information is kept outlining this process and its outputs. 6.2.2 Planning to achieve environmental objectives The standard advises on the elements that need to be determined to ensure objectives can be achieved. This can be thought of in terms of what needs to be done, when it needs to be done by, what resources are required to achieve it, who is responsible for the objectives being achieved, how results are to be measured and progress ensured, and consideration on how these objectives can be implemented into existing business systems 7.Support 7.1 Resources Simply put, the standard advises the organization that resources to achieve stated objectives and show continual improvement must be made available. 7.2 Competence Employee competence must meet the terms of the ISO 14001:2015 standard by ensuring that the people given responsibility for EMS tasks are capable and confident. Related to this, it stands to reason that the experience, training, and/or education of the individual must be of the required standard, and that any training required is identified and delivered – with measurable actions taken externally or internally to ensure that this level of competence exists. Predictably, this process and its outputs need to be recorded as documented information for the EMS. 7.3 Awareness Awareness is closely related to competence in the standard. Employees must be made aware of the environmental policy and its contents, any current and future impacts that may affect their tasks, what their personal performance means to the EMS and its objectives, including the positives or improved performance, and what the implications of poor performance may be to the EMS 7.4 Communication 7.4.1 General Processes for internal and external communication need to be established and recorded as documented information within the EMS. The key elements that need to be decided, actioned, and recorded are what needs to be communicated, how it should be done, who needs to receive the communication, and at what intervals it should be done. It should be noted here that any communication outputs should be consistent with related information and content generated by the EMS for the sake of consistency. 7.4.2 Internal communication The standard advises the organization that information should be communicated at various levels and with various frequencies as deemed suitable, and to ensure that the nature and frequency of communication allows continual improvement to result from the communication process itself. 7.4.3 External communication Once again, the organization is advised by the standard to ensure that communication relevant to the EMS takes place as per the established process, with the goal of ensuring compliance obligations and objectives are met. 7.5 Documented information 7.5.1 General “Documented information,” which you will have seen mentioned several times during this guide, marks another change implemented in the 2015 standard. The change is designed to allow each organization to have the ability to shape documented information to their own requirements in general, with the exception of the mandatory components mentioned specifically in the standard and, therefore, this guide. The ISO 14001:2015 standard advises us that the EMS should include all documented information that it declares mandatory, and also anything viewed as critical to the EMS and its operation. It should also be noted that the amount of documented information that an organization requires will differ according to the size, operating sector, and complexity of compliance obligations faced by the business. 7.5.2 Creating and updating The standard advises that documentation created by the EMS should be available and fit for purpose where and when needed, reasonably protected against damage or loss of integrity and identity, and the processes of distribution, retention, access, retrieval, preservation and storage, control and disposition are adequately provided for. It should be noted that documented information from external sources should be similarly controlled and handled, and that viewing and editing access levels should be carefully considered and controlled. 7.5.3 Control of documented information The standard advises that documentation created by the EMS should be available and fit for purpose where and when needed, reasonably protected against damage or loss of integrity and identity, and the processes of distribution, retention, access, retrieval, preservation and storage, control and disposition are adequately provided for. It should be noted that documented information from external sources should be similarly controlled and handled, and that viewing and editing access levels should be carefully considered and controlled.

July is BIPOC Mental Health Awareness Month — and too many Black women are silently suffering behind “I’m fine.”

The cultural weight of the Strong Black Woman ideal has led us to normalize high-functioning depression and anxiety. We keep smiling and achieving, even when we’re breaking inside.

✨ That’s why I’m hosting Sis, You Good? — A Soul Care Experience for the Strong Friend on July 19 in Houston.

Join me for an unforgettable evening of:
🔥 Real talk on the Strong Black Woman Syndrome
🔥 Guided journaling + affirmation rituals
🔥 Deep sisterhood circles
🔥 And yes… a Twerk Out the Trauma session so we can literally shake it off! 🪩🍑

This isn’t just another wellness event or group therapy. It’s a sacred space designed for high-achieving Black women to drop the cape, release what we’ve been carrying, and reconnect with ourselves and each other. 

If you’re the friend everyone leans on, but you don’t feel like you have anywhere to lean — this space was created for you.

🗓️ Early bird sold out! GA + VIP tickets still available.

#100DaysOfCode | Days 7–20 Update
Continuing my #100DaysOfCode DSA Challenge
From Jan 30 to Feb 12, I maintained consistency and focused on strengthening core Data Structures & Algorithms concepts.

Problems Covered:
🔹 Arrays & Two Pointers
-Two Sum
-Move Zeroes
-Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag Algorithm)
-Rearrange Array Elements by Sign
🔹 Bit Manipulation
-Single Number
🔹 Math / Logical Thinking
-Missing Number
🔹 Greedy Algorithms
-Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
🔹 Dynamic Programming
-Maximum Subarray (Kadane’s Algorithm)
🔹 Hashing
-Longest Consecutive Sequence
🔹 Trees
-Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
-Lowest Common Ancestor

Key Learnings:
- Converting brute-force approaches into optimized O(n) solutions
- Recognizing common problem-solving patterns
- Improving recursion clarity in tree problems
- Writing cleaner and more structured Java code
Day by day, I’m building stronger algorithmic thinking.
Still learning. Still improving.
On to the next phase of the challenge

post_text: Every facilitation room is developmentally diverse—even when the topic, role, or level looks the same. Starting in 1 Hour Friday, Jan 16th, Noon Central Time: Virtual - 45 Minutes LinkedIn Live Event (Please RSVP) https://lnkd.in/gHZm3tdb Participants don’t experience learning the same way. Facilitators don’t experience the room the same way either. In this live session, we’ll explore developmental diversity and why it matters so much for learning and transformation. First, we’ll look at how people at different developmental orientations experience facilitation: what feels supportive what feels threatening what feels confusing or clarifying what kinds of struggle help—or hinder—learning Then we’ll turn the lens back on us as facilitators. Because our own developmental orientation quietly shapes: what we notice in the room what feels urgent or uncomfortable when we step in—and when we struggle to hold back This session isn’t about labels or stages. It’s about understanding why the same moment in a room can feel productive to one person and unsettling to another—and how that difference affects learning. In the world of training and facilitation, a subtle question often appears beneath the surface: Is it more important to focus on expression — being authentic as a facilitator — or on impression — how participants perceive us? The answer is clear: both are essential, and neither works alone. Expression is about authenticity. Research and thought leadership from Brené Brown highlight that authenticity builds trust and psychological safety — two foundations of effective learning. When facilitators express ideas genuinely, show curiosity, and respond honestly, participants feel safe to engage, ask questions, and share real challenges. However, facilitation is also a performative role. According to Erving Goffman’s Impression Management theory, people naturally form judgments based on presence, communication style, clarity, and confidence. Studies cited by Harvard Business Review show that first impressions strongly influence perceived credibility and learning engagement — often within the first few minutes of a session. In training rooms, overemphasizing expression without managing impression can lead to confusion or loss of authority. Being “authentic” but unclear, unstructured, or unaware of group dynamics can weaken learning impact. On the other hand, focusing only on impression — polished slides, perfect delivery, controlled persona — without authentic expression results in shallow engagement and low transfer of learning. Effective facilitators master the balance. They express themselves with authenticity, while being intentional about how that expression lands. They adapt tone, language, pacing, and examples based on the participants’ context, culture, and energy. In facilitation, expression gives depth. Impression gives access. Learning happens when both align. Every facilitation room is developmentally diverse—even when the topic, role, or level looks the same. Starting in 1 Hour

Friday, Jan 16th, Noon Central Time: Virtual - 45 Minutes

LinkedIn Live Event (Please RSVP)
https://lnkd.in/gHZm3tdb

Participants don’t experience learning the same way.
Facilitators don’t experience the room the same way either.

In this live session, we’ll explore developmental diversity and why it matters so much for learning and transformation.

First, we’ll look at how people at different developmental orientations experience facilitation:
what feels supportive
what feels threatening
what feels confusing or clarifying
what kinds of struggle help—or hinder—learning

Then we’ll turn the lens back on us as facilitators.

Because our own developmental orientation quietly shapes:
what we notice in the room
what feels urgent or uncomfortable
when we step in—and when we struggle to hold back

This session isn’t about labels or stages.
It’s about understanding why the same moment in a room can feel productive to one person and unsettling to another—and how that difference affects learning.

By the end of the session, you’ll have greater clarity around:
why facilitation can feel heavier than expected
how developmental diversity influences responsibility, struggle, and silence
and what actually belongs to you as a facilitator—and what doesn’t

This is a conversation for facilitators who want learning to stick, not just land—and who are ready to see the room (and themselves) more clearly.

No slides.
No techniques.
Just distinctions that change how facilitation works.

🏠⚠️ 𝗪𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗵𝗼𝗺𝗲? It’s easier than you think! Taking a few proactive steps can help protect your property and ensure a healthy living environment. Here are some key tips to get you started:

1️⃣ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗶𝗱𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝘀 – Keep it below 60% to stop mold from thriving.
2️⃣ 𝗙𝗶𝘅 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗸𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗹𝘆 – Water is mold's best friend, so act fast!
3️⃣ 𝗘𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 – Especially in damp areas like bathrooms and kitchens.
4️⃣ 𝗖𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗿𝘆 𝘄𝗲𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀 quickly to avoid moisture buildup.

Don't wait until it's too late—stay ahead of mold with simple yet effective precautions. Ready to keep your home safe, dry, and mold-free? 🌟

I’m beyond excited to share that I’ve just started a new role as Development & Communications Manager for Big Bend Conservancy!

Big Bend Conservancy is the official philanthropic partner of Big Bend National Park, working to preserve, enrich, and conserve the park’s incredible landscapes, wildlife, water, and cultural heritage. We directly support critical initiatives in Big Bend National Park and along the Rio Grande Wild & Scenic River, in partnership with the National Park Service.

This park has shaped so much of my conservation journey, including some of my first-ever fieldwork! Some of my favorite memories from A&M come from research trips to Big Bend, where I helped collect park visitation data as a part of Texas A&M Department of Rangeland, Wildlife and Fisheries Management's Human Dimensions of Natural Resources lab.

I feel incredibly lucky to return in a new role and give back to a place that has meant so much to me and to so many others. 💚🌄

This week’s 40 for 40 features Jon Thorson, CEO of USM North America, who reminds us that great design doesn’t just look good—it lasts. His pick for the most iconic design of the past 40 years? The USM Credenza. Iconic, adaptable, and part of The Museum of Modern Art's permanent collection, it’s a piece that proves longevity is innovation.

Jon sees a shift happening—from unchecked consumerism to a more conscious “buy-better” mindset. As our needs evolve, he believes the future of design lies in flexible systems that grow with us—products and spaces that adapt, endure, and solve problems collaboratively.

What designs have stood the test of time in your world?

Some students believe boot camps and quick skills training can replace higher education. While this might work for landing a job in the short term, it’s not a sustainable long-term strategy.

What happens if the specific skill they learn becomes obsolete? Do they have the ability to adapt and learn a new profession on their own?

This is where higher education plays a critical role. It doesn’t just teach you a trade, it equips you with critical thinking skills, adaptability, and the ability to continue learning throughout life.

Higher education prepares you to be a productive, resilient member of society, no matter how the world changes.

It doesn’t just teach you a trade, it equips you with critical thinking skills, adaptability, and the ability to continue learning throughout life. I’ve learned that for many Black women — myself included — depression doesn’t always look like sadness. Sometimes it looks like overworking. We cope by staying busy. By saying “yes” to everything. By showing up even when we’re running on empty. Because slowing down feels unsafe — like we might finally have to face the heaviness we’ve been carrying. In the workplace, this often gets misunderstood. Instead of being seen as a sign of struggle, it’s praised. “You’re so hardworking.” “You always deliver.” “You’re so strong.” What people don’t realise is that sometimes, that ‘strength’ is survival. It’s the way we hold ourselves together when we’re falling apart inside. And yet, when you keep performing at that level, colleagues and managers assume you can handle more. The pile of work grows, the pressure builds, and the silence around mental health — especially for Black professionals — deepens. One of the biggest takeaways from networking with my training buddies this week was this:

If you’re removed from the operational side of a business, how well do you really understand it?

Systems, dashboards, and KPIs are valuable — but they only tell part of the story.

My advice for anyone wanting to get ahead: spend time on the warehouse floor. Shadow every function for a week — goods in, picking, packing, despatch, and fault finding.

You’ll gain a level of product knowledge, process understanding, and operational awareness that no spreadsheet or computer screen can provide.

The best commercial and operational decisions are made by people who understand how the business truly works from the ground up.

#pharmaceuticals #medicine #warehousing #operations

Lowest bidder changes for #DubaiMetro Blue Line.

The team of Spain’s #FCC, Beijing-based China State Construction Engineering Corporation (#CSCEC) and France’s #Alstom has emerged as the low bidder for the Blue Line extension to the Dubai Metro network after revised #bids were submitted on 21 November.

The team submitted an offer of AED19.8bn after the project client, Dubai’s Roads & Transport Authority (#RTA), asked bidders to submit proposals with alternatives to reduce the price.

The consortium’s price is nearly 18% lower than its original base offer of AED24.1bn submitted on 8 October.

The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Railway (also called the Gulf Railway or Gulf Cooperation Council Railway) is a regional infrastructure project to link all six GCC countries (Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Oman) by rail. Kuwait Times+2 Gulf News+2 The total planned length is about 2,177 km (≈ 2,100-2,200 km). Arab News+2 Gulf News+2 The railway is intended for both passenger and freight transport. Kuwait Times+2 Railway Supply+2 Speeds planned for passenger trains are up to 200 km/h, and freight somewhat lower (often ~120 km/h) on many sections. Kuwait Times+1 Kuwait-to-UAE (and via) Route & Key Sections For the specific connection between Kuwait and the UAE, here is how Kuwait’s segment fits in, and how the UAE portion is developing, plus how the network links up. Kuwait’s section: Kuwait signed a contract in April 2025 with Turkish consultancy Proyapi to design its section of the GCC Railway. GulfBase+3 Arab News+3 MEP Middle East+3 That section is 111 km long, from Al-Shadadiya (where a major station will be built, on a ~2 million m² site) to Nuwaiseeb on the border with Saudi Arabia. MEP Middle East+2 Arab News+2 The design and planning phase includes route mapping, soil testing, preparing tenders, etc. The advisory/design contract value is about KD 2.5 million (~US$8.1 million). MEP Middle East+2 Arab News+2 UAE and adjacent sections: The UAE is pushing forward with its Etihad Rail project, which is a key section in the network. GCC Railway+2 Kuwait Times+2 Also relevant is the Hafeet Rail project (UAE-Oman link, from Abu Dhabi to Sohar) which will connect into the wider GCC system. Kuwait Times+2 Gulf News+2 Timeline & Status The goal is for completion by 2030. Gulf News+2 Arab News+2 As of 2025, just moving into the design/planning phase in Kuwait. Terrain and geography: Some segments may pass through difficult environments (deserts, borders etc.). Lowest bidder changes for #DubaiMetro Blue Line.

The team of Spain’s #FCC, Beijing-based China State Construction Engineering Corporation (#CSCEC) and France’s #Alstom has emerged as the low bidder for the Blue Line extension to the Dubai Metro network after revised #bids were submitted on 21 November.

The team submitted an offer of AED19.8bn after the project client, Dubai’s Roads & Transport Authority (#RTA), asked bidders to submit proposals with alternatives to reduce the price.

The consortium’s price is nearly 18% lower than its original base offer of AED24.1bn submitted on 8 October.

post_text: Had a say on Amul's latest topical toon riffing on the 'Coldplay-Astronomer' news, for Financial Express, thanks to Christina Moniz . I believe it was in poor taste (pun unintended, considering it is Amul!). While a few brands have used the 'Coldplay scandal' theme (including IKEA Singapore), they seem to think that they are merely riffing on the two people in the concert (the CEO and the HR head). But the ads also, unintentionally, bring to mind people who are affected by this scandal - Andy's and Kristin's families. It's one thing for Astronomer (the company, and another affected party) for making light of the scandal by bringing in Gwyneth Paltrow (Chris Martin's ex-wife) as 'temporary spokesperson', but entirely another for unrelated entities like Amul to make a joke out of it. For someone like me who has only seen Amul ads being praised, to see a whole lot of people denouncing an Amul ad, particularly on LinkedIn and Twitter/X, was quite a surprise. But this should be par for the course for Amul, though. They produce so many topical ads month after month, year after year, and only a few get talked about. A whole lot of them are very average and do not get talked about at all. And a few of them also attract outrage. In terms of lessons for other brands who want to use topical news for social media content, the first, and most important part of a moment marketing campaign is to consider multiple viewpoints before taking it live. Always designate someone in the team as the 'compulsive naysayer' (or, 'Devil's Advocate') and ask them to counter the theme or idea as logically as possible. Then consider if your campaign theme can still be defended, or does the counter seem stronger, more meaningful? This is a standard operating procedure in PR agencies already, for media interactions and press conferences where the PR agency thinks up the worst possible/most antagonistic questions and gives the client spokesperson directional responses. This worst-case-scenario planning helps deal with the fires before they could happen or avoid a fire entirely. #crisis #crisiscommunications #PR #advertising #momentmarketing

post_text_html:
Had a say on Amul's latest topical toon riffing on the 'Coldplay-Astronomer' news, for Financial Express, thanks to Christina Moniz. I believe it was in poor taste (pun unintended, considering it is Amul!). While a few brands have used the 'Coldplay scandal' theme (including IKEA Singapore), they seem to think that they are merely riffing on the two people in the concert (the CEO and the HR head). But the ads also, unintentionally, bring to mind people who are affected by this scandal - Andy's and Kristin's families. It's one thing for Astronomer (the company, and another affected party) for making light of the scandal by bringing in Gwyneth Paltrow (Chris Martin's ex-wife) as 'temporary spokesperson', but entirely another for unrelated entities like Amul to make a joke out of it.

For someone like me who has only seen Amul ads being praised, to see a whole lot of people denouncing an Amul ad, particularly on LinkedIn and Twitter/X, was quite a surprise. But this should be par for the course for Amul, though. They produce so many topical ads month after month, year after year, and only a few get talked about. A whole lot of them are very average and do not get talked about at all. And a few of them also attract outrage.

In terms of lessons for other brands who want to use topical news for social media content, the first, and most important part of a moment marketing campaign is to consider multiple viewpoints before taking it live. Always designate someone in the team as the 'compulsive naysayer' (or, 'Devil's Advocate') and ask them to counter the theme or idea as logically as possible. Then consider if your campaign theme can still be defended, or does the counter seem stronger, more meaningful? This is a standard operating procedure in PR agencies already, for media interactions and press conferences where the PR agency thinks up the worst possible/most antagonistic questions and gives the client spokesperson directional responses. This worst-case-scenario planning helps deal with the fires before they could happen or avoid a fire entirely.

post_text: In this Knowledge Economy that we are in, it is pertinent that we strive everyday to learn and commit ourselves to keep learning. Awareness - Be aware of where you lack in knowledge or skills, then decide where you want to improve. Remember, one of the signs of being wise is admitting how much knowledge you do not know (or even aware of). Develop a deep hunger for knowledge. This is a crucial first step - a MUST. New knowledge can be anything - it could be Shakespeare or it could also be the history of lasagna. Essentially everything is knowledge, so to speak. BE OPEN MINDED - You cannot learn, unlearn and learn new things and expand your brain if reject everything you read or hear. USE GOOD SOURCES - Using google scholar and even Wikipedia is better than random pieces on random internet websites. Also use Quora, the community is very knowledgeable. READ, READ, READ. Book, Newspaper, FB News, Twitter, anything you can get your hands on. Currently, I am building a map in my brain of knowledge of the world - through time and ideas. So what happened 65 million years ago? What happened 100,000 years ago..and I am creating this timeline and a mind palace of this knowledge. That will help with organization, and more importantly with remembering all the stuff. Gather Ancient Knowledge - Books on Ancient philosophy, ancient history, ancient religions, ancient science. Why? Because they form the bedrock of much of the recent knowledge. Get a basis for the foundation. Now you do not have to read the “actual” books but rather get a quick version or a summary version if you would like. Summary texts also help you to identify where/which you want to follow deeper and then you can read the seminal text e.g. you realise you love Descartes’ idea on life or want to delve into Plato’s ideas, so then you read his Meditations or Plato’s Republic. Also, this helps to build the history of human kind in your world. Watch TedTalks - Why? They cut down massively the time it takes to read multiple books into 18 minute segments on Youtube. They are free too! Plus, you can get hordes of information quickly and also get with exposed to new researchers and cutting-edge thoughts in a certain field. Science - Pick up any high-school or college (depending on your current knowledge) science textbook on physics, biology, chemistry and environmental science - they will help you immensely to understand the world around us. It will also help with the research lingo. On a side note, you realise for example cooking is so similar to a chemistry experiment. Watch Documentaries - Instead of gorging on mindless TV, I watch 2 documentaries a day. Documentaries make stories come alive and they are usually (not always) done by people passionate and highly knowledgeable about a certain field. Then watch another or few other documentaries under the same topic - to see if they contradict or agree with each other. Documentaries also help me remember things easily because I can put names and faces to the stories I have heard. Google - any question you have. In the middle of the night you want to know if shrimps have bones (random..the things I think about sometimes) or weird things such as the US Military Daily Schedule, just Google it. And try to do it immediately or write it down if you are studying/working. It is good to find answers to random questions that pop up and expand your knowledge base. Google Scholar - Use Google Scholar for deeper research, not just for assignments. It has access to gazillion journals and amazing research. Maybe I am the only person who reads journal articles for fun. In the long run it will also boost your research capabilities such as how to use key words to come up with better searches. Social Media - Use Social Media to your advantage by ‘liking’, ‘following’ and ‘connecting’ with insightful people and pages be it on Facebook, Quora, Twitter, Instagram and LinkedIn. I actually get so much knowledge about the business world (e.g. upcoming tech or Big Data) from LinkedIn. LinkedIn information will also help with career prospects no doubt as you have insight into the minds and thoughts of business leaders and leaders of companies you may aspire to work for or emulate. Moreover, getting info/news from social media saves time. MOST IMPORTANTLY though - is the comments sections - you get altering views in real time from real people (not always, sometimes they might be bots haha). I have actually ‘unfollowed’ all my friends on Facebook and follow just news channels, NatGeo, The Economist, and other leading thinktanks because they post links to their articles and research. Its easy since I am on FB most days anyway. Travelling - Travelling in the role of knowledge acquisition is very unique. It allows you to learn about yourself just as much as about other people. HOWEVER, a caveat in travelling is do not just lose yourself entirely when you are visiting a place. For example, if you are like me, I would learn more from visiting villages in Bali and taking photos and talking to the people there. Others might prefer to get drunk and high all the time and just party - I am sure that is another method of learning too (so no judging). Be open minded (Point 2 above) and embrace every opportunity. Be a Mindful learner – Think Deeply about issues, almost meditatively. I use every class assignment to think about issues asked very deeply. I go way over what I am expected to read not to show off but because I imagine how this knowledge will help me in the future. Moreover, understand that each piece of knowledge is only ONE view point/experience, and there is a myriad of experience. Understand for example biases, motivations in history that what a Queen has to say about an event will differ from what a maid or a lady-in-waiting has to say about the same event. The human experience is coloured through so many lenses. Read more about this from Ellen Langer (Harvard Psychologist) – her Tedtalk, her books (‘Mindfulness’ and ‘The Power of Mindful Learning’). Writing – A daily journal of noting down every piece of knowledge (or a summary if you don’t have the time) you have learnt that day such as what did you learn from documentaries and Ted Talks for that day. It is also good to reflect on a particular day. Mind Palace /Timeline – Briefly talked about this earlier, create a mental map of all the knowledge and realise how awesome humanity is and yet how far we have to go. I think I learnt about it first from Sherlock Holmes. It really helps me organising all of history in terms of time and ideas. Be a life-long learner – Understand that you cannot and will not read every book in the entire world – however you can promise to be committed to life-time learning and maximise your potential and brain power for the rest of your life. Note that time is are only real limit to acquire all of this knowledge – so optimize as much as you can e.g. listen to Tedtalks while cleaning your room or watch a documentary in place of a Netflix show. MEDITATE, MEDITATE, MEDITATE - Specifically Mindfulness Meditation. And live a happy and fulfilling life. Be a DEEP learner. Use every single opportunity to learn about yourself and the world around you. In a way this is how I practice gratitude, which helps to alleviate stress and makes me feel good. Finally, I am in constant awe of the world - if you see a random girl staring up at the sky in the middle of the day and being amazed by how its so blue - it may or may not be me…

post_text: 🚀 Just finished reading “Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models” (AAAI-24) — and it really made me think. LLMs are learning to reason — not just respond. Here’s how reasoning has evolved, from stateless outputs to fully stateful, graph-structured thought 👇 ⚙️ Basic Input–Output — Stateless Why: The model processes the prompt once and produces an output — no internal reasoning steps are remembered. Example: Q: “Plan a trip to Japan.” A: “Visit Tokyo and Kyoto.” A direct answer — quick, but shallow. 🔗 Chain of Thought (CoT) — Minimally Stateful Why: Keeps a linear state — one reasoning path, step by step, but can’t explore alternatives or backtrack. Example: “Fly to Tokyo → Stay 3 days → Visit Kyoto → Return.” A clear sequence, but no flexibility — one reasoning chain. 🌲 Tree of Thoughts (ToT) — Partially Stateful Why: Maintains multiple reasoning branches (different possible trip plans) and picks the best after exploring options. Example: Path A: Tokyo + Kyoto (culture-focused) Path B: Tokyo + Okinawa (relaxation-focused) It evaluates both and chooses one — partially stateful, but branches don’t interact. 🌐 Graph of Thoughts (GoT) — Fully Stateful Why: Builds a network of connected ideas where different reasoning paths interact, merge, and update each other. Example: While planning a trip, the model links multiple factors: 🏙️ Destinations (Tokyo, Kyoto, Okinawa) 💰 Budget (flights ↔ hotels ↔ attractions) 🌦️ Weather (affects destination choices) 📅 Schedule (updates based on costs and weather) The model dynamically adjusts one idea based on another — e.g., “If it rains in Kyoto, shift to Okinawa; update budget and timing accordingly.” That’s graph reasoning — interconnected states influencing each other toward an optimal, consistent plan. 🧠 What struck me most is how GoT mirrors human reasoning — refining ideas through feedback, context, and connection. From chains → trees → graphs, LLMs are evolving from linear logic to adaptive, interconnected thought. #AAAI24 #GraphOfThoughts #LLM #AIResearch #Reasoning #MachineLearning #ArtificialIntelligence Reference: https://lnkd.in/gCkqjvPi

However, these methods often suffer from: Brevity bias – simplifying prompts too much and losing critical domain insights. Context collapse – rewriting prompts repeatedly until important details disappear. 💡 How ACE works ACE treats contexts as living playbooks that grow and refine themselves via three modular agents: 1. Generator – produces reasoning trajectories. 2. Reflector – analyzes successes and failures to extract insights. 3. Curator – updates the playbook incrementally. This approach preserves knowledge over time and adapts efficiently, even without labeled data. 📊 Key results +10.6% improvement on agent tasks and +8.6% on financial reasoning benchmarks. 86.9% lower adaptation latency and reduced rollout costs. “Temperature” Means in Large Language Models (LLMs) When you experiment with LLMs like GPT, Claude, or open-source models, one of the most important settings you’ll come across is the Temperature parameter. Many beginners adjust it without really understanding what it controls. Here’s the simplest explanation: Temperature controls how predictable or creative the model’s output will be. A lower temperature makes the model more focused and deterministic. A higher temperature makes the model more diverse and creative. Low Temperature (0.0 – 0.3): • Accurate, factual, repeatable responses • Best for coding, math, legal, technical tasks • The model chooses the most likely next word almost every time Medium Temperature (0.4 – 0.7): • Balanced responses • Good for general writing, explanations, and structured tasks High Temperature (0.8 – 1.5): • Creative, varied, unconventional answers • Best for brainstorming, storytelling, marketing ideas • More randomness in word choice and direction Why Temperature Matters The same prompt at different temperatures can produce completely different responses. Instead of rewriting prompts repeatedly, adjusting the temperature is often the fastest way to change the tone and style of the output. In this work, we systematically compare open-ended generation and multiple-choice selection across reasoning and knowledge-intensive tasks. Using six models (from SmolLM 1.7B to Gemini 2.0 Flash) and two datasets (DisambiguationQA and TinyTruthfulQA), we explore how iterative self-correction unfolds over multiple refinement rounds. 🔍 Key insights: • Generation adapts quickly — early iterations fix many errors — but later revisions introduce semantic drift and over-correction. • Multiple-choice is far more stable, i.e., correct answers persist, yet suffers from logit inertia: once wrong, the model rarely flips to the right answer. • The trade-off is clear: adaptability vs. stability. 🎯 Takeaway: the structure of the output space fundamentally shapes self-correction. data, defining its own optimization steps, and updating its own weights through reinforcement learning. It’s like giving the model not just a “brain,” but the ability to rewrite its own synapses. 🧠 2️⃣ Agentic Context Engineering (Stanford, SambaNova, UC Berkeley) https://lnkd.in/gP427FJR Proposes ACE, a system where an LLM continuously improves its prompts, memories, and reasoning traces — learning from experience without changing weights. Think of it as a model that keeps rewriting its notebook of strategies to become more effective over time. What’s fascinating is how these two directions complement each other: 💡 SEAL → focuses on internal self-modification (weights, finetuning). 💡 ACE → focuses on external self-modification (context, prompts, memory). 🚀 Just finished reading “Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models” (AAAI-24) — and it really made me think.

LLMs are learning to reason — not just respond.
Here’s how reasoning has evolved, from stateless outputs to fully stateful, graph-structured thought 👇

⚙️ Basic Input–Output — Stateless
Why: The model processes the prompt once and produces an output — no internal reasoning steps are remembered.

Example:
Q: “Plan a trip to Japan.”
A: “Visit Tokyo and Kyoto.”
A direct answer — quick, but shallow.

🔗 Chain of Thought (CoT) — Minimally Stateful
Why: Keeps a linear state — one reasoning path, step by step, but can’t explore alternatives or backtrack.

Example:
“Fly to Tokyo → Stay 3 days → Visit Kyoto → Return.”
A clear sequence, but no flexibility — one reasoning chain.

🌲 Tree of Thoughts (ToT) — Partially Stateful
Why: Maintains multiple reasoning branches (different possible trip plans) and picks the best after exploring options.

Example:
Path A: Tokyo + Kyoto (culture-focused)
Path B: Tokyo + Okinawa (relaxation-focused)
It evaluates both and chooses one — partially stateful, but branches don’t interact.

🌐 Graph of Thoughts (GoT) — Fully Stateful
Why: Builds a network of connected ideas where different reasoning paths interact, merge, and update each other.

Example: While planning a trip, the model links multiple factors:
🏙️ Destinations (Tokyo, Kyoto, Okinawa)
💰 Budget (flights ↔ hotels ↔ attractions)
🌦️ Weather (affects destination choices)
📅 Schedule (updates based on costs and weather)
The model dynamically adjusts one idea based on another — e.g., “If it rains in Kyoto, shift to Okinawa; update budget and timing accordingly.”
That’s graph reasoning — interconnected states influencing each other toward an optimal, consistent plan.

🧠 What struck me most is how GoT mirrors human reasoning — refining ideas through feedback, context, and connection.
From chains → trees → graphs, LLMs are evolving from linear logic to adaptive, interconnected thought.

post_text: In the contemporary enterprise, "Customer Centricity" is frequently treated as a cultural aspiration, yet for an organization to truly revolve around its users, it must move beyond sentiment and into a deliberate structural architecture. This architecture is governed by the integration of the CRM triad: the Strategic, the Operational, and the Analytical. When these three dimensions are harmonized, Customer Experience (CX) ceases to be a departmental function and becomes the institutional heartbeat, ensuring that every touchpoint is as intentional as it is efficient. Strategic CRM serves as the foundational layer, the "North Star" that dictates organizational behavior and long-term value over short-term transactional gains. As leaders, our role in this sphere is to ensure that the brand promise is not just a marketing slogan but a lived reality across every facet of the business, from product development to post-sale support. Without this strategic anchor, any attempt at automation or data mining is merely efficient noise; we are not just managing customers, we are cultivating long-term customer equity and institutional trust. The translation of this philosophy into the real world occurs within the realm of Operational CRM, the "engine room" where strategy is mechanized to remove friction from the customer journey. Through the sophisticated application of Marketing Automation and Sales Force Automation (SFA), we transition from generic broadcasting to highly personalized, behavior-triggered lifecycles. This level of automation strips away administrative burdens, allowing teams to pivot from data entry to relationship-building, ensuring that the organization remains responsive to the customer’s immediate context at scale. Finally, Analytical CRM provides the intellectual backbone of the entire system, transforming raw information into predictive intelligence. By systematically mining customer-related data, analyzing historical behaviors, sentiment, and engagement metrics, we move from a reactive posture to a proactive one. This empirical layer does not merely "inform" the business; it validates our strategic pivots and optimizes our operational efficiency. It allows us to stop guessing what the market wants and start anticipating what it needs before those needs are even articulated. Ultimately, sophisticated leadership in this space is defined by the strength of the feedback loop between these three pillars. Analytical insights must refine the Strategic vision, which in turn must be flawlessly executed through Operational excellence. In an increasingly crowded professional landscape, the real competitive advantage lies with the leader who can orchestrate these complex human-technical systems to build an unbreakable cycle of value.

In the contemporary enterprise, "Customer Centricity" is frequently treated as a cultural aspiration, yet for an organization to truly revolve around its users, it must move beyond sentiment and into a deliberate structural architecture. This architecture is governed by the integration of the CRM triad: the Strategic, the Operational, and the Analytical. When these three dimensions are harmonized, Customer Experience (CX) ceases to be a departmental function and becomes the institutional heartbeat, ensuring that every touchpoint is as intentional as it is efficient.

Strategic CRM serves as the foundational layer, the "North Star" that dictates organizational behavior and long-term value over short-term transactional gains. As leaders, our role in this sphere is to ensure that the brand promise is not just a marketing slogan but a lived reality across every facet of the business, from product development to post-sale support. Without this strategic anchor, any attempt at automation or data mining is merely efficient noise; we are not just managing customers, we are cultivating long-term customer equity and institutional trust.

The translation of this philosophy into the real world occurs within the realm of Operational CRM, the "engine room" where strategy is mechanized to remove friction from the customer journey. Through the sophisticated application of Marketing Automation and Sales Force Automation (SFA), we transition from generic broadcasting to highly personalized, behavior-triggered lifecycles. This level of automation strips away administrative burdens, allowing teams to pivot from data entry to relationship-building, ensuring that the organization remains responsive to the customer’s immediate context at scale.

Finally, Analytical CRM provides the intellectual backbone of the entire system, transforming raw information into predictive intelligence. By systematically mining customer-related data, analyzing historical behaviors, sentiment, and engagement metrics, we move from a reactive posture to a proactive one. This empirical layer does not merely "inform" the business; it validates our strategic pivots and optimizes our operational efficiency. It allows us to stop guessing what the market wants and start anticipating what it needs before those needs are even articulated.

Ultimately, sophisticated leadership in this space is defined by the strength of the feedback loop between these three pillars. Analytical insights must refine the Strategic vision, which in turn must be flawlessly executed through Operational excellence. In an increasingly crowded professional landscape, the real competitive advantage lies with the leader who can orchestrate these complex human-technical systems to build an unbreakable cycle of value.
