post_text: Understanding every fee that will be charged to you is the best way to prepare for the high cost of purchasing a property. Whether you're buying your first house or the tenth, sticking to your budget and getting the math right will make the process go more smoothly. To understand the fees, we break them down into 5 categories: 1. Mortgage Down Payment Bank Mortgage Processing Fee Property Valuation Fee Mortgage Payments 2. Government DLD (Dubai Land Department) Transfer Fee DLD (Dubai Land Department) Property Registration Fee DLD (Dubai Land Department) Mortgage Registration Fee Oqood Certificate (if off-plan) 3. Service Security Deposit Agency Fee Conveyance Fee 4. Maintenance Maintenance Fee DEWA (Dubai Electricity and Water Authority) Gas AC Internet 5. Insurance Life Insurance Property Insurance (recommended) The list might seem long but not all of these costs are upfront. You will have to include upfront costs in your home buying budget while ongoing costs are part of your living expenses. Upfront vs. Ongoing costs Upfront costs Down Payment Bank Mortgage Processing Fee Property Valuation Fee DLD Transfer Fee DLD Property Registration Fee DLD Mortgage Registration Fee Oqood Certificate (if off-plan) Conveyance Fee Agency Fee Security Deposit Ongoing costs Life Insurance Property Insurance (recommended) Mortgage Payments Maintenance Fee DEWA (Dubai Electricity and Water Authority) Gas AC Internet How much are the upfront costs? 1. Mortgage Down Payment This is the initial up-front partial payment. The amount saved for a down payment is typically one of the factors which affect how much the bank is agreeing to lend for a mortgage. This is normally a minimum of 20% of the loan amount. Bank Mortgage Processing Fee For buyers completing their purchase with a mortgage, this fee is payable to the bank. The processing fee is usually 0.5% of the loan amount + 5% VAT, but it varies depending on the bank. Property Valuation Fee Another fee payable to the bank for a mortgage buyer is the property valuation fee. The rate varies for this fee too, and it is dependent on each bank. The rate ranges from AED 2,500-3,500 + 5% VAT. 2. Government Costs paid to the government are to the Dubai Land Department (DLD), established to manage the sale and purchase of land. They approve, organize and document the real estate in Dubai. DLD Transfer Fee All property purchases must be registered with the Dubai Land Department (DLD). The amount is paid by the buyer and usually at 4% of the Purchase Price + AED 580. DLD Property Registration Fee A registration fee, payable by the buyer to DLD at the rate of AED 4,000 + 5% VAT. DLD Mortgage Registration Fee If the buyer is buying the property through a mortgage, a mortgage registration fee to the DLD is also applicable at 0.25% of the loan amount + AED 290. Oqood Certificate (if the property is off-plan) It ensures that the property is registered with the name of the buyer. Issuance fee for Oqood Certificate is AED 5,250. 3. Service Security Deposit When buying a property on secondary market transactions, the buyer is required to pay a deposit to secure the purchase. The amount is typically 10% of the purchase price payable to the seller via cheque. This amount is collected by the authorized agent (a RERA registered broker) who holds the deposit until the property is successfully transferred. Agency Fee Payable on completion of property purchase to your agent at the rate of 2% of the property price plus 5% VAT. Conveyance Fee Appointing a conveyancer ensures all the legal terms and contracts are accurately stated as per the UAE law and protects the interests of all parties involved. The amount is payable directly to the conveyancer with the range from AED 6,000-10,000. How much are the ongoing costs? 1. Mortgage This is the amount you pay every month towards your mortgage. 2. Maintenance Maintenance Fee This fee is for the upkeep and maintenance of the residential communities or buildings. The charges are usually calculated based on the square foot. DEWA / Gas / AC / Internet DEWA, which stands for Dubai Electricity and Water Authority, is the company that manages water and electricity supply in Dubai. I often ask myself, what do people really want in their lives and from their work?

The more time I spend around people — teams, founders, students, executives irrespective of gender, backgrounds, and cultures — the more I realize something simple: We are all fighting the same silent battles. And leaders who understand this lead very differently. We all want:

- To matter: To wake up knowing our work isn't just activity, it has meaning and purpose
- To be seen and heard: Not as a role or a number, but as a human being with a story, a voice, and an option
- To grow: To feel today is a step forward, not just another loop of the same day
- To have freedom: The space to make decisions, to create, and to think without fear
- To feel safe: Emotionally, financially, and professionally
- To experience moments of joy: Not just at the end of the project, but along the way and to enjoy the journey
- To work together: As one team.

And behind all of that, we have the same fears that we rarely admit out loud:

- Failing where others can see
- Reaching the end and realizing we played it too small
- Being alone with our struggles
- Not being enough — no matter how hard we try
- Losing control of the things that matter most
- Looking back with regret instead of pride

Leadership isn't about leading people and managing tasks. It's about understanding hearts. The best leaders don't erase fear; they make it safe for people to dream bigger than it. They give clarity when people are overwhelmed. They listen and give trust when people doubt themselves. They show and give courage simply by showing they care.

So, what do you want from life and what are you afraid of?

post_text_html:
Coinciding with R U OK day I happened to read Emma Seppalas’ HBR article ‘Burnout at Work Isn’t Just About Exhaustion. It’s Also About Loneliness’. It contains some interesting information (UK stats):



  • “Compared with roughly 20 years ago, people are twice as likely to report that they are always exhausted”

  • “Close to 50% of people say they are often or always exhausted due to work”

  • “…there is a significant correlation between feeling lonely and work exhaustion…”

  • “…we found that 50% of people — across professions, from the nonprofit sector to the medical field — are burned out…”

  • “…while obesity reduces longevity by 20%, drinking by 30%, and smoking by 50%, loneliness reduces it by a whopping 70%. In fact, one study suggests that loneliness increases your chance of stroke or coronary heart disease — the leading cause of death in developed countries — by 30%...”

  • “…loneliness is an emotionally painful feeling; it even registers as physical pain in the brain…”


Emma offers up some advice on action that can be taken:



  • Promote a workplace culture of inclusion and empathy

  • Encourage employees throughout the organization to build developmental networks. These developmental networks can be task orientated or for emotional support

  • Celebrate collective successes. It helps build a sense of belonging and that what you do matters, perhaps contributing to a sense of Purpose


What are my thoughts on what can be done – a step you may be able to take is simply ask R U OK ? Have a look at the site, there may be something you find helpful.


Also mentioned in the article is of Workplace Engagement which you may be interested in.

Hotel Lakeview Ooty

#TravelAZ #hotel #travel #review
West Lake Road , Ooty, Ooty Lake, Ooty, India, 643004
Experience Comfort and Convenience at Hotel Lakeview OotyNestled just over a kilometer from the vibrant heart of Ooty, Hotel Lakeview offers an ideal retreat for travelers seeking both tranquility and accessibility. Established in 1988 and thoughtfully renovated in 2023, this charming hotel combines timeless appeal with modern amenities, ensuring a comfortable stay amidst the scenic beauty of the Nilgiri Hills. With 117 well-appointed rooms, guests can enjoy spacious accommodations designed for relaxation and convenience.

Whether you're arriving from the airport, approximately 210 minutes away, or exploring the local attractions, Hotel Lakeview provides a welcoming atmosphere with flexible check-in from 2:00 PM and check-out until 11:00 AM. The hotel also warmly welcomes children aged 6 to 8, who can stay free of charge, making it an excellent choice for family vacations....

post_text: Mastercard announced that QNB Group was granted a Mastercard license to extend its issuing and acquiring activities in Syria. Read More - https://lnkd.in/gE452xuX The move, which follows the memorandum of understanding signed between Mastercard and the Central Bank of Syria in September to support the modernisation of the country’s digital payments infrastructure, will expand access to seamless, secure and innovative digital transactions. The alliance marks an important milestone for Mastercard and QNB in their joint efforts to enhance digital banking experience, drive financial inclusion and create new opportunities through technology. “At Mastercard, we are deepening our commitment to Syria as early investors in a market undergoing meaningful transformation. By empowering our partner banks, we are enabling millions of citizens to access modern financial services and laying the foundations for a robust, future-ready payments ecosystem. Our work supports the country’s vision for sustainable economic progress, delivered with full respect for regulatory and compliance standards,” said Adam Jones , division president, West Arabia, Mastercard. “At Mastercard, we are deepening our commitment to Syria as early investors in a market undergoing meaningful transformation. From GCSE Uncertainty to the World Bachelor in Business: Shaye Bhattessa-sharma’s Journey with LessonWise

Roughly four years ago, Shaye joined LessonWise as a GCSE student in Year 10. At the time, his grades were fluctuating between 5s and 6s in key subjects like Maths and Science. He was clearly capable—but like many students—he needed the right support, structure, and guidance to realise his potential.

We got to work.

We carefully matched Shaye with a team of our best tutors, offering trial lessons to ensure the right fit and chemistry. What followed was a true collaboration: Shaye’s relentless work ethic combined with the support of expert tutors and ongoing mentoring from our team. By Year 11, he had transformed his academic trajectory, achieving 8s and 9s across the board in his GCSEs.

Then came the A levels. The familiar shock most students face when met with a curriculum that demands so much more independence and is so much denser in every aspect. The step up was abrupt, and Shaye initially struggled with the volume and the complexity. Within less than a week, we matched him with some of our top A-level tutors, who helped him break down the content, build routines, and regain his footing. Six months later, he wasn’t just keeping up, he was excelling. His confidence had returned, and he was ready to sit his mock exams.

Then came university admissions planning.

Shaye, an exceptionally gifted young entrepreneur, set his sights high: the World Bachelor in Business (WBB)—one of the most competitive and prestigious business programmes in the world. Offered jointly by Università Bocconi, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, and USC Marshall School of Business, the WBB admits only 40 students per cohort worldwide.

Together, we mapped out the process: SATs, essays, timelines. Shaye began SAT preparation with one of our top tutors, and after months of dedicated practice, he achieved an outstanding score of 1480.

Today, Shaye is predicted straight As in his A levels and has been offered a place on the WBB programme—a remarkable achievement by any standard.

✨ This is what we exist for at LessonWise: to help students and families not just prepare for exams, but reach life-changing milestones. We walk the journey with them—from GCSEs to A levels, through applications and admissions—with carefully matched tutors, continuous mentorship, and hands-on guidance throughout.

A huge congratulations to Shaye for everything he’s achieved so far. His discipline, drive, and determination have been nothing short of inspiring, and we couldn’t be prouder. 

Shaye’s story is a testament to his incredible character—and a reflection of our mission: To unlock potential, and help every student we work with take their education further than they imagined.

#education #tutoring #edtech #studentstories #universityadmissions #sat #alevels #gcse #mentorship #bocconi

Over the years building custom apps and helping no-code and AI-powered tools get past launch at Appstuck.com , I’ve seen the decision come up time and again, often too late in the game. Here’s a quick breakdown to help you make the right call *before* you commit to the wrong toolset: 👷♂️ No-Code (e.g. Webflow, Glide, Bubble) ✅ Great for: Fast iterations, MVPs, simple SaaS, landing pages, internal dashboards 🚫 Watch out for: Platform limitations, lack of deep integrations, difficult handoff to developers 🧱 Low-Code (e.g. FlutterFlow, OutSystems) ✅ Great for: Scaling apps from MVP to MMP, faster time-to-market, moderate custom functionality 🚫 Watch out for: Learning curves, vendor lock-in, performance bottlenecks at scale 💻 Full-Code (e.g. React Native, custom backends) ✅ Great for: Complex UI/UX, long-term scaling, tight security & data compliance 🚫 Watch out for: Higher budgets, longer timelines, need for experienced dev teams 💡 Rule of thumb? Start with no-code if: You need validation fast and don’t have dev resources yet. Upgrade when: You're hitting limitations, or need maintainability, integrations, or better performance. Start with full-code if: You’re building a product where scale, customization, or data security is non-negotiable from day one. The trap I see most often is starting with a no-code tool, gaining some traction, then realizing it’s almost impossible to scale or extend without rebuilding it all-which costs more than just starting right. At Appstuck, we help teams bridge these exact situations-whether you're stuck mid-process or just planning out a build that needs to *work* long term. Angola’s Lobito Atlantic Railway Expands with Arrival of 275 New Container Wagons

Terminal at Nador West Med, Morocco’s flagship Mediterranean deep-water port, positioning it as a cornerstone for enhanced regional trade flows and attractive concessions for global infrastructure investors Building on the overarching framework agreement signed on October 28, 2024, between the Tanger Med Group and CMA CGM, Marsa Maroc and CMA Terminals today announced a binding partnership accord enabling the latter’s entry into the equity of the concession-holding entity for the terminal. Upon regulatory approvals, Marsa Maroc will retain a controlling 51% stake in both capital and voting rights, with CMA Terminals securing 49%—a structure that balances local operational dominance with international scale to optimize throughput and revenue generation. Set for phased commissioning starting in 2027, the terminal will feature 900 linear meters of quay at an 18-meter draft, 37.5 hectares of dedicated yard space across a 60-hectare footprint, and up to eight ship-to-shore (STS) gantry cranes. At full tilt, it promises annual capacity of 1.8 million TEUs, unlocking substantial escalatory upside for concession-linked cash flows amid Morocco’s accelerating export diversification and nearshoring trends. This alliance marries CMA CGM’s expansive global liner network—poised to funnel high-volume traffic streams—with Marsa Maroc’s entrenched operational acumen and regional footprint, cultivating a state-of-the-art facility attuned to premier international benchmarks for efficiency and interconnectivity. For institutional allocators, the partnership signals robust risk-adjusted returns in port concessions, leveraging transshipment synergies to elevate Nador West Med as a Mediterranean pivot and amplify Morocco’s gravitational pull on major maritime trade lanes. Strategically sited in Betoya Bay at the Oued Kert estuary—mere nautical miles from the Gibraltar Strait—the port’s geographic primacy complements CMA CGM’s existing Western Mediterranean assets, post_text: Some exciting news ✨ As I kick off my third year, I'm eager to share that I'll be serving in the Association for the Study of Higher Education - Council on Ethnic Participation (CEP) as the 2023-2024 Graduate Representative. I'm grateful for this full circle moment as this was the first home I found in the field. I am looking forward to learning from so many amazing scholars and other graduate students over the next year. This pivot was all about purpose, serving and spreading joy for me, and I'm walking in it boldly. I also received an acceptance to present my research at the ASHE conference this November. 🌾🌾 BIOMASS-
• Biomass usage is expected to nearly triple this financial year, reaching 2.5 million tonnes, up from earlier projections of 1.75 million tonnes.

• This surge is driven by the SAMARTH Biomass Mission, under the Ministry of Power, aiming to convert agricultural residue into energy in an eco-friendly and cost-effective manner.

• India generates around 230 million tonnes of surplus agricultural residue annually, but only 3.2 million tonnes are currently used for energy.

• The government is promoting torrefaction technology, which enhances biomass efficiency by converting it into charcoal-like pellets that are more energy-dense and durable, selling at ₹28,000–₹35,000 per tonne.

• Custom Hiring Centres have been set up to provide baling machines, helping farmers collect and sell crop residue instead of burning it.

• If India utilizes 100 million tonnes of biomass for biofuel, it could unlock a ₹65,000 crore market opportunity.

post_text: You may have heard that Healthscope has gone into administration. Does that mean the business is fundamentally bad? Not at all.... There’s lots of reasons why businesses go broke. Sometimes it’s not enough demand. But in Healthscope’s situation it’s not a lack of demand. The ageing population and growth in healthcare services is well above GDP growth. That means it’s down to a few key factors: 1. Debt vs Equity A business can be profitable (before interest) but in tough times with margins low, high interest costs can mean expenses are more than the net income. That’s clearly an issue here. Hence it's wise to ensure your debt / equity stack will get you through the leaner times. 2. Occupancy costs Rents as a percentage of turnover may be too high. That shouldn’t be the landlord’s problem but if you are going bust then that’s a place to review costs. A business can only wear so much of their turnover on occupancy costs. A business should know exactly how much in occupancy costs as a percentage of revenue it can afford to pay. At the same time, if your business is not viable in the long run at the cost of real estate, you need a change your model. Many retailers are finding this out. 3. Wages / overheads As much as we (and all the medical professions who bill in private hospitals) would love to keep getting paid more, if the wage to revenue ratio is too high, then it’s not possible to keep increasing costs while revenue (largely private insurance subsidies) grow a lot less. Every business needs to know their labour efficiency ratio and make sure stays within those profitable parameters. At a high level, the healthcare sector is an incredible investment opportunity, whether that be the businesses who run healthcare or the real estate partners who support them. The future growth is significant. However the fundamentals need to make sense…the right rents and the right cost structure (not to mention the right capital stack). Whatever happens, Healthscope will still be around in one form or another. Health services aren’t going away! But the fundamentals need to make sense.

In simple terms, if a business with 50+ employees has someone on the plan develop $100,000/year in medical claims, the employer can expect premiums to go up $120,000 at the renewal, and there is only one way to escape it --> a Taft Hartley plan. A Taft Hartley plan works because everyone gets the same increase regardless of how their health was that year. The trick is to find a Taft Hartley plan that underwrites groups before allowing them on so that renewal rates can be stable over time. If a plan doesn't do this, the rates are bound to skyrocket because only high-claims businesses will want to join, and then everybody will share in having massively high premiums which will cause the You need two basic things to start a healthcare company. - A license to provide care - A business model However, who grants your license to provide care can vary greatly, so I recommend doing the right research before you find yourself down the wrong rabbit hole. #2: How to Enter? Here are the ways to get a license: - Buy an existing HC business (w/ license) - Buy an existing HC license (no business) - Start from scratch Each option has it’s own pros and cons. There is no blanket approach in choosing a best option. #3: Deciding Here is the basic difference between buying and starting from scratch. Buying: You inherit a team, brand and liability. That can be very good... or a very, VERY bad Starting from scratch: You can build EXACTLY as you want... for a price & time! #4: Liability Unless you are cash pay, many payers will take back payments through audits of your services. Don't comply w/ MCR? They'll levy your account. Poor documentation? No authorization. It is as simple as that. #5: Investment Okay, so you've modeled out those mouthwatering returns and calculated your months to profitability/payback. That is great! Now you just need to take your budget/timeline and DOUBLE IT. Seriously? Yes, seriously… Here's one of my own timelines to collections: Projected: 180 days Actual: 301 days Healthcare can be rewarding work and an AMAZING investment, but if you don't understand what you're doing, you will set yourself up for a lot of heartache! post_text_html:
You may have heard that Healthscope has gone into administration. Does that mean the business is fundamentally bad? Not at all....

There’s lots of reasons why businesses go broke. Sometimes it’s not enough demand. But in Healthscope’s situation it’s not a lack of demand. The ageing population and growth in healthcare services is well above GDP growth.

That means it’s down to a few key factors:

1. Debt vs Equity

A business can be profitable (before interest) but in tough times with margins low, high interest costs can mean expenses are more than the net income. That’s clearly an issue here. Hence it's wise to ensure your debt / equity stack will get you through the leaner times.

2. Occupancy costs

Rents as a percentage of turnover may be too high. That shouldn’t be the landlord’s problem but if you are going bust then that’s a place to review costs. A business can only wear so much of their turnover on occupancy costs. A business should know exactly how much in occupancy costs as a percentage of revenue it can afford to pay. At the same time, if your business is not viable in the long run at the cost of real estate, you need a change your model. Many retailers are finding this out.

3. Wages / overheads

As much as we (and all the medical professions who bill in private hospitals) would love to keep getting paid more, if the wage to revenue ratio is too high, then it’s not possible to keep increasing costs while revenue (largely private insurance subsidies) grow a lot less. Every business needs to know their labour efficiency ratio and make sure stays within those profitable parameters.

At a high level, the healthcare sector is an incredible investment opportunity, whether that be the businesses who run healthcare or the real estate partners who support them. The future growth is significant.

However the fundamentals need to make sense…the right rents and the right cost structure (not to mention the right capital stack).

Whatever happens, Healthscope will still be around in one form or another. Health services aren’t going away! But the fundamentals need to make sense.

🚢 MarLEN Kick-off Meeting in Brussels! 🌍⚓

Today, the MarLEN consortium gathered at APRE - Agenzia per la Promozione della Ricerca Europea in Brussels for our official kick-off meeting, joined by the Project Monitor Officer Gerd Muysewinkel, Policy officer, and Head of Unit DR RTD. The meeting was a productive session with constructive discussions on the consortium agreement, first funding calls, and evaluation procedures.

🔹 What is MarLEN?
Led by Forschungszentrum Jülich, the Maritime Low Emission Network (MarLEN) is a collaboration of European ministries and funding organisations responsible for maritime technology research funding. The project is funded by European Commission through #HorizonEurope, and our goal is to strengthen the European Research Area by coordinating national and regional maritime research programs, fostering synergies, and aligning with the Zero Emission Waterborne Transport (ZEWT) partnership.

📅 Project Duration: January 2025 – June 2029

🌊 MarRI-UK's Role in MarLEN
MarRI-UK will lead the Projects Monitoring work package, developing a robust evaluation and monitoring framework to assess the impact of funded projects and drive forward maritime innovation.

🤝 UK Collaboration in MarLEN
The UK maritime sector plays a vital role in international collaboration, and we look forward to building stronger partnerships through MarLEN. Our UK partners include:
✅ Innovate UK (IUK)
✅ MarRI-UK
✅ MSE International

Stay tuned for updates on MarLEN’s progress and how it will shape the future of maritime innovation! 🌱🚢

With the rates of preventable – and potentially fatal – congenital syphilis rising, it’s vital that our healthcare system can respond early and effectively to syphilis during pregnancy. At a recent meeting of the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC), the committee recommended that the PBS listings for benzathine benzylpenicillin (Prescriber Bag and the General Schedule) to allow prescribing by endorsed midwives. Benzathine benzylpenicillin is used in the treatment of syphilis. This is an important step forward in supporting midwives as primary maternity care providers and will strengthen Australia’s national syphilis response by enabling timely treatment and prevention of congenital syphilis. post_text: Getting a second passport via citizenship by investment (CBI) program gives you ultimate global mobility , CBI is a means to obtain a new passport that opens up the world to the holder and gives the freedom of travel , and provides a new status that can be referred as a true global citizen . This is the ultimate luxury for those who can afford it and a solid Plan B for those who need it. However, CBI is not limited to giving global mobility to its holders, it has something more to offer: FINANCIAL FREEDOM . One may think that how a CBI removes the shackles of rigorous financial structures that have been put in place by their home country and how it can give the elite the ability to maintain and grow their wealth. Financial freedom can be defined in many forms, but CBI offers the most complete package for a global investor . The first financial benefit the CBI gives to its investors is the freedom from tedious taxation . Many of businessmen see their finances bleed due to the high taxes, and they have no choice but to abide by a tax structure that takes a lot, and in many cases, does not offer much in return. The recent pandemic greatly highlighted how fragile the global economic system is . A few made money off the pandemic, but mostly lost hefty amounts, and their businesses, and the bigger you are, the harder you fall. As governments struggled to deal with the economic crisis worldwide, the first reaction is to take a look at their imposed taxes with a plan to raise the taxes in order to cope with the financial burden thrust upon them, then the governments started imposing more “wealth tax”. CBI solves this by offering investors another option, that is more lenient and allows the investors more control over the wealth that they have accumulated over time through hard work. Besides becoming citizens of a more tax-friendly country , CBI also gives investors the option to open bank accounts in countries that have more user-friendly banking procedures . For the investors who belong to countries that have financial sanctions or complicated banking regulations, this could give them more freedom in moving their money throughout the world without the need to worry every time they make a transaction. Doing business also becomes easier , as Caribbean CBI countries, allow simple registration of companies as well as a simple process for establishing corporations that allow for simpler business transactions than those you would find in some nations throughout the world. Countries such as Turkey and Montenegro also offer citizenship by investment, the Caribbean nations offer the greatest financial freedom to investors through their citizenship by investment programs. Antigua & Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St. Kitts & Nevis, and St. Lucia offers the world’s most prominent citizenship programs. Their CBIs have reasonable prices, investment to get a passport starts at just $100,000 , the processing time for applications is as little as 3 months and gives applicants and their family members a strong passport. These countries are considered as tax-havens and the investors can safeguard their wealth from the high amount of taxes imposed by their home countries. There are many countries worldwide that are considered as tax-havens like Ireland and the UAE, but neither of these countries offers citizenship and also these do not have the kind of favorable tax regime you’d find in the Caribbean. Global income tax, inheritance tax, capital gains tax, and wealth tax are not imposed in the Caribbean, which means that you are truly free to enjoy the wealth you have worked tirelessly collecting. No greedy government hands dipping The Caribbean nations adopted the UK’s common law (with the exception of St. Lucia which has a hybrid of UK common law and French civil law), meaning investors can rest assured that they are protected within a familiar legal structure. These countries are also members of the CARICOM and the OECS. Investors who obtain the CBI of one of the nations are free to live, work, and take advantage of the economic landscape of all members of these unions. The revenue from CBIs in the Caribbean provides investment for either government-managed development funds or real estate investments. This helps the governments diversify their economy, create sustainable economic ventures, and help boost tourism and create jobs for the local population. Not everyone can obtain a Caribbean passport, these countries also have strict due diligence process as they want to bring in the best the world has to offer By selecting specific criteria and a robust due diligence process, they can ensure they bring the best to their shores. High net-worth individuals have a habit of making money right and left. The Caribbean nations want them to continue doing so in a relaxed environment, which may lead to higher job creation, attracting more businesses to their shores, and overall economic diversification and growth. The truth about tax-havens is that these are not the countries that are not strict or regulated enough, but the exact opposite. Tax-havens are nations that identify the true benefit of letting businesses and people thrive, they have the foresight to see the actual benefits of a lack tax regime. The Caribbean CIPs are much more than just a passport in return for investment or donation. Investors get global mobility and financial freedom , they also get the peace of mind knowing that if there is any political or economical instability in their home country, they have a plan B . The Caribbean countries of Antigua & Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St. Kitts & Nevis, and St. Lucia may not have the resources of the UK or USA. Still, they make up for it with their innovation and without bleeding their population dry with high taxes. post_text: Three Projects, One Team, No Winner Monday begins with alignment. The leadership team agrees on three priorities. Project A, Project B, Project C. All important. All funded. All assigned. The plan is parallel progress. By Tuesday afternoon, Project A needs a decision. Not a big one. Just clarity on scope. The person who could decide is in meetings. The question sits in a thread. No one escalates. No one owns it. The thread goes quiet. Project B has momentum. Two people are energized. They ship something small. It feels good. Project C gets mentioned in a standup. Someone asks about timing. The answer is vague. Everyone nods. Wednesday morning, an executive asks about Project B. Suddenly it feels urgent. Project C gets deprioritized without anyone saying so. Project A is still waiting on that decision. Thursday, a client escalates. Project C becomes the priority. Project B loses its two energized people. Project A's thread is now buried. Friday, all three projects feel stuck. Not because they're hard. Because attention fractured. --- The team worked all week. Calendars were full. Slack was active. People were responsive. But responsiveness is not progress. Whoever spoke loudest got focus. Whoever interrupted first got attention. The team didn't choose priorities. They reacted to pressure. No one decided to stop Project A. It just lost momentum. No one deprioritized Project B. It just got quieter. No one abandoned Project C. It just waited. --- This pattern repeats. Organizations create multiple initiatives expecting teams to sustain parallel progress. But human attention doesn't work that way. Deep focus requires singular direction. Context-switching depletes capacity faster than overwork. Without a forced sequence, teams default to reactive mode. The result feels paradoxical. Everyone works harder. Everything moves slower. Busyness increases. Completion decreases. By December, the year ends with no major wins. Three projects ran. None finished strong. --- The problem isn't effort or talent. It's that parallel priorities demand a kind of attention humans cannot reliably provide. When everything is important, nothing survives the week intact.

a €500 million project is nearly impossible. Running 500 projects at €1 million each is boring, manageable, and delivers. Clear scope, clear owner, clear done. Any competent team handles a million-euro scope without needing a steering committee to decide what colour the status report should be. This is not a new insight. It's not even a controversial one. Every experienced practitioner nods when they hear it, and then goes back to work inside a monolithic program that does the exact opposite. The interesting question isn't how to decompose—any decent architect can break scope into pieces over a long lunch. The interesting question is what the monolith protects. Because it always protects something. A €500 million program is a career structure. It justifies director-level positions, dedicated PMOs, quarterly board reporting, and enough governance layers that no single decision is ever traceable to a single person. Fifteen small deliverables don't offer that. Fifteen small deliverables have visible owners, measurable outcomes, and a point where someone has to say \"done\" or \"failed\" out loud. That visibility is exactly what large organizations engineer away. Complexity isn't the problem—complexity is the solution to a different problem, which is accountability. When everything is connected to everything and the dependencies span three org charts, failure becomes environmental. Nobody's fault. Just the inherent difficulty of operating at scale. Three Projects, One Team, No Winner

Monday begins with alignment.
The leadership team agrees on three priorities. Project A, Project B, Project C. All important. All funded. All assigned.
The plan is parallel progress.
By Tuesday afternoon, Project A needs a decision. Not a big one. Just clarity on scope. The person who could decide is in meetings. The question sits in a thread. No one escalates. No one owns it. The thread goes quiet.
Project B has momentum. Two people are energized. They ship something small. It feels good.
Project C gets mentioned in a standup. Someone asks about timing. The answer is vague. Everyone nods.
Wednesday morning, an executive asks about Project B. Suddenly it feels urgent. Project C gets deprioritized without anyone saying so. Project A is still waiting on that decision.
Thursday, a client escalates. Project C becomes the priority. Project B loses its two energized people. Project A's thread is now buried.
Friday, all three projects feel stuck.
Not because they're hard. Because attention fractured.


---
The team worked all week. Calendars were full. Slack was active. People were responsive.
But responsiveness is not progress.
Whoever spoke loudest got focus. Whoever interrupted first got attention. The team didn't choose priorities. They reacted to pressure.
No one decided to stop Project A. It just lost momentum.
No one deprioritized Project B. It just got quieter.
No one abandoned Project C. It just waited.


---
This pattern repeats.
Organizations create multiple initiatives expecting teams to sustain parallel progress. But human attention doesn't work that way. Deep focus requires singular direction. Context-switching depletes capacity faster than overwork.
Without a forced sequence, teams default to reactive mode.
The result feels paradoxical. Everyone works harder. Everything moves slower. Busyness increases. Completion decreases.
By December, the year ends with no major wins. Three projects ran. None finished strong.


---
The problem isn't effort or talent.

original_post_text:
Three Projects, One Team, No Winner

Monday begins with alignment.
The leadership team agrees on three priorities. Project A, Project B, Project C. All important. All funded. All assigned.
The plan is parallel progress.
By Tuesday afternoon, Project A needs a decision. Not a big one. Just clarity on scope. The person who could decide is in meetings. The question sits in a thread. No one escalates. No one owns it. The thread goes quiet.
Project B has momentum. Two people are energized. They ship something small. It feels good.
Project C gets mentioned in a standup. Someone asks about timing. The answer is vague. Everyone nods.
Wednesday morning, an executive asks about Project B. Suddenly it feels urgent. Project C gets deprioritized without anyone saying so. Project A is still waiting on that decision.
Thursday, a client escalates. Project C becomes the priority. Project B loses its two energized people. Project A's thread is now buried.
Friday, all three projects feel stuck.
Not because they're hard. Because attention fractured.


---
The team worked all week. Calendars were full. Slack was active. People were responsive.
But responsiveness is not progress.
Whoever spoke loudest got focus. Whoever interrupted first got attention. The team didn't choose priorities. They reacted to pressure.
No one decided to stop Project A. It just lost momentum.
No one deprioritized Project B. It just got quieter.
No one abandoned Project C. It just waited.


---
This pattern repeats.
Organizations create multiple initiatives expecting teams to sustain parallel progress. But human attention doesn't work that way. Deep focus requires singular direction. Context-switching depletes capacity faster than overwork.
Without a forced sequence, teams default to reactive mode.
The result feels paradoxical. Everyone works harder. Everything moves slower. Busyness increases. Completion decreases.
By December, the year ends with no major wins. Three projects ran. None finished strong.


---
The problem isn't effort or talent.
It's that parallel priorities demand a kind of attention humans cannot reliably provide. When everything is important, nothing survives the week intact.

post_text: The list of possible stochastic patterning issues for EUV lithography keeps growing longer: CD variation, edge roughness, placement error, defects [1]. The origins of stochastic behavior are now well-known. For a given EUV photon flux into the resist, a limited fraction are absorbed. Since the absorption is less than 5% affected by dose [2], the absorbed photon number per unit area practically follows a Poisson distribution [3]. The Poisson distribution is much like a normal distribution whose standard deviation is the square root of the mean, yet truncated at zero (no negative values allowed). Prior work has already shown that the stochastic edge appearance is smoothed by resist blur [4]. The resist blur is taken to be a continuous function (e.g., Gaussian with sigma=2nm), but this does not take into account the actual random secondary generation yield [5] following EUV photon absorption. Ionized electrons do not need to ionize other electrons to release energy; they can also lose energy through plasmons and vibrational excitations [6]. In this article, we will explore the electron number randomness as an extra stochastic factor in EUV lithography. The electron yield per absorbed photon is estimated to be ~3 for organic chemically amplified resists [6], and ~8 for metal oxide resists [7]. Instead of being fixed numbers, these should be taken to be typical or average values; the actual number comes from a second Poisson distribution, distinct from that for photon absorption. Then the blur amplitude should naturally be scaled according to the actual electron number. Thus, secondary electrons effectively compound the stochastic behavior. Edge deformation is a natural generalization of edge roughness, one of the known manifestations of stochastic behavior. The most obvious manifestation of this is a deviation of a contact or via shape from circularity. For a ~20 nm feature size, Figure 1a shows the edge deformation when electron yield per photon is fixed, whereas Figure 1b shows the same when electron yield per photon follows a Poisson distribution for an average value of 3 electrons per photon. The resist blur is modeled with 4x Gaussian convolution (sigma=1 nm), giving an effective sigma of 2nm. Figure 1a. 16 simulation runs with 2nm blur and fixed secondary electron yield. The assumed resist layer absorption is 18% and the dose 60 mJ/cm2. Grid pixel size is 1 nm x 1 nm. Figure 1b. 16 simulation runs with 2nm blur and secondary electron yield following a Poisson distribution with mean=3 electrons per photon. The same conditions as in Figure 1a were assumed. Even without calculating the individual via areas, the difference in appearance is already striking. Besides increasing the photon dose, increasing the electron yield per photon is also suggested to keep stochastic effects in check, by reducing the standard deviation/mean ratio. Even so, electron number is constrained by the energy needed for ionization (~10 eV); EUV has only enough energy for no more than 9 ionized electrons per photon. A higher photon energy, i.e., shorter wavelength, can raise the upper limit. However, increasing the electron number also increases the range of electron paths [8]. This increases blur, which is fundamentally detrimental to resolution [9]. post_text: In a previous article, I pointed out that we no longer have to ensure every dataset is perfectly formatted to get our data analytics programs off the ground. Once equipped with the right tools and capabilities to pull out raw data as and when it is needed, we can turn our attention to an agile approach for deploying data analytics. To build a data-driven culture across our business, we need to choose the right use cases for analytics and business intelligence from the get-go. And when we use a phased approach, we can learn from both our mistakes and our triumphs, while building competence and confidence in data analytics across our business. To help you get started, here’s some advice we often offer clients to help them develop the right pilot programs. Don’t get preoccupied with cost – Once money enters the equation, there is a tendency for us to harshly and prematurely judge the results or implementation process. The reverse can happen too. When large sums of money have been invested, the tendency is to become overly protective of a solution to the point where it hampers progress. Either way, the result is a tendency to spend too much time trying to attain an elusive perfection, rather than getting the use case underway. Focus on the business, not the technology – As is the case with building a data warehouse, analytics implementations can get bogged down in technical details. While your IT team does play a key role in getting an analytics use case off the ground, we need to remain focused on the business problem we are trying to solve. Focusing on the needs of the users allows us to work backward to deploying an analytics solution that actually delivers. Be security conscious, not compliance obsessed – The growing importance of data privacy and security regulations have many of us jumping at shadows. While it’s essential to keep sensitive and critical data secure, we can still make data available for analytics uses cases without compromising security. For example, Qlik allows you to mask sensitive fields so in the instance of a retail situation, you can restrict some fields for users at individual branches but allow individual stores to compare their results to the rest of the branches in the data set. By adopting a phased approach, we can gain an understanding of where each dataset resides and put the necessary protective measures in place. Celebrate your mistakes – Though it sounds cliché, mistakes are opportunities to learn and improve. We need to make a few mistakes during an agile analytics implementation if we want to improve. The fixes that we implement to resolve these problems serve as valuable lessons to future use cases. More importantly, allowing the team to identify and implement solutions to resolve early hiccups goes a long way towards building confidence in the project. Create your own methodology – Mistakes and solutions are only truly valuable when we record them for future use. Every business is different and will have unique methodologies that allow use cases to be deployed more easily. By keeping and maintaining your own best practices when it comes to deploying analytics, organisations create continuity for future deployments undertaken by different personnel. Becoming a data-driven business doesn’t happen overnight, but we can get there iteratively by focusing first on the key problems we want to solve today. Once we see and understand the power of analytics, we can begin deploying them towards more powerful and transformative goals.

Big funds like Blackstone and TPG are doing great. Smaller funds? Raising money is harder than ever. Here’s what is going on: Bain says there are about 29,000 companies sitting in PE portfolios. That’s about $3.6 trillion still waiting to be sold. And still, the big players are strong. Blackstone, Carlyle, and TPG keep raising billions, bringing in record money, and closing huge deals. Why? Because investors now want: Big platforms Global reach The power to do billion-dollar deals This is good for mega funds. But for founders and smaller managers, it makes life tough. Here’s the truth: There are two kinds of private equity partners: 1. allocators who only write checks. 2. Execution partners who work with you to grow. At Enventure , we choose the second. We don’t just give capital. We help founders fix operations, scale with focus, and be ready for exit from day one. We have been founders ourselves. We know the wins, the misses, and the grind. So when you give equity, it should not be to “private equity.” It should be to a partner who believes in your vision and works beside you. Capital without alignment is a risk. Capital with clarity builds legacy. If you are a founder facing growth, succession, or your first round of outside funding, you don’t need the biggest fund. You need a partner who understands your journey and helps you execute it. DM me if you want to talk about how that looks in practice. post_text: Approximately 30-40% of the food in the United States goes uneaten every year, according to the USDA . This amounts to 135 billion pounds of wasted food, worth $161 billion. Meanwhile, more than 48 million people — 13% of the population — are food insecure, meaning they don’t get enough daily calories or nutrients necessary to stay healthy. Sandeep Srinivas , a PhD student in business administration at Gies College of Business at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is writing his dissertation on the impact of technology on the food supply chain, and when he learned about this discrepancy between food supply and demand, he wondered if there was anyone working on the problem. He learned there were food banks that took donations of unsold food from supermarkets and used it to feed the food-insecure population. Most of the donated food were boxed and canned nonperishable items, not the fresh dairy, meat, and produce that’s essential to a healthy diet. He also learned that there were a number of businesses, known as foodtech platforms, that are trying to reduce food waste by selling surplus food from various points in the food supply chain at a discount. Imperfect Foods, for instance, distributes food that’s considered too “ugly” for supermarket shelves, and Too Good to Go sells restaurant leftovers as takeout. Srinivas was particularly interested in Flashfood , a Toronto-based app that connects supermarkets that have extra merchandise with customers who want to buy it for less than the market rate. “What this platform is essentially trying to do is provide a midway point,” Srinivas explains. “It’s not exclusively placing the burden [of feeding people] on the retailers or the food banks. It’s bringing the cost down and passing that on to consumers.” Was it possible, Srinivas wondered, that, without knowing it, these foodtech platforms were also helping to redistribute the food supply and feed the food insecure population? A marketplace solution between food banks and supermarkets With his academic advisors Gautam Pant and Ujjal Mukherjee , Srinivas set out to measure the impact of Flashfood on food insecurity in local populations. This study is especially important now, given the uncertainty surrounding government aid programs. Srinivas, Pant, and Mukherjee recently presented their findings in a new paper, “From Waste to Welfare: The Effect of Foodtech Platforms on Food Insecurity.” Srinivas began by using the Map the Meal Gap dataset from Feeding America, which measures the percentage of the food insecure population at a county level, and data from the Flashfood website that showed when the app expanded into different counties. He analyzed the data using a difference-in-differences approach that compared the levels of food insecurity in counties where Flashfood was available and demographically similar counties where it wasn’t both before and after Flashfood launched. He discovered that, on average, one Flashfood store reduces a county-level food insecurity rate by 0.090 percentage points. This translates into approximately 860 people per county or 146,000 people across all the counties where Flashfood operates. The impact of Flashfood’s entry into a community was strongest in more vulnerable areas with higher poverty levels. “The results that this for-profit platform is able to cause such a positive effect was actually a little bit surprising,” Srinivas says, “although it was not totally unexpected because nobody else had looked at for-profit platforms in the context of food insecurity.” He was also curious how the for-profit platforms affected the nonprofit food banks. Were people abandoning the food banks now that Flashfood made supermarket groceries more affordable? Or were they using both? He discovered that Flashfood and the food banks were, in fact, complementing each other, largely because they offered different types of food. People continued to get canned and nonperishable pantry items through the food banks. But through Flashfood, they could supplement that food with fresh produce, meat, and dairy. This makes perfect sense to Srinivas: “Not everyone wants to rely on canned products or frozen food or carbs.” Srinivas shared his findings with Nick Bertram, then the Flashfood CEO. “This is something they didn’t know how to test,” says Srinivas, “so they were very excited when we showed them those results.” Implications for policy, platforms, and partnerships Although Flashfood was originally developed as an environmentally conscious solution to the problem of food waste, and its founders never considered that affordability might also be an attraction for customers, Bertram and his team were pleased that it had the additional benefit of reducing food insecurity, especially in more vulnerable areas. Mukherjee, an associate professor of business administration at Gies Business, points out that Flashfood could use Srinivas’ data to focus its expansion efforts. But the paper’s findings have the potential to make an impact beyond this one foodtech platform. “It can be used by the government because the government can actually use Flashfood to supplement or complement their efforts to reduce food insecurity,” Mukherjee says. “It can provide infrastructure to connect this platform with the food bank platforms to encourage complementarity. It can build informational infrastructure like broadband and WiFi access for people to use this platform in an efficient manner. And the retailers can also, from this research, quantify the effects of subscribing to the platform. So it’s very useful from a business and social perspective.” The paper has already received acclaim: it won the Doctoral Research Showcase Award at the Decision Sciences Institute Conference in November. Srinivas, Pant, and Mukherjee plan to continue researching the effects of technology on the food supply chain, including how blockchain can be used to reduce food contamination and recalls. “This is a good way to meet the objective of reducing hunger in the U.S. using all possible mechanisms,” Srivinas says.

post_text: Introduction Enterprises are constantly seeking innovative solutions to meet their growing network and security needs while driving operational agility. Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) is one such solution that has been gaining popularity. However, a common misconception has started to emerge: the idea that a single vendor can deliver a comprehensive SASE solution. This article will debunk that myth and shed light on why outcome-based services from Managed Service Providers (MSPs) and Managed Security Service Providers (MSSPs) are often the better choice. So, what is in the SASE Framework? The SASE solution stack comprises a blend of conceptual IT management principles and tangible technologies, coming together to create a comprehensive and secure environment. Here’s a breakdown: Core Principles Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) : The foundation of ZTNA is a "never trust, always verify" approach. Every user and device must be authenticated and authorized before they gain access to the network, minimizing the risk of inside threats and data breaches. Identity-Driven : In a SASE architecture, access and security policies are tied to user and device identities, not their physical locations. This tenet ensures that policies remain consistent and are enforced, irrespective of where the user or device is connecting from. Globally Distribute d: SASE solutions are designed to be cloud-native and globally distributed, providing optimized access, secure, and with a consistent experience to all users, regardless of their location. Technologies Software-Defined Wide Area Networking (SD-WAN) : The networking backbone of SASE is SD-WAN. It connects disparate enterprise networks – including data centers, remote offices, and mobile users – to provide reliable and efficient orchestration of network connectivity. Secure Web Gateway (SWG) : SWG provides real-time web content filtering and malware detection. It ensures secure internet access by blocking malicious content and websites down to users through network and cloud-based enforcement points. Firewall-as-a-Service (FWaaS) : Delivering inbound firewall capabilities via the cloud, FWaaS provides comprehensive threat protection and enforces security policies across all inbound network traffic; depending on the capabilities, these can also be called Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) and are used to inspect inbound traffic from the internet to servers. Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) : CASB allows organizations to extend their security policies to SaaS applications, providing visibility, threat protection, and data security. They provide more than just binary access control and can be used to restrict functional access based on conditions. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) : DLP tools monitor and control data movements across the network, datastores, and endpoints, ensuring the protection of sensitive information. Together, these conceptual tenets and technologies create a unified SASE framework that ties together network infrastructure and security services. This integration results in improved user experience, heightened security, and enhanced operational efficiency. Understanding SASE and How It Differs from Just “SD-WAN + Security” In simple terms, SASE is a comprehensive model that integrates network security and wide area networking (WAN) capabilities with cloud-based orchestration. However, SASE is more than just SD-WAN coupled in parallel with security tools. While SD-WAN focuses on connecting diverse networks, and standalone security services aim to protect specific systems, functions, or endpoints, SASE merges these functionalities, providing seamless and secure network access regardless of user location. While integrating SD-WAN into a security solution might seem like a straightforward way to combine network management and security, it's crucial not to treat these as two separate functions. It’s vital that your SD-WAN solution governance is seamlessly integrated with security in a unified policy framework; this integration is more important than technological or platform integration a single vendor solution seeks to achieve. Without this governance integration, there is a risk of creating an environment where the network and security components operate in silos. This will lead to inconsistent policy enforcement, gaps in security, and complexities in management. The key is to ensure that SD-WAN and security elements within SASE are inherently interwoven enabling coherent policies and streamlined management, thus truly unlocking the potential of SASE as a consolidated networking and security platform. You can reveiew my previous article on planing a network tranformation and adopting SD-WAN here: SASE and Security Frameworks: A Complementary Relationship While SASE provides a technology framework to support the secure transmission of data and secure access to applications and resources, it should not be viewed as a replacement for established security frameworks such as NIST, CIS, or ISO27001. These frameworks provide comprehensive guidelines on how to secure information and establish strong cybersecurity controls. They cover a range of elements, from risk assessment and identity management to incident response and recovery procedures. SASE complements these security frameworks by providing the technological means to implement their principles. For instance, the Zero Trust principle of SASE aligns with the access control and identity verification requirements emphasized in these security frameworks. The cloud-native and globally distributed architecture of SASE also resonates with these frameworks’ emphasis on resilience and recovery. Moreover, SASE can aid in regulatory compliance for industries bound by strict regulations and where maintaining data security and privacy is paramount, such as healthcare (under HIPAA) or finance (under GDPR). Here, the unified visibility and control offered by the SASE technology framework is critical. The Overpromise of Single Vendor SASE Solutions The allure of single vendor solutions is understandable. They promise simplicity, integration, and a single point of contact for support. However, in practice, finding a single vendor that excels in all the areas encompassed by SASE can be a daunting, if not impossible, task, and that’s before layering in the unique requirements of your business. Network solutions and security are complex fields, each comprising multiple sub-disciplines. It's rare to find a single vendor with top-tier expertise in all these areas. Besides, sticking with a single vendor can lead to vendor lock-in, reducing flexibility and potentially leading to higher costs in the long run. The Right Solution (for most): Outcome-Based Services from MSPs or MSSPs This is where MSPs and MSSPs come into the picture. They provide businesses with access to a pool of experts in various fields, offering customized solutions based on each company's unique needs. MSPs and MSSPs monitor, manage, and secure your network infrastructure, providing outcome-based services that ensure your IT operations are effective and efficient. They can leverage best-in-class vendors for each part of the SASE tech stack but reduce the friction that can be caused by having multiple solutions. Secondly, staffing your own company with experts is often a Herculean task. According to (ISC)2, at the end of 2022, there was a global cybersecurity worker gap of 3.4 million skilled individuals. This is a staggering figure that highlights the critical shortage of cybersecurity professionals. Moreover, when it comes to hiring highly qualified cybersecurity experts, the cost can be prohibitive for many businesses. Entry-level analysts can easily cost upwards of $100k with benefits, while seasoned leaders and architects can be $250k+. By partnering with an MSSP, businesses can gain access to a team of seasoned cybersecurity experts at a fraction of the cost of hiring in-house. This not only alleviates the pressure of finding and retaining top talent but also ensures that your security posture is continuously updated and fortified by professionals who live and breathe cybersecurity. Choosing MSPs and MSSPs over a DIY solution allows IT teams to focus on their core competencies and aligning strategic initiatives to the needs of the business, while leaving their management of network and security needs in the hands of trusted experts. This approach drives enhanced security, access to the latest technology, cost savings, and most importantly, peace of mind through risk abatement. SASE? Sign Me Up! But how do I get Started? As your business prepares to adopt a SASE solution stack, there are four critical steps to kickstart your evaluation process: Define Your Business Requirements : Start by identifying your unique business needs and objectives. What challenges are you trying to solve? How do you envision SASE addressing these issues? Consider your business's size, nature, the geographical spread of offices, remote work policies, and specific industry regulations you must comply with. Assess Your Current Infrastructure : Examine your current network and security infrastructure. Determine what's working and what isn't. This assessment will help you understand what needs to change and where SASE can fill the gaps. Identify Potential Vendors and Partners : Research potential vendors, focusing on their ability to meet your specific needs. Look into their expertise, track record, the comprehensiveness of their SASE solution, customer support, and cost. Benchmark Solutions : Create a requirements rubric that allows you to standardize, normalize, and compare vendors and partners that you are considering. You will need to consider both quantitative data like price, licensing model, and term, as well as qualitative assessments from your stakeholder about ability to deliver, internal technical acumen, and integration into your operations. As you undertake this evaluation process, here are key questions to consider: What are our main business objectives that a SASE solution should support? How do your users access data and tools today and how might that change in the future? What are the security and networking challenges you are currently facing? How will adopting a SASE solution improve our current infrastructure? What kind of network traffic and security policies do you need to enforce? How capable are you in managing a SASE solution in-house? What is your budget for implementing and maintaining a SASE solution? What is your timeline for SASE adoption? What level of customer support will you require from the SASE vendor or MSSP? What are the business impacts of a security event? Additionally, quantitative data plays a crucial role in your SASE evaluation, allowing you to assess your needs and evaluate potential solutions more accurately. Here are some key data points you should gather: Number of Network Users : This includes full-time employees, part-time staff, contractors, partners, and customers who access your network. User Locations : Determine how many of your network users are in-office, remote, or mobile. This should include geographical data on distributed offices or remote employees. Device Count and Types: Count the total number of devices accessing your network, including laptops, smartphones, tablets, IoT devices, etc. Knowing the types of devices will help ensure the SASE solution can handle all device requirements. Application Usage : Identify the applications your business uses, the data they handle, and the network resources they consume. This data can help you understand your bandwidth needs and security requirements. Current Network Performance Metrics : This includes latency, packet loss, and jitter, which can indicate the quality of your current network and identify areas for improvement. Security Incidents : Gather data on the number, type, and severity of past security incidents. This can guide your focus on specific security features in a SASE solution. Cost Data : Calculate the total cost of your current network and security infrastructure, including hardware, software, maintenance, and personnel costs. This will provide a benchmark for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of a SASE solution. Compliance Requirements : Quantify the number of regulations your business needs to comply with, which could affect your SASE requirements. Also consider any specific requirements from your cybersecurity insurance or client agreements. Network Traffic Data : Understand your average and peak network traffic levels. This can help ensure your SASE solution can scale to meet your needs. 30 open deviations is not a capacity problem.

It is a systems problem.

That distinction matters because the two have different solutions. A team that is behind needs more hours. A system that generates work faster than it resolves it needs a different architecture.

The signal most quality leaders recognize but rarely name: the backlog does not build because of one bad week. It builds because the system requires manual effort at every stage. Triaging. Categorizing. Routing. Chasing effectiveness checks. Each step is reasonable on its own. Together they create a queue that compounds faster than any team can clear it.

The teams running clean backlogs are not carrying more headcount. They have removed the manual steps between an event and a closed record. Routing is automatic. Trending is continuous. Effectiveness checks trigger without someone remembering to schedule them.

The result is not just efficiency. It is visibility. A clean backlog tells leadership what the quality function actually sees. A full one obscures it.

The real goal isn’t to become better at firefighting. It’s to understand why the fire keeps starting in the first place. That’s where process improvement begins: → Identify the pattern → Find the root cause → Fix the process → Measure the result → Prevent recurrence A strong operations team shouldn’t measure success only by how many problems it resolves. It should also ask: “How many recurring problems have we eliminated?” Because operational excellence isn’t just about fixing today’s problem. READINESS | 005 A problem can be visible to everyone and still remain invisible to the organization. The people closest to the work usually see it first. They discuss it. They work around it. They report it. But as information moves up, detail is removed, urgency is softened, and the constraint becomes another status update. Startups value people who solve problems, not people who simply point at them. That is reasonable. But “don’t bring me a problem without a solution” becomes dangerous when the problem crosses functions or exceeds the authority of the person who found it. Modern continuous-improvement systems follow a better standard: Solve problems at the lowest capable level. Escalate them when they cross organizational boundaries or require greater authority and resources. That requires more than pointing out what is wrong. A useful escalation defines the condition, provides evidence, explains the impact, identifies what has already been attempted, and states the decision or support required. The standard is not complaint. It is structured problem solving. But even well-defined problems must be prioritized. In The Crux, Richard Rumelt argues that strategy requires identifying the challenge that is both critical and solvable. The point where focused action can have the greatest impact. A Readiness Assessment brings these disciplines together. It connects frontline insight across functions, separates symptoms from constraints, identifies the crux, and directs ownership and resources toward it. It is Not another status meeting. Massive inventory buildup, burned-out teams, and zero increase in final output. The breakthrough comes from applying Eliyahu M. Goldratt’s Theory of Constraints (TOC): \"Any manageable system is limited in achieving more of its goals by a very small number of constraints.\" Optimizing non-bottlenecks creates an illusion of efficiency without improving the bottom line. True throughput increases only when you manage the single limiting factor. Goldratt’s 5 Focusing Steps provide a structured cycle for continuous improvement: 1. IDENTIFY the Constraint: Pinpoint the exact step or resource that dictates total system speed. 2. EXPLOIT the Constraint: Maximize the bottleneck's efficiency with existing resources (zero idle time, zero wasted capacity). 3. SUBORDINATE Everything Else: Align all other processes to match the pace of the bottleneck to prevent excess inventory and overload. 4. ELEVATE the Constraint: Invest capital or resources to expand the bottleneck's capacity if demand still exceeds output. 5. REPEAT (Prevent Inertia): Once the constraint breaks, it shifts somewhere else. Return to Step 1 without letting old habits become the new bottleneck. Operational excellence isn't about making everything run at maximum speed—it's about harmonizing the entire system around the constraint. 30 open deviations is not a capacity problem.

It is a systems problem.

That distinction matters because the two have different solutions. A team that is behind needs more hours. A system that generates work faster than it resolves it needs a different architecture.

The signal most quality leaders recognize but rarely name: the backlog does not build because of one bad week. It builds because the system requires manual effort at every stage. Triaging. Categorizing. Routing. Chasing effectiveness checks. Each step is reasonable on its own. Together they create a queue that compounds faster than any team can clear it.

The teams running clean backlogs are not carrying more headcount. They have removed the manual steps between an event and a closed record. Routing is automatic. Trending is continuous. Effectiveness checks trigger without someone remembering to schedule them.

The result is not just efficiency. It is visibility. A clean backlog tells leadership what the quality function actually sees. A full one obscures it.

If you want a grounded read on where your system sits between reactive backlog and continuous execution, the quality score takes five minutes: https://hubs.ly/Q04rF7R60

post_text: Stepping into the Acting Team Lead role for the SA Field Team at Vocus has been such a rewarding challenge. post_text:
Es wird dunkel. Die Sonne bleibt gefährlich. ⚠️ 

Eine Sonnenfinsternis ist ein faszinierendes Naturschauspiel – und gleichzeitig ein Moment, in dem wir besonders auf unsere Augen achten sollten. 

Denn auch wenn die Sonne teilweise vom Mond verdeckt wird, kann direkte Sonnenstrahlung die Netzhaut schädigen. Das Tückische: Eine solche Schädigung muss nicht sofort schmerzhaft sein. 
Beim direkten Blick in die Sonne können die empfindlichen Sinneszellen der Netzhaut geschädigt werden. Diese sogenannte solare Retinopathie kann zu Sehstörungen führen. 

Deshalb gilt: Wer eine Sonnenfinsternis beobachten möchte, sollte ausschliesslich einen geeigneten, geprüften Sonnenschutz verwenden. Eine normale Sonnenbrille bietet dafür keinen ausreichenden Schutz. 
Schützen Sie Augen – damit aus einem faszinierenden Erlebnis keine bleibende Erinnerung wird. 
 
❓ Schauen Sie sich die Sonnenfinsternis heute an?

#Vista #Augengesundheit #Sonnenfinsternis #Augenschutz #Sehen #Ophthalmologie

Result: The same packaging may be ✅ mandatorily compostable here ⚠️ unnecessary there ⛔ prohibited elsewhere We need clarity to accelerate the circular economy. Instead, we are creating confusion for manufacturers, local authorities, certifiers and citizens. How can we harmonise sorting labels if the rules themselves change at every border ? (*) about a Belgian draft law that has undergone so many amendments and compromises that it has become unreadable and impossible to implement. _________________ I'm Philippe Dewolfs, engineer turned - almost 30 years ago - certification geek for #compostable , #biodegradable , #renewable & #biobased products. V. , Bundesverband Güterkraftverkehr Logistik und Entsorgung (BGL) e.V. , and DIE PAPIERINDUSTRIE has jointly written to four Federal Ministers, raising the alarm about the implementation of new EU waste shipment rules. From 21 May 2026, EU Regulation 2024/1157 becomes operational. Two requirements are set to cause serious disruption: 🔴 The DIWASS digital platform is not ready – Technical specifications were published late, key functions are still missing, and registration processes are incomplete. Yet from May 2026, any shipment not processed through DIWASS risks being classified as illegal – not because of any environmental violation, but due to a formal requirement that may not yet be technically fulfillable. 🔴 A 2-working-day advance notice for 'Green List' shipments is unworkable – In recycling and waste logistics, dispositions often happen within hours. Fluctuating customer needs, truck load optimisation, and spontaneous returns make rigid advance deadlines a serious threat to established supply chains. What the industry is demanding: ✅ A binding 12-month transition period ✅ Penalty-free use of alternative submission methods in the interim ✅ Abolition or flexible application of the 2-day deadline ✅ A uniform, pragmatic enforcement approach across Germany A regulation designed to strengthen environmental and resource protection must not end up paralyzing the very circular economy it aims to support. The clock is ticking. As Heidi Sanborn, MPA Sanborn, Executive Director/CEO of the National Stewardship Action Council (NSAC), explained in the article: “Extended Producer Responsibility laws are public policies passed by legislatures and implemented with government oversight. They create clear, consistent rules so all producers contribute fairly to the cost of recycling and waste management, which is very different from voluntary corporate initiatives or private agreements among companies.” With nearly four decades of industry-related experience, Heidi, often referred to as the “Godmother of EPR in the United States” has shaped many of the policies guiding the transition to a circular economy, including California's SB 54. Over the past decade, NSAC has passed more circular economy laws than any other organization in the nation, working alongside policymakers, agencies, companies, recyclers, and communities to move policy from concept to implementation. The Industrial Accelerator Act, published today, marks a key moment for Europe’s clean industry. The law correctly identifies the challenges Europe needs to tackle: reducing supply chain vulnerabilities, increasing demand for low‑carbon products and materials, and derisking the investments needed to scale up clean industries and technologies. 💡These are the areas where clarity and ambition are needed most. It is also encouraging to see that low‑carbon solutions form the strategy’s backbone, even if it will take time to fully assess whether all the details and numbers are aligned with industry needs. 🌍 As negotiations on the law begin, it’s essential to refrain from framing this as “local versus clean”. Focusing on local content without linking it to sustainability would be a missed opportunity. Other regions are investing massively in clean technologies and global competition is accelerating. The IAA can unlock major investment and strengthen Europe’s leadership in clean industries. 🎯Shaping Europe’s clean industrial ecosystem also requires rules on public procurement and circularity, still to be tabled. And all of this work needs to be aligned with the EU’s 2040 climate target to enable businesses and investors to move with confidence and plan for the future. A lot of uncertainty was created by the multiple delays in tabling the IAA. 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗮 𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗹 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗲
 
To paraphrase our Belgian Prime Minister (*) : " 𝑤𝑒 𝑤𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝑎 𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑒ℎ𝑜𝑟𝑠𝑒, 𝑏𝑢𝑡 𝑤𝑒 𝑔𝑜𝑡 𝑎𝑛 𝑢𝑔𝑙𝑦, 𝑠𝑚𝑒𝑙𝑙𝑦 𝑐𝑎𝑚𝑒𝑙 " ...
 
A European #PPWR intended to harmonise ...
which leaves it up to each Member State to decide which packaging must be compostable ( art 9.2 ).
 
Result:
The same packaging may be
✅ mandatorily compostable here
⚠️ unnecessary there
⛔ prohibited elsewhere
 
We need clarity to accelerate the circular economy.
Instead, we are creating confusion for manufacturers, local authorities, certifiers and citizens.

How can we harmonise sorting labels if the rules themselves change at every border ?


(*) about a Belgian draft law that has undergone so many amendments and compromises that it has become unreadable and impossible to implement.
 
_________________
I'm Philippe Dewolfs, engineer turned - almost 30 years ago - certification geek for #compostable, #biodegradable, #renewable & #biobased products.
Helping to make certification rigorous and science based ... but not boring.
