post_text: Most fire protection engineers would agree that there are many misconceptions about fire damage and suppression equipment. While no amount of fire protection can guarantee absolute immunity, a careful analysis of hazards, combined with the proper selection of fire protection systems, can drastically reduce potential damage. Unfortunately, laymen often misunderstand the recommendations given by fire protection professionals. And since “unfriendly” fires do not happen to most of us on a regular basis, we have images of fires seen in movies or on television. In order to offer the viewer a clear picture, movie directors typically use clean-burning natural gas flames in the fire scenes, which are unrealistic at best. To accurately portray most fires, the director would have to show a black screen. Misconceptions like these often make people confused about fire protection. The following are some of the most common fire protection-related myths. Myth 1. Keep sprinklers away from electricity: Electrical fires can produce large quantities of opaque, corrosive, and toxic smoke. This smoke makes any manual fire fighting efforts-such as using a portable extinguisher-extremely difficult. Most electrical and electronic equipment exposed to sprinkler water can be cleaned, rinsed with deionized water, and dried. Almost always, the fire protection layman opposes the presence of sprinklers in an electrical room because of “personnel hazard.” This argument is weak because everyone should already have left the room long before a sprinkler actuates. In most cases, hazards caused by the fire and its products of combustion are much greater than that of the water discharge or potential for contact with a live circuit. Even in a case where sprinklers actuate with a person in the room, such as if he was unconscious, the chances of being harmed by the water discharge are much less than from the deadly smoke. Myth 2. Don’t use water on flammable liquid/oil fires: While it is true that a straight stream of water when applied to a flammable liquid fire can actually spread the burning liquid, it is a poor reason to exclude the use of water at all. Water is an excellent fire suppression agent used to successfully control and extinguish flammable liquid fires, if properly applied. Let’s take a brief look at the physics of burning liquids. Every flammable/combustible liquid has a flash point-the temperature at which the liquid gives off a flammable vapor in sufficient concentration with ambient air to generate an ignitable mixture. So in reality, it is not actually the liquid that burns, but the vapor. The proper application of water to a flammable liquid or oil fire has several effects. 1. Water absorbs convective heat above the fire. If it is not absorbed, this heat can cause structural damage and ignite other nearby combustibles. 2. When applied to structural members, water provides a cooling effect to keep the materials from failing (for example, structural steel begins to weaken at 800 F). 3. Water extracts heat from the liquid itself, so that when the liquid is cooled to below its flash point, the fire self-extinguishes. The method of water application is the key to properly extinguishing a flammable liquid fire. Trained fire fighters use a spray or fog pattern from their hoses in order to accomplish the three items discussed above. Fixed sprinkler and waterspray systems achieve the same effect, but begin suppression earlier, distribute water more evenly, and cause much less damage than the fire department would, assuming that they even attempt offensive fire fighting. Another important aspect of flammable liquid fire control is proper spill containment. If a pool or “burning” liquid flows outside a sprinkler-protected area, no sprinkler system will do the job. Therefore, containment must be limited to the areas protected by the fire suppression system, and for ease of control, the area should be subdivided into smaller sections. Myth 3. Sprinklers do more damage than fire: Sprinklers provide early control of a fire, thus providing safety and limiting the damage. With the exception of the deluge sprinkler/waterspray system (which is only used for specific high-hazard applications), sprinkler heads only operate when heat released by a fire melts the fusible link that keeps the sprinkler closed, and the open sprinklers can be expected directly above the fire seat. Every individual head must be triggered in that fashion. Myth 4. Sprinklers may go off accidentally: The failure rates for sprinkler heads are extremely small (on the order of 1 in 16 million or a probability of 6.25×10 -8 ). Inadvertent discharge of sprinklers is extremely rare and usually attributed to mechanical damage or poor system design. It is so rare, in fact, that there are not enough data to be more precise. It is estimated that 1 in 2.5-million installed sprinkler systems will discharge inadvertently (probability of 4.0×10 -7 ). To ensure reliability and performance, sprinkler system components, design, and installation are meticulously controlled by the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standard, NFPA 13, Installation of Sprinkler Systems, the nation’s foremost design and installation standard on the subject. Proper selection and location of sprinkler heads, and proper system design, minimize the possibility of inadvertent discharge. Myth 5. Plants that meet fire and building codes don’t need additional protection: Fire and building codes objectives are to get the occupants out safely before conditions become hazardous, rather than to protect the building from fire. Since industrial fires have not historically resulted in extensive loss of life, most building and fire codes tend to be fairly lenient in industrial facilities. In addition, these codes usually do not concern themselves with the adequacy of fire suppression systems, but merely address whether or not their presence is required. Industrial fire losses do, however, constitute a high percentage of the annual property losses, a factor that the codes usually do not address. Also, model codes used by most jurisdictions only contain minimum requirements, even though builders and owners often look at them as maximum requirements. If the “codes” don’t address property loss prevention, how can you make sure that your plant is adequately protected? Industrial insurance carriers with a technical background can offer a wealth of information and support ranging from management loss prevention programs to special hazard fire suppression protection. Myth 6. It is better to rely on manual fire suppression: Manual fire fighting efforts are a last resort when attempting to confine and contain a fire within a plant. By the time the local fire department is notified and arrives at the scene of a working fire, extensive damage to the building and contents has already occurred. Add to that the extensive water damage from 1-3/4 or 2-1/2-in. hose streams (250-500 gpm). In the case of large fires or high-hazard buildings, the officer in command may decide to take the defensive position of letting the fire burn itself out and protecting neighboring structures rather than jeopardizing the safety of firefighters. Effective fire fighting is much harder than portrayed on television and in movies. Few people realize that a typical fire extinguisher provides only 10-15 sec of agent discharge. Unless the fire extinguisher is used in the incipient stage of a fire and the operator is familiar with the extinguisher’s proper use, they are of little benefit to facility protection. Often, valuable time is wasted emptying fire extinguishers when the fire department should have been notified immediately. Using a fire hose can be much harder than it looks. Many 1-1/2-in. “occupant” hoses are inadequately maintained and could result in injury if used. Smoke quickly impairs visibility, and products of combustion can turn a room into a deadly trap within minutes. For anything other than small, incipient fires, the best thing to do is to leave the area immediately, notify the fire department from a safe location, and let the suppression system (if installed) do its job. Myth 7. Firefighters know fire protection systems: While surveying an industrial plant, the inspector noted that the preaction sprinkler system valve protecting a fairly large building of wood construction had been turned off. When questioned, the facility’s safety officer replied that he would check with another employee who was a retired firefighter, which he did promptly. The retired firefighter informed the safety officer that the impaired sprinkler system was “legal” because plant personnel were concerned about inadvertent sprinkler discharge and that someone would open the system valve (located in the fire area) in case of fire. This incident reaffirms the misconception that firefighters know all about sprinklers and other fire suppression systems. Had the retired firefighter been familiar with the operation of the plant’s suppression systems, he would have known that the concerns were unsubstantiated because preaction sprinkler systems are virtually unsusceptible to inadvertent discharge and that the valve would not be safely accessible during a fire. The fact is that firefighters are trained to deal with fire fighting tactics and rescue; their training and knowledge on fixed fire protection systems is usually limited. Fire protection systems are engineered mechanical, electrical, and structural systems whose evaluation should be left to fire protection engineers and their care to experienced contractors. Myth 8. If the plant has sprinklers, it’s protected: While sprinklers have an excellent record of protecting people and buildings from fire, the mere presence of a sprinkler system does not mean that it can adequately deal with a fire. This point is especially true in facilities with often-changing hazards. Sprinkler systems are matched to the occupancy of a building, meaning that the higher the expected heat release of a fire, the more water a sprinkler system must be able to deliver. The density, or water flow over a unit area, is a balance between the available water supply (flow and pressure) and friction resistance of the sprinkler piping. Engineering calculations are used in the sprinkler system layout and the pipe selection. Therefore, a sprinkler system that was adequate 10-yr ago may not necessarily offer adequate protection today. Myth 9. Halon is toxic and illegal: At this time, no laws or regulatory agencies in the U.S. prohibit the use of Halon as a fire suppressant. When used as intended as a total flooding or local application fire suppression agent, no adverse health effects have been reported from the use of Halon 1301 and 1211 over the past 30 yr. At the typical 5-7% concentration, the volume of Halon is insufficient to displace a significant percentage of oxygen. Exposure to Halon at high concentrations only causes temporary adverse health conditions. Decomposition products of Halon from exposure to flame or surface temperatures over 900 F can be harmful. However, products of combustion from the fire itself (carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride) are a greater danger. As long as occupants leave the area within 15 min of a Halon system discharge, do not reenter it immediately after a fire, and the space is well ventilated after a discharge, Halon is a safe fire suppression agent. Myth 10. Testing diesel fire pumps is bad: I have heard numerous comments from maintenance personnel, such as: “We have reduced the speed of the diesel driver to lessen wear on the engine.” “We would like to install a clutch between the engine and pump, which we can disengage during our weekly tests to minimize wear on the engine.” “We want to install a high-temperature cut-out to prevent the engine from overheating.” These points may be appropriate reasoning for a truck or industrial engine, but they could be the cause for catastrophic losses if a diesel fire pump fails when needed. The main focus behind any fire protection equipment is maximum reliability when needed. As such, fire pumps and their diesel engine are intended for emergency service, not for maximum mileage and wear, as in the case of the truck engine. Therefore, it is imperative that only the minimum necessary mechanical and electrical systems be provided, as deemed necessary by the manufacturer, listing agency, and fire protection experts. While it is true that wear increases due to poor lubrication when the diesel engine is started under full load and brought up to its rated speed within 1-2 sec, a fire pump engine should not log more than 30 hr/yr, including weekly and annual testing. Excessive wear over the engine’s life should not be an issue. When problems with diesel drivers are occasionally encountered, it is usually due to poor maintenance and/or operating procedures. For example, infrequent oil changes can result in corrosion, due to the moisture content in the oil; or leaks in hoses can result in overheating, due to low coolant level. With the proper care, as recommended by the manufacturer and NFPA, a diesel fire pump assembly should give many years of troublefree service. This service is the case with thousands of fire pump installations throughout the U.S. and the world.

The proper application of water to a flammable liquid or oil fire has several effects.

1. Water absorbs convective heat above the fire. If it is not absorbed, this heat can cause structural damage and ignite other nearby combustibles.

2. When applied to structural members, water provides a cooling effect to keep the materials from failing (for example, structural steel begins to weaken at 800 F).

3. Water extracts heat from the liquid itself, so that when the liquid is cooled to below its flash point, the fire self-extinguishes.

The method of water application is the key to properly extinguishing a flammable liquid fire. Trained fire fighters use a spray or fog pattern from their hoses in order to accomplish the three items discussed above. Fixed sprinkler and waterspray systems achieve the same effect, but begin suppression earlier, distribute water more evenly, and cause much less damage than the fire department would, assuming that they even attempt offensive fire fighting.

Another important aspect of flammable liquid fire control is proper spill containment. If a pool or “burning” liquid flows outside a sprinkler-protected area, no sprinkler system will do the job. Therefore, containment must be limited to the areas protected by the fire suppression system, and for ease of control, the area should be subdivided into smaller sections.

Myth 3. Sprinklers do more damage than fire:

Sprinklers provide early control of a fire, thus providing safety and limiting the damage. With the exception of the deluge sprinkler/waterspray system (which is only used for specific high-hazard applications), sprinkler heads only operate when heat released by a fire melts the fusible link that keeps the sprinkler closed, and the open sprinklers can be expected directly above the fire seat. Every individual head must be triggered in that fashion.

Myth 4. Sprinklers may go off accidentally:

The failure rates for sprinkler heads are extremely small (on the order of 1 in 16 million or a probability of 6.25×10 -8 ). Inadvertent discharge of sprinklers is extremely rare and usually attributed to mechanical damage or poor system design. It is so rare, in fact, that there are not enough data to be more precise. It is estimated that 1 in 2.5-million installed sprinkler systems will discharge inadvertently (probability of 4.0×10 -7 ).

To ensure reliability and performance, sprinkler system components, design, and installation are meticulously controlled by the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standard, NFPA 13, Installation of Sprinkler Systems, the nation’s foremost design and installation standard on the subject. Proper selection and location of sprinkler heads, and proper system design, minimize the possibility of inadvertent discharge.

Myth 5. Plants that meet fire and building codes don’t need additional protection:

Fire and building codes objectives are to get the occupants out safely before conditions become hazardous, rather than to protect the building from fire. Since industrial fires have not historically resulted in extensive loss of life, most building and fire codes tend to be fairly lenient in industrial facilities. In addition, these codes usually do not concern themselves with the adequacy of fire suppression systems, but merely address whether or not their presence is required.

Industrial fire losses do, however, constitute a high percentage of the annual property losses, a factor that the codes usually do not address. Also, model codes used by most jurisdictions only contain minimum requirements, even though builders and owners often look at them as maximum requirements.

If the “codes” don’t address property loss prevention, how can you make sure that your plant is adequately protected? Industrial insurance carriers with a technical background can offer a wealth of information and support ranging from management loss prevention programs to special hazard fire suppression protection.

Myth 6. It is better to rely on manual fire suppression:

Manual fire fighting efforts are a last resort when attempting to confine and contain a fire within a plant. By the time the local fire department is notified and arrives at the scene of a working fire, extensive damage to the building and contents has already occurred. Add to that the extensive water damage from 1-3/4 or 2-1/2-in. hose streams (250-500 gpm). In the case of large fires or high-hazard buildings, the officer in command may decide to take the defensive position of letting the fire burn itself out and protecting neighboring structures rather than jeopardizing the safety of firefighters.

Effective fire fighting is much harder than portrayed on television and in movies. Few people realize that a typical fire extinguisher provides only 10-15 sec of agent discharge. Unless the fire extinguisher is used in the incipient stage of a fire and the operator is familiar with the extinguisher’s proper use, they are of little benefit to facility protection. Often, valuable time is wasted emptying fire extinguishers when the fire department should have been notified immediately.

Using a fire hose can be much harder than it looks. Many 1-1/2-in. “occupant” hoses are inadequately maintained and could result in injury if used. Smoke quickly impairs visibility, and products of combustion can turn a room into a deadly trap within minutes.

For anything other than small, incipient fires, the best thing to do is to leave the area immediately, notify the fire department from a safe location, and let the suppression system (if installed) do its job.

Myth 7. Firefighters know fire protection systems:

While surveying an industrial plant, the inspector noted that the preaction sprinkler system valve protecting a fairly large building of wood construction had been turned off. When questioned, the facility’s safety officer replied that he would check with another employee who was a retired firefighter, which he did promptly. The retired firefighter informed the safety officer that the impaired sprinkler system was “legal” because plant personnel were concerned about inadvertent sprinkler discharge and that someone would open the system valve (located in the fire area) in case of fire.

This incident reaffirms the misconception that firefighters know all about sprinklers and other fire suppression systems. Had the retired firefighter been familiar with the operation of the plant’s suppression systems, he would have known that the concerns were unsubstantiated because preaction sprinkler systems are virtually unsusceptible to inadvertent discharge and that the valve would not be safely accessible during a fire.

The fact is that firefighters are trained to deal with fire fighting tactics and rescue; their training and knowledge on fixed fire protection systems is usually limited. Fire protection systems are engineered mechanical, electrical, and structural systems whose evaluation should be left to fire protection engineers and their care to experienced contractors.

Myth 8. If the plant has sprinklers, it’s protected:

While sprinklers have an excellent record of protecting people and buildings from fire, the mere presence of a sprinkler system does not mean that it can adequately deal with a fire. This point is especially true in facilities with often-changing hazards.

Sprinkler systems are matched to the occupancy of a building, meaning that the higher the expected heat release of a fire, the more water a sprinkler system must be able to deliver. The density, or water flow over a unit area, is a balance between the available water supply (flow and pressure) and friction resistance of the sprinkler piping. Engineering calculations are used in the sprinkler system layout and the pipe selection. Therefore, a sprinkler system that was adequate 10-yr ago may not necessarily offer adequate protection today.

Myth 9. Halon is toxic and illegal:

At this time, no laws or regulatory agencies in the U.S. prohibit the use of Halon as a fire suppressant. When used as intended as a total flooding or local application fire suppression agent, no adverse health effects have been reported from the use of Halon 1301 and 1211 over the past 30 yr. At the typical 5-7% concentration, the volume of Halon is insufficient to displace a significant percentage of oxygen. Exposure to Halon at high concentrations only causes temporary adverse health conditions.

Decomposition products of Halon from exposure to flame or surface temperatures over 900 F can be harmful. However, products of combustion from the fire itself (carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride) are a greater danger. As long as occupants leave the area within 15 min of a Halon system discharge, do not reenter it immediately after a fire, and the space is well ventilated after a discharge, Halon is a safe fire suppression agent.

Myth 10. Testing diesel fire pumps is bad:

I have heard numerous comments from maintenance personnel, such as: “We have reduced the speed of the diesel driver to lessen wear on the engine.” “We would like to install a clutch between the engine and pump, which we can disengage during our weekly tests to minimize wear on the engine.” “We want to install a high-temperature cut-out to prevent the engine from overheating.”

These points may be appropriate reasoning for a truck or industrial engine, but they could be the cause for catastrophic losses if a diesel fire pump fails when needed. The main focus behind any fire protection equipment is maximum reliability when needed. As such, fire pumps and their diesel engine are intended for emergency service, not for maximum mileage and wear, as in the case of the truck engine. Therefore, it is imperative that only the minimum necessary mechanical and electrical systems be provided, as deemed necessary by the manufacturer, listing agency, and fire protection experts.

While it is true that wear increases due to poor lubrication when the diesel engine is started under full load and brought up to its rated speed within 1-2 sec, a fire pump engine should not log more than 30 hr/yr, including weekly and annual testing. Excessive wear over the engine’s life should not be an issue.

When problems with diesel drivers are occasionally encountered, it is usually due to poor maintenance and/or operating procedures. For example, infrequent oil changes can result in corrosion, due to the moisture content in the oil; or leaks in hoses can result in overheating, due to low coolant level. With the proper care, as recommended by the manufacturer and NFPA, a diesel fire pump assembly should give many years of troublefree service. This service is the case with thousands of fire pump installations throughout the U.S. and the world.

post_text: 🙌 Took a break after COP30 and I’m back! My first sit-down interview was with Mr Xin Wei Low , Assistant Chief Executive (Energy Technologies Division) at the Energy Market Authority (EMA) . Here's the link to the interview: https://lnkd.in/gs79PwMY But tl;dr, Singapore has one of the most reliable power grids in the world. In 2024, the Republic’s average frequency of sustained interruptions per customer account, also known as System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI), is 0.26 minutes. This is in stark contrast to the global average of 300 to 400 minutes and even surpasses the best-performing U.S. city, the District of Columbia, which recorded a SAIDI of 32.6 minutes. Mr Low emphasised that, by building capabilities in forecasting, rapid response and adaptability, Singapore can ensure the reliability of its power grid for at least the next five to eight years. To account for both planned and unplanned outages, Singapore ensures its spare generation capacity remains at least 27% above peak electricity demand. According to projections by EMA, Singapore is expecting a total power supply of 11.7 gigawatts, and a system peak demand of 8.5 gigawatts in 2026; the reserve margin is estimated to reach a substantial 38%. As energy systems become increasingly complex amid the global energy transition, climate change, and geopolitical shifts, Mr Low drew on a strategic metaphor from Sun Tzu's The Art of War: "Fūrinkazan" (Wind, Forest, Fire, Mountain), to describe an ideal power grid. "The grid needs to respond to outages swiftly as the wind, coordination happens steadily as the forest, stability maintained relentlessly as the fire, and reserves provided immovable as the mountain," he said. We also delved into innovative solutions like Virtual Power Plants and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology. Many thanks to Leonie Tan and Ki Kym Ang for facilitating this story and for their understanding! p.s. I’m still adjusting to the news cycle (CUES The Scientist by Coldplay 😆), but I'm ready for pitches and coffee chats! #energy #power #politics #climate #sustainability #unitedstates

Bloomberg outlook for 2026 is a stark reminder that the global energy transition is entering a decisive and dangerous phase. While geopolitical shifts in the US and China will shape markets and technology flows, countries like Indonesia will bear the real consequences of delayed action. Indonesia stands at a crossroads. On one hand, we are seeing falling renewable energy costs, growing access to clean technologies, and clear evidence from other developing countries that a rapid transition is possible. On the other, Indonesia continues to lock itself into coal through PLTU extensions, captive coal plants for industry, and false solutions framed as “transition fuels.” What this global trend analysis makes clear is that the energy transition will not wait for political comfort. Data centers, EV supply chains, and clean tech manufacturing are reshaping the global economy and countries that cling to fossil fuels risk being left behind, economically and socially. 🙌 Took a break after COP30 and I’m back!

My first sit-down interview was with Mr Xin Wei Low, Assistant Chief Executive (Energy Technologies Division) at the Energy Market Authority (EMA).

Here's the link to the interview: https://lnkd.in/gs79PwMY

But tl;dr, Singapore has one of the most reliable power grids in the world. In 2024, the Republic’s average frequency of sustained interruptions per customer account, also known as System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI), is 0.26 minutes.

This is in stark contrast to the global average of 300 to 400 minutes and even surpasses the best-performing U.S. city, the District of Columbia, which recorded a SAIDI of 32.6 minutes.

Mr Low emphasised that, by building capabilities in forecasting, rapid response and adaptability, Singapore can ensure the reliability of its power grid for at least the next five to eight years.

To account for both planned and unplanned outages, Singapore ensures its spare generation capacity remains at least 27% above peak electricity demand.

According to projections by EMA, Singapore is expecting a total power supply of 11.7 gigawatts, and a system peak demand of 8.5 gigawatts in 2026; the reserve margin is estimated to reach a substantial 38%.

As energy systems become increasingly complex amid the global energy transition, climate change, and geopolitical shifts, Mr Low drew on a strategic metaphor from Sun Tzu's The Art of War: "Fūrinkazan" (Wind, Forest, Fire, Mountain), to describe an ideal power grid.

"The grid needs to respond to outages swiftly as the wind, coordination happens steadily as the forest, stability maintained relentlessly as the fire, and reserves provided immovable as the mountain," he said.

We also delved into innovative solutions like Virtual Power Plants and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology.

Many thanks to Leonie Tan and Ki Kym Ang for facilitating this story and for their understanding!

p.s. I’m still adjusting to the news cycle (CUES The Scientist by Coldplay 😆), but I'm ready for pitches and coffee chats!

post_text:
Jimmy Connors won 1,274 professional tennis matches.

I wondered what that actually represents.

He played 1,557 tour-level matches over a career that stretched across more than two decades (1972 to 1996).

But the number that interests me isn’t 1,274.

It’s the repetition.

Win. Recover. Travel. Practice. Compete again.

Lose 283 times — and come back for the next one.

Watch younger players arrive stronger, faster and hungrier — and find a way to remain competitive.

We talk a lot about what it takes to reach the top.

Maybe we don’t talk enough about what it takes to stay there.

In sport, as in business, one great year can make you successful.

Remaining relevant for decades requires something else entirely.

Talent gets you into the conversation.

Consistency, adaptation and resilience keep you there.

1,274 wins weren’t one extraordinary achievement.

They were 1,274 separate occasions when Jimmy Connors had to show up and win again.

As Robert Mazzucchelli would say, it’s a long game.

Jimmy Connors won 1,274 professional tennis matches.

I wondered what that actually represents.

He played 1,557 tour-level matches over a career that stretched across more than two decades (1972 to 1996).

But the number that interests me isn’t 1,274.

It’s the repetition.

Win. Recover. Travel. Practice. Compete again.

Lose 283 times — and come back for the next one.

Watch younger players arrive stronger, faster and hungrier — and find a way to remain competitive.

We talk a lot about what it takes to reach the top.

Maybe we don’t talk enough about what it takes to stay there.

In sport, as in business, one great year can make you successful.

Remaining relevant for decades requires something else entirely.

Talent gets you into the conversation.

Consistency, adaptation and resilience keep you there.

1,274 wins weren’t one extraordinary achievement.

They were 1,274 separate occasions when Jimmy Connors had to show up and win again.

As Robert Mazzucchelli would say, it’s a long game.

post_text: Op donderdag 29 januari 2026 heeft Brussels Centre for Law, Government and Society (BruCeL) lid Jorien Van Belle haar doctoraat, getiteld “Subjectivering versus toegang tot de Raad van State: de “paradox van de rechtsbescherming"”, met succes publiek verdedigt. In haar doctoraat, heeft Jorien onderzocht hoe de rol van de Raad van State verschuift van een objectieve wettigheidstoetsing naar een toetsing waar de individuele rechtsbescherming, de belangen van de burger meer centraal komen te staan. Haar doctoraat werd begeleid door professor Aube Wirtgen. ---- Le jeudi 29 janvier 2026, Jorien Van Belle, membre du Brussels Centre for Law, Government and Society (BruCeL), a soutenu avec succès sa thèse de doctorat intitulée « Subjectivisation versus accès au Conseil d'État : le « paradoxe de la protection juridique » ». Dans sa thèse, Jorien a examiné comment le rôle du Conseil d'État évolue d'un contrôle objectif de la légalité vers un contrôle davantage axé sur la protection juridique individuelle et les intérêts des citoyens. Sa thèse a été supervisée par le professeur Aube Wirtgen. ---- On Thursday, 29 January 2026, Brussels Centre for Law, Government and Society (BruCeL) member Jorien Van Belle successfully defended her doctoral thesis entitled ‘Subjectivation versus access to the Council of State: the “paradox of legal protection”’. Jorien's doctoral thesis examines how the role of the Council of State is shifting from an objective review of legality to a review that focuses more on individual legal protection and the interests of the citizen. Her doctoral thesis was supervised by Professor Aube Wirtgen

Honored to announce the participation of Fabiola Duro in the upcoming thematic session at #Balkonnect2025, where she will present #DigitalTour as a success story of digital innovation in tourism. A project with strong potential for regional replication beyond Albania, DigitalTour demonstrates how digital tools can reshape tourism experiences and foster sustainable growth.

The session, titled “Tourism–Agri–Food–Processing Innovation, Sustainability and Economic Growth,” will explore key opportunities and business models focused on:

Seasonal tourism & agri-rural development
Traditional and sustainable food processing
Regional cooperation & cross-border (agri-eco) tourism

Digitalisation and innovation in food and tourism
Investment and financing strategies

Moderated by Shkelzen Marku (Yunus Social Business Balkans), the panel includes:
✅ Aleksandar Prelevic – ITEX
✅ Fabiola Duro – INNVEST
✅ Flori Uka – UkaFarm/Winery
✅ Gladiola Dona – Hospitality and Tourism Academy (HAT)

Honored to announce the participation of Fabiola Duro in the upcoming thematic session at #Balkonnect2025, where she will present #DigitalTour as a success story of digital innovation in tourism. A project with strong potential for regional replication beyond Albania, DigitalTour demonstrates how digital tools can reshape tourism experiences and foster sustainable growth.

The session, titled “Tourism–Agri–Food–Processing Innovation, Sustainability and Economic Growth,” will explore key opportunities and business models focused on:

Seasonal tourism & agri-rural development
Traditional and sustainable food processing
Regional cooperation & cross-border (agri-eco) tourism

Digitalisation and innovation in food and tourism
Investment and financing strategies

Moderated by Shkelzen Marku (Yunus Social Business Balkans), the panel includes:
✅ Aleksandar Prelevic – ITEX
✅ Fabiola Duro – INNVEST
✅ Flori Uka – UkaFarm/Winery
✅ Gladiola Dona – Hospitality and Tourism Academy (HAT)
✅ Blerta Harxhi-Begolli – Peja Municipality

Join us for this engaging discussion:
🗓️ May 23 | 🕑 14:00–15:30 | 📍 Strauss/Emerald

post_text: “AUTOSAR kills creativity.” I’ve heard this statement many times in embedded software discussions. But does it really? I see two common perspectives: Some people say AUTOSAR limits creativity Working within standardized architectures, predefined interfaces, layered software, and strict processes can sometimes feel restrictive. There’s less room for “quick clever solutions,” and innovation may seem replaced by configuration, compliance, and documentation. From this perspective, creativity appears constrained. Others say AUTOSAR actually demands creativity I see strong arguments here too. AUTOSAR doesn’t remove creativity — it changes where creativity is applied. Creativity moves into: - Designing robust architectures within constraints - Optimizing timing, memory, and performance - Solving integration challenges across complex ECUs - Building reusable, scalable software designs - Finding elegant solutions while staying compliant with safety and process requirements Anyone can be creative without constraints. Real engineering creativity often appears because of constraints. Maybe AUTOSAR doesn’t kill creativity. Maybe it forces us to redefine it. What do you think — does AUTOSAR limit innovation, or does it channel it in a different way? #AUTOSAR #EmbeddedSoftware #AutomotiveSoftware #SoftwareArchitecture #FunctionalSafety #Engineering #Innovation #EmbeddedSystems

Standardisation of platform features: Commonly used vehicle functions were standardised and bundled into a \"platform\", naming it Basic software. The basic software was defined in a way to provide a hardware and system agnostic application software. The realisation of each function in the platform was defined. The application developer would configure the commonly used functions invoking a platform API. Instead of rewriting the platform software when hardware or network configuration changes, the application developer uses the same platform with a different configuration and probably swaps the API. This reduced the costs and encouraged reuse. This brought parallelism into the software development lifecycle, where application developers could start component development while feature development in platform continued in parallel. 3. Methodology : The methodology was standardised - the tooling aspects. AUTOSAR defined generic input configuration formats, moving away from the traditional formats like DBC, Flexray that were tied to communication systems . The methodology of defining system and exchange formats was standardised, making it easy for new and old players of automotive to collaborate and share. This eventually also led to incorporation of new communication protocol like TCP/IP and Ethernet into AUTOSAR as the architecture itself was generic and the methodology also enabled it. More about this in later posts. Conclusion: These 3 high level steps defined a pivot for the industry, it was slower change in a traditional industry but eventually the industry moved. Sure, AUTOSAR is complex for a new player to understand and there is the problem of over-engineering but the benefits outweigh the drawbacks. AUTOSAR introduced a way that allows hardware and software to evolve independently. It is the first and most critical step toward the Software-Defined Vehicle (SDV). can’t just wake up randomly and start working 😂 That’s when I discovered: ⚡ Runnable Entities ⚡ Events And suddenly AUTOSAR started feeling less like magic and more like a well-managed office system 😄 Here’s how I understood it 👇 Imagine an office building 🏢 The employees = SWCs The tasks employees perform = Runnables A Runnable is basically: “A small piece of executable logic.” Example: ✔ Read sensor value ✔ Calculate vehicle speed ✔ Turn ON warning lamp But here’s the interesting part 👇 Employees don’t work 24/7 nonstop. Someone tells them WHEN to work. That “someone” is Events ⚡ AUTOSAR Events trigger Runnable execution. Different events = different triggers. The main ones I learned today 👇 🔹 Timing Event ⏰ “Run every 10ms.” Example: Reading wheel speed periodically. Like an office alarm reminding employees every hour 😂 🔹 Data Received Event 📩 Runnable executes when new data arrives. Example: New sensor value received. Like: “Boss sent an email → now start working.” 🔹 Operation Invoked Event ☎️ Triggered when another SWC requests a service. Example: Diagnostic request arrives. Like getting a phone call: “Hey, can you do this task?” Today’s biggest “aha moment” 👇 SWCs themselves are mostly passive. Runnable + Events are what make the system alive. Without events… nothing actually happens. 😄 And honestly? AUTOSAR CAN Driver — More Than Just “Sending CAN Messages” While learning AUTOSAR COM Stack deeply, I realized something important: The CAN Driver is not just a low-level transmit/receive module. It is the real-time bridge between software and physical CAN hardware. Behind a simple API like: Can_Write() there is a complete chain of operations happening internally: ✔ L-PDU conversion into hardware-specific format ✔ Hardware mailbox allocation using HTH ✔ Interrupt/Polling-based transmission handling ✔ Tx confirmation callbacks to CanIf ✔ Controller state management ✔ Bus-Off and Wakeup handling ✔ Thread-safe reentrant behavior ✔ CAN FD frame handling and bitrate switching One concept I found especially interesting was: 🔥 Priority Inversion Even though CAN bus itself supports priority-based arbitration, improper driver implementation can still delay high-priority messages. ➡ Inner Priority Inversion A low-priority message occupying the same Tx buffer blocks a high-priority message. ➡ Outer Priority Inversion A lower-priority frame from another node wins arbitration because the higher-priority frame was not ready before Inter-Frame Space ended. This shows that: “Real-time performance depends not only on CAN protocol, but also on driver architecture.” Another interesting learning was CAN Driver State Management: Power ON ↓ CAN_UNINIT ↓ Can_Init() STOPPED ↓ Can_SetControllerMode(CAN_CS_STARTED) STARTED And during low power operation: STARTED → SLEEP → Wakeup → STOPPED/STARTED Wakeup can happen either through: ✔ Interrupts ✔ Polling using APIs like: Can_CheckWakeup() and EcuM_CheckWakeup(). Also explored how AUTOSAR handles: ✔ Reentrant APIs ✔ Atomic hardware access ✔ Mutex/critical section protection ✔ Polling main functions ✔ ISR-based notifications One more powerful enhancement in modern systems: 🔥 CAN FD CAN FD keeps arbitration at normal bitrate but switches to higher bitrate during payload transmission using the BRS bit. Result: ✔ Faster communication ✔ Up to 64-byte payload ✔ Better bandwidth efficiency The deeper I go into AUTOSAR CAN Driver internals, the more I understand that robust automotive communication is AUTOSAR vs Zephyr RTOS: not a replacement — a different operating model for automotive software After working across both AUTOSAR programs and more recently Zephyr-based automotive prototypes, I’ve come to a simple conclusion: these aren’t competing solutions for the same problem. They optimize for very different engineering models. Classic AUTOSAR optimizes integration at scale. It gives OEMs and Tier-1s a standardized framework for supplier interoperability, generated integration layers, and predictable software integration across large programs. Zephyr optimizes iteration speed. It gives smaller teams direct hardware access, modern open-source workflows, broad upstream driver support, and CI-native development. In practice: • Classic AUTOSAR → large domain ECUs in mature supplier ecosystems • Zephyr → edge controllers, zonal nodes, body electronics, prototyping, SDV transition systems • The future → coexistence, not replacement AUTOSAR is already evolving toward Classic + Adaptive. That actually creates space for lighter platforms like Zephyr in specific ECU classes. The real gap isn’t another RTOS. It’s the missing production tooling around diagnostics, validation, flashing, and lifecycle automation that makes open platforms viable in automotive programs. That’s where I see the biggest opportunity over the next few years. “AUTOSAR kills creativity.”
I’ve heard this statement many times in embedded software discussions.

But does it really?

I see two common perspectives:

Some people say AUTOSAR limits creativity
Working within standardized architectures, predefined interfaces, layered software, and strict processes can sometimes feel restrictive.
There’s less room for “quick clever solutions,” and innovation may seem replaced by configuration, compliance, and documentation.

From this perspective, creativity appears constrained.

Others say AUTOSAR actually demands creativity
I see strong arguments here too.

AUTOSAR doesn’t remove creativity — it changes where creativity is applied.

Creativity moves into:

- Designing robust architectures within constraints
- Optimizing timing, memory, and performance
- Solving integration challenges across complex ECUs
- Building reusable, scalable software designs
- Finding elegant solutions while staying compliant with safety and process requirements

Anyone can be creative without constraints.
Real engineering creativity often appears because of constraints.

Maybe AUTOSAR doesn’t kill creativity.
Maybe it forces us to redefine it.

What do you think — does AUTOSAR limit innovation, or does it channel it in a different way?

The cover represents water and proton transport in tiny metallic carbon nanotube pores. While traditional hydrodynamics assumes walls are just boundaries, but Aleksandr Noy and his team have uncovered a game-changing discovery: the electronic properties of carbon nanotube porins (CNTPs) significantly affect water permeability! They compared transport in metallic and semiconducting nanotubes of identical diameter and noticed a consistent enhancement in metallic nanotubes. 
This suggests that the electronic nature of the nanotubes, rather than just their size, determines permeability 😉

For the Eu3+→Eu2+ reduction, the H2 atmosphere proved to be the most effective, with a solution energy as low as 0.02 eV/defect, significantly lower than in O2 or N2 atmospheres. The Zn'Al antisite defect is identified as the most favorable native defect and is associated with modifications in the material's luminescent properties. In doped systems, Eu2+ preferentially substitutes Zn2+ sites, whereas Eu3+ favors Al3+ sites; however, the presence of interstitial Eu3+ is also expected due to the ionic radius mismatch. Crystal field modeling indicates that Eu3+ ions occupy sites with local C3 symmetry. Surface energy calculations show that the (001) and symmetrically equivalent surfaces govern the growth morphology, while the (002) surface is the most stable at equilibrium. Furthermore, Al–Al terminations dominate ZnAl2O4 surfaces, influencing defect migration and potentially affecting the material's optical properties. These findings provide atomistic insights into the structure–property relationships of ZnAl2O4:Eu, with implications for optoelectronic applications. 📄 Full article available at: 👉 Henrique Prado Silva, Joéslei Lopes de Oliveira Lucena, and Marcos Vinicius dos Santos Rezende 📍 Department of Physics, Federal University of Sergipe – Brazil Na3V2(PO4)2F3 has been attracting a lot of attention as a positive electrode material for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). The deformation of local structure caused by rare-earth ions and intrinsic defect properties in Na3V2(PO4)2F3 as a positive electrode for SIB have been investigated with atomistic simulation based on the lattice energy minimization. A good reproduction of the Na3V2(PO4)2F3 structure is obtained. It is revealed that Na Frenkel defect, which is formed by sodium interstitial and vacancy pair, is the most favorable type of intrinsic defect. This leads to the formation of stable sodium vacancy required for the Na-ion diffusion. The results indicate that trivalent rare-earth dopants at the V3+ site are the most energetically favorable dopants for Na3V2(PO4)2F3, and that the incorporation at the Na and P site could be used as a strategy to increase the sodium vacancy and interstitial, respectively. The deformation in the local structure by the rare-earth ions doping at the V site is also investigated as helpful in improving the rate performance of SIBs. 📄 Full article available at: 👉 Jackson 📍 Department of Physics, Federal University of Sergipe – Brazil Atomistic simulation is performed to study the defect properties and spectroscopy in the MgGa2O4 structure. The calculations indicate that the most favorable type of intrinsic defect is generated by the cation antisite defect, in which there is an exchange of positions between Mg2+ and Ga3+ ions. The calculation also indicates that the incorporation of Eu3+ dopant at the Ga3+(2) site is the most energetically favorable. According to a spectroscopic study using the crystal field approach, Eu3+ replaces the Ga3+ site occupying a combination of C4 and C4h symmetries while maintaining the same amount of the non-null crystal field parameters. This result is important for the reproduction of experimental energy sublevels and ΔE (7F1) manifold splitting. 📄 Full article available at: 👉 https://lnkd.in/d9R6rqth . 🌟 New cover for Nature Magazine (Materials)!
Carbon Nanoubes Revolutionize Hydrodynamic Concepts

The cover represents water and proton transport in tiny metallic carbon nanotube pores. While traditional hydrodynamics assumes walls are just boundaries, but Aleksandr Noy and his team have uncovered a game-changing discovery: the electronic properties of carbon nanotube porins (CNTPs) significantly affect water permeability! They compared transport in metallic and semiconducting nanotubes of identical diameter and noticed a consistent enhancement in metallic nanotubes.
This suggests that the electronic nature of the nanotubes, rather than just their size, determines permeability 😉

post_text: Many people think connecting a tool like Google Analytics to an AI agent (or LLM) is easy and they’re probably right. Connecting them is easy, but making them work reliably and not hallucinate is another story. Sometimes things work perfectly on the first try (usually the first simple test). Then I add a bit more complexity… and suddenly it doesn’t work as expected, for various reasons. It reminds me a bit of vibe building, where I build something and make it somewhat work, especially with platforms like Base44 that let me build things super quickly. (btw I really like base44 and the user experience there.) It’s really cool and creative, but once I have something that works, I realize that now I actually have to understand how it works and the logic behind my app.. It looks like it’s similar with MCPs, tools, and agents. I have been spending a lot of time connecting marketing tools like Google Search Console, DataForSEO, Google Sheets, and slack (a bit of a nightmare, or maybe i just dont understnad..). Sometimes the agent calls the right one immediately. Sometimes it takes a few tries. The smarter the model, the easier the iteration, but it’s not really reliable in my opinion. Every tool has its own parameters, use cases, and edge cases. You can’t just throw everything at the agent and expect it to magically figure things out. From what I see, there are simpler MCPs and more extensive MCPs. They can actually be very different. And having an OpenAPI spec doesn’t mean things will “just work.” Also, the hierarchy of tools being exposed to the agent should be designed carefully. You don’t want to give the agent too little info, but you also don’t want to overload it with everything from the start. It feels like there’s a “vibe MCPing” going around, just trust Chatty to figure it out. And it works… until it doesn’t. Have you already connected a tool to your LLM? Which one?

post_text: When a company like Google talks about procurement, it isn’t talking about “three quotes and a PO.” In his keynote at the 8th Annual CPO Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Ron Ng, APAC Head of Procurement for Google Asia Pacific, framed a very different expectation: procurement as a strategic partner that co-creates value with the business, accelerates time-to-market end-to-end, and manages risk as both an operational and reputational concern. For CPOs and procurement leaders across APAC, the message is clear. To be taken seriously by global digital players, and by their own boards, procurement must move beyond transactional excellence and become a business-first, data-driven, AI-ready function. This article unpacks what that actually means in practice, and how procurement teams can align. 1. Business-first partnerships, not procurement-first processes Global digital companies start from the business model and work backwards. Procurement is expected to understand how the organisation makes money, what drives growth and retention, and where risk really lives. In a traditional setup, the business unit writes a brief, procurement “runs the process,” and everyone is asked to squeeze their needs into a standard RFx template. Success is reported as percentage savings and policy compliance, even if the process slowed things down or missed opportunities to improve outcomes. The co-creation model flips this sequence. The starting point is the business engine, not the sourcing template. Take payroll as an example. For a company like Google, the priority is not simply the unit cost per payslip. Accuracy across markets, regulatory compliance, and employee experience are often far more important. In marketing, the real levers are speed to launch, creative quality, and the ability to reallocate budget quickly when a campaign under- or over-performs. Pure rate reduction means very little if it undermines those goals. A business-first procurement team sits down with stakeholders, finance, HR, marketing, IT, and defines success in those terms. Uptime, SLA adherence, data security, employee NPS, campaign ROI, ESG outcomes: these become part of the brief. Strategic suppliers are then engaged as potential co-creators who can bring new ideas, automation and data capabilities, not just a sharper quote. Only after this alignment does the RFx and contract framework take shape. Instead of generic templates, requirements and scoring criteria are anchored to the business levers that actually matter. This is exactly the spirit of the CPO Summit agenda when it emphasised stronger business partnerships and a reinvention of procurement’s value proposition. For suppliers, the implication is clear. When dealing with a “Google-style” buyer, they are judged not just on price, but on their ability to plug into the client’s business model and help deliver outcomes. 2. Time-to-market: procurement as a speed enabler In digital businesses, speed is not a nice add-on; it is a competitive weapon. New products, market entries and campaign pivots are often measured in weeks or days, not quarters. That reality puts procurement under a different kind of pressure: can you support this rhythm without sacrificing governance? The critical questions become: how quickly can you move from idea to shortlist to contract? How fast can you onboard a new supplier for a pilot without tying the business in knots? Once a pilot works in one market, can you scale it across the region without starting from zero each time? The FMM Supply Chain Webinar that SupplyCart supported broke this down into three practical capabilities: robust supplier management, digital sourcing, and disciplined contracts and performance. Digital sourcing is often where the speed uplift comes from. Instead of scattered emails and inconsistent templates, structured e-RFx flows channel everything through a single process. Vendor submissions are secure, time-stamped and directly comparable. Automated scoring and dashboards help teams evaluate, shortlist and iterate far faster than manual spreadsheets ever could. In some transformations, end-to-end procurement cycle times have been reduced by as much as 70%, while actually improving transparency and trust. Vendors value seeing uniform rules, clear deadlines and consistent communication. For a buyer like Google, that is simply the baseline: procurement should shorten the distance between business intent and supplier execution, not lengthen it. Platforms such as ADAM-Procure are designed with this reality in mind, digitising the journey from vendor registration through RFx to PR→PO with governance built into the flow rather than bolted on afterwards. 3. Risk is both operational and reputational Tech companies operate under intense public and regulatory scrutiny. When a supplier fails, the consequences are rarely contained to a single delayed delivery. Data breaches, labour issues, environmental violations or outages can quickly escalate into front-page stories and regulator attention. This dual character of risk, operational and reputational, is increasingly visible in how procurement is regulated and benchmarked in markets like Malaysia. Policy directions such as the Malaysia Procurement Bill 2025 emphasise open competition, digital transparency and vendor accountability. They call for structured review panels, appeals mechanisms and standardised practices across the public sector. Conversations at CPO2025 echoed the same theme: procurement is expected to deliver on ESG, resilience and compliance as part of its core remit. From the perspective of a global tech buyer, a strategic procurement partner in APAC must therefore demonstrate three things. First, they need a deep understanding of their vendor network. It should be clear which suppliers are genuinely critical, where the single points of failure are, which vendors have weaker ESG or financial profiles, and where concentration risk is emerging. Second, they must monitor performance and risk using real data, not just initial paperwork. On-time delivery, quality incidents, response times, cyber posture, audit findings and sustainability credentials all feed into the risk picture. A vendor that was low-risk at contract signature may look very different two years later if performance is deteriorating or their risk profile has changed. Third, they must be able to prove that sourcing and contracting decisions are defensible. When regulators, auditors or internal stakeholders ask “why this supplier?”, it is no longer sufficient to point to a folder of emails. Decisions need to be backed by structured scoring, documented trade-offs, and complete audit trails. Digital platforms like ADAM-Procure are built with this in mind. They don’t only record which supplier was selected; they show how and why: the criteria used, the weightings, the individual evaluations, the approval path, and the history of performance since. For global tech buyers, that level of traceability is part of how they manage reputational risk in complex markets, not a nice-to-have feature. 4. Data and auditability: the foundations for AI-ready sourcing Organisations such as Google are already experimenting with AI across back-office and procurement workflows. But the more advanced the conversation, the more one principle comes up: AI is only as good as the data and governance it sits on. In practice, that means a strategic procurement partner is expected to have clean, structured vendor data rather than unsearchable free text; centralised digital RFx records with machine-readable scoring and outcomes; and clear links between events, contracts and performance data. With these foundations in place, agentic AI can start to do useful, safe work. For example, AI can draft RFx documents aligned to standard criteria and past best practice instead of starting from a blank page. It can suggest suppliers based on patterns in performance, risk and ESG history rather than simple category tags. It can flag anomalies in bids, unusual pricing patterns or deviations in contract performance that warrant human attention. It can generate first-pass evaluations and summaries that save time for evaluators, while leaving final judgement in human hands. Without structured data and auditability, AI pilots become risky and hard to trust, especially in organisations that are already under scrutiny. The risk of amplifying bias or making opaque decisions is simply too high. Here, solutions like ADAM-Procure act as AI enablers. By enforcing structure in vendor records, RFx events and approval flows, they create the digital evidence base that allows agentic AI to operate within clear guardrails instead of improvising around gaps. 5. What a “strategic procurement partner” looks like to Google-style buyers When you pull these threads together, a clear profile emerges. To a global tech company, a strategic procurement partner in APAC is one that starts with business outcomes and co-designs requirements, criteria and KPIs with stakeholders. It frames sourcing decisions in terms of revenue impact, resilience and experience, not just unit cost. It treats key suppliers as innovation partners and is willing to share enough transparency for genuine collaboration on ESG, risk and performance. It also operates at digital speed without losing control. Processes are standardised and supported by platforms; RFx and contracting timelines are compressed; pilots and roll-outs can be executed quickly across markets because the underlying templates and workflows are reusable. On the risk side, it can demonstrate strong due diligence, ongoing monitoring and early-warning mechanisms for both operational and reputational issues. When challenged, it can show that evaluations were fair and transparent. Finally, it is data-rich and AI-ready. Records are structured enough to feed advanced analytics and AI agents, and there is a clear understanding that AI augments human judgement rather than bypassing governance. Organisations that reach this level don’t just negotiate sharper deals. They become trusted counterparts that global digital players want to work with when they plan to grow in APAC. Where to start: align RFx and supplier strategy For many teams, the biggest gap between aspiration and reality sits in the RFx and supplier co-creation layer. Criteria live in offline templates, scoring is inconsistent or hard to reconstruct, and neither stakeholders nor suppliers have a clear view of how decisions were reached. Addressing this layer is often the fastest way to prove a more business-first mindset to internal stakeholders and demonstrate maturity to global partners. It also creates the structured data foundation needed for any serious AI initiative later on. This is where platforms like SupplyCart’s ADAM-Procure are focused: enabling business-first RFx design and scoring, supporting collaborative supplier engagement, and embedding the controls and audit trails that global tech buyers expect, while integrating all of that into vendor management and P2P processes. The expectations set out on stage in Kuala Lumpur are high, but they are not theoretical. They describe how leading organisations already work with their procurement partners today. The opportunity for APAC teams is to close that gap deliberately, one well-designed process and one well-governed RFx at a time. A focused demonstration can show: How criteria and scoring can be aligned to real business outcomes. How vendor masking, approval chains, and audit trails protect both you and your suppliers. post_text: People often ask why Node.js is common in smaller services while .NET dominates large systems. The reason is mostly architectural. Node.js runs on a single-threaded, event-driven model. That makes it extremely good at handling lots of I/O requests at the same time, things like real-time updates, APIs, chats, and dashboards. It’s lightweight, quick to build, and easy to scale horizontally, which is why startups and fast-moving teams love it. But once business logic becomes heavy or CPU-intensive, managing performance and long-term maintainability gets harder. .NET, on the other hand, is designed with scale and structure in mind. It supports true multi-threading, handles CPU-heavy workloads more efficiently, and enforces strong typing. That matters a lot when you’re dealing with large microservice ecosystems, complex business rules, strict security requirements, and systems that are expected to run and evolve for years. This is exactly why banks, insurance platforms, ERPs, and government systems rely on it. Summary: Node.js shines when speed and flexibility are the priority. .NET shines when reliability, complexity, and long-term scale matter. Network failures, timeouts, and duplicate webhook events are normal operational realities. Critical operations such as payments, order creation, and state transitions must be idempotent by design. A resilient system assumes duplication and handles it safely. 𝟮. 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 Frameworks evolve. Database mistakes persist. Schema design, indexing strategy, normalization vs denormalization decisions, and query planning directly impact scalability and performance. A well-designed database reduces future technical debt more than any framework migration ever will. 𝟯. 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝗡𝗲𝗴𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 Production systems require traceability. At minimum: • Structured logging • Correlation/request IDs • Clear error categorization • Centralized monitoring If an issue cannot be diagnosed quickly, operational maturity is lacking. Backend engineering is fundamentally about building predictable, maintainable, and scalable systems not just functional APIs. People often ask why Node.js is common in smaller services while .NET dominates large systems. The reason is mostly architectural.

Node.js runs on a single-threaded, event-driven model. That makes it extremely good at handling lots of I/O requests at the same time, things like real-time updates, APIs, chats, and dashboards. It’s lightweight, quick to build, and easy to scale horizontally, which is why startups and fast-moving teams love it. But once business logic becomes heavy or CPU-intensive, managing performance and long-term maintainability gets harder.

.NET, on the other hand, is designed with scale and structure in mind. It supports true multi-threading, handles CPU-heavy workloads more efficiently, and enforces strong typing. That matters a lot when you’re dealing with large microservice ecosystems, complex business rules, strict security requirements, and systems that are expected to run and evolve for years. This is exactly why banks, insurance platforms, ERPs, and government systems rely on it.

Summary:
Node.js shines when speed and flexibility are the priority.
.NET shines when reliability, complexity, and long-term scale matter.

Different tools — different problems.

post_text: 'I never knew you had that on.' If you've heard this from a customer, you have a £3 problem. I speak to hundreds of businesses a month. They all say the same thing. "Not enough leads." "Want more customers." "People say they never knew we had that on." If you serve a local area, there's one thing that fixes this. Costs £3 a day. Here's the setup: → One campaign on Meta → £3/day budget → Demographics only (age, gender) → Drop a pin. 1 mile radius of your location. → Add your best organic content — anything that performed above average → When frequency hits 5 for the week, switch the creative That's it. Now everyone within a mile knows exactly what you've got on. Every week. Over and over. So when it's a cold, wet Tuesday night and someone's thinking "where should we go?" They go to you. Not because you're the best. Because you're the one they remembered.

'I never knew you had that on.' If you've heard this from a customer, you have a £3 problem.

I speak to hundreds of businesses a month.

They all say the same thing.

"Not enough leads." "Want more customers." "People say they never knew we had that on."

If you serve a local area, there's one thing that fixes this.

Costs £3 a day. Here's the setup:

→ One campaign on Meta
→ £3/day budget
→ Demographics only (age, gender)
→ Drop a pin. 1 mile radius of your location.
→ Add your best organic content — anything that performed above average
→ When frequency hits 5 for the week, switch the creative

That's it.

Now everyone within a mile knows exactly what you've got on.

Every week. Over and over.

So when it's a cold, wet Tuesday night and someone's thinking "where should we go?"

They go to you.

Not because you're the best.

Because you're the one they remembered.

post_text: From the age of 6, I was always an athletic and active child despite being chubby. I played netball, short distance running and even took a stab at basketball which today, is my first love and is honestly, all I would like to do. You know how people like asking “what’s the one thing you could do forever if money wasn’t a problem?” My answer would be, “to play basketball.” Sports has become more than a passion, but rather a way of life. It is where I have faced my greatest challenges, learnt about resilience, discipline and teamwork. It has not only shaped who I am, but how I approach life and has opened doors for me in spaces I never imagined myself in. The world of sports introduced me to some of the most amazing people and organisations including the Ekhuruleni Basketball Association where my journey with basketball was harnessed. It is no surprise that my passion has grown beyond the courts; from playing for Gauteng, travelling to the shores of Italy to compete, receiving a sports bursary to play for and study at University of the Witwatersrand amongst many life changing opportunities, to now pursing my masters in Sports Administration at the Russian International Olympic University . For my Master’s thesis at RIOU, I explored The Media Framing of Intersex Athletes in Track and Field: Cases from Southern Africa. The inspiration for my topic stemmed from the widely publicized case of our global sports icon, Caster Semenya , whose story has become a focal point in the global debate on gender, race, and inclusion in elite sport. With my research, I wanted to investigate how different media platforms portray women with DSD (Differences of Sexual Development) in track and field, the influence on public perception and the effect on the athletes themselves. I noticed how intersex athletes from Southern Africa have been represented in mainstream sports media, often through biased, invasive, or dehumanizing narratives. I examined the impact this framing has not only on public opinion but also on policy, eligibility rules, and athlete well-being. It intrigued my mind to learn that the World Athletics regulations on DSD athletes mainly affected athletes from Africa and parts of Asia. Further into my research, I gained a deeper understanding on the DSD conditions as well as the debates raised by different institutions in their arguments at the World Athletics, The Court of Arbitration for Sports and the recent European Human Rights Court ruling. With this, I also wanted to contribute to academic research in the field of media studies in sports, to show that certain narratives portrayed by the media can heavily influence the view of the public, especially in our current generation where the media is the primary source of information. Media has the potential to educate but can also harm and cost people their livelihoods. This leaves the media with a huge responsibility as agents that are part of building the society we live in and experience. This thesis process sharpened my analytical thinking, research design capabilities, and policy evaluation skills, tools I will carry into the professional world. More importantly, I have learnt that sport is not just about performance, it is also about identity, justice, and the right to belong. Caster Semenya’s recent victory at the European Court of Human Rights where it was concluded that Semenya was not afforded a thorough review in her appeal to the CAS, that her rights to a fair hearing were indeed violated. This case served as a powerful reminder that the struggle for dignity and equality is ongoing, and worth pursuing- for the current generation but also, for generations to come. What did my research journey teach me? Let your topic choose you – Research can be daunting and working on something that moves you emotionally, makes the long nights endurable and worth it. Challenge dominant narratives – Especially in media studies, ask: Who is being left out of the story? Who is most and least affected by the decisions made? People get annoyed by the question “why” 😂 but trust me, your courage to ask questions is what will change the reality for many to come. Don’t fear complexity – Issues like gender and identity in sport are and have always been messy. Sit with the discomfort- that is where the learning happens. One doesn’t have to look too far for an example: Banyana Banyana, despite the incredible Desiree Ellis leading them to their first-ever WAFCON title (2022) and recent round of 16 performance, continue to struggle for sponsorship and media coverage. Meanwhile, their male counterparts, Bafana Bafana, receive significantly more support and publicity. This despite not matching the same level of international success. It’s uncomfortable to have these discussions but how else will we change our society? Tell stories with care – Especially when researching marginalized groups. These are not “case studies” but they are people. They are you and me, and many others around us whose voices have been silenced and ignored. Be gentle and sensitive with people’s realities. This thesis would not have been possible without the support of two professors who guided me throughout this journey. To Professor Cora Burnett , thank you for your valuable insights and continuous support, which deepened my understanding of gender in sport. To Professor Rosa López Espinoza Rosa Lopez de D’Amico, your advice and guidance helped me structure my ideas and stay focused. You have truly been a great inspiration in my research. Thank you to the Russian International Olympic University for providing a platform and an enriching program that has contributed meaningfully to my personal and professional growth in sport. To my family, though physically absent during my time in Sochi, your unwavering support, prayers, confident and pride in me, carried me throughout this chapter of my life. I dedicate this achievement to my parents, Emmanuel and Mapule Selwadi, my sister Katleho Selwadi who later joined me for my graduation ♥️, and my younger siblings Tshiamo and Oratile, whose love and belief in me have been my pillars. I am deeply grateful. To anyone standing at the edge of something unfamiliar: take the leap. The unknown might just be the best teacher you will ever have. How did Michigan get its speed limits? For over 20 years, federal policy restricted how high states could set speed limits. It started in 1974 when Nixon implemented a 55 mph national maximum speed limit. One might think this was a safety measure, but it was actually to preserve fuel during the oil embargo. 

After the maximum speed limit was raised to 65 in 1987, Michigan politicians debated raising speed limits on select rural freeways. Then-Gov. Blanchard originally refused to support the increase unless legislation included banning "fuzz busters," or radar detectors. Blanchard eventually had a change of heart and accepted other forms of stricter traffic enforcement.

Once Clinton repealed the national maximum speed limit in 1995, states were free to determine their own speed limits. Limits on freeways across the state gradually rose to 70-75 mph in the following years. Has this made freeways safer? Some may believe so. However, research links speed limit increases with increased traffic fatalities.

This article was interesting and fun to write about! I hope you all enjoy. https://lnkd.in/eFtSYcHZ
